Is physical abuse an acceptable reason for divorce?

Physical abuse is a grave sin, and the Bible never treats violence lightly, but Scripture does not give a simple verse that says, “abuse automatically equals divorce.” In the case of severe, ongoing, unrepentant abuse, many faithful Christians would say separation is not only wise but necessary for protection, and some also conclude that such hard-hearted, covenant-breaking conduct can fall under the biblical grounds of desertion or marital unfaithfulness principles, though believers differ on whether that always permits divorce and remarriage.

The clearest biblical starting points are God’s hatred of oppression and His protection of the vulnerable, along with the seriousness of the marriage covenant, for example Malachi 2:16; Ephesians 5:25-29; 1 Corinthians 7:10-15. A husband is never allowed to use force or domination against his wife, because Christ loves and nourishes His church, not brutalizes her.

If you are in danger, leave and get to a safe place now, and contact emergency services and trusted believers in your church immediately. Scripture supports seeking wise protection, and you should also speak with your pastor or elders as soon as possible for help, accountability, and a safety plan.

Why is “You shall not steal” in the Ten Commandments?

“You shall not steal” is in the Ten Commandments because God is holy, and He created human life to be marked by justice, trust, and love of neighbor, not by taking what belongs to others. It protects **private property**, the dignity of the person, and the covenant community from greed and exploitation, since theft is not merely a social offense but sin against God and one’s neighbor (Exodus 20:15; Leviticus 19:11; Ephesians 4:28).

The command also reveals our hearts. God forbids stealing because He opposes covetousness, deceit, and the selfish desire to gain apart from honest labor. In Christ, believers are not only called to stop stealing, but to work honestly so they can share with those in need, which is a beautiful picture of sanctified love (Ephesians 4:28).

A good next step is to ask God to search you for any dishonest gain, and to make your life marked by integrity, contentment, and generosity.
What does it mean that “His mercy endures forever” (Jeremiah 33:11 and Psalm 136)?

“His mercy endures forever” means God’s steadfast covenant love does not run out, fail, or get exhausted, because it rests on His faithful character, not on our deserving it. In Psalm 136 the repeated phrase celebrates that the LORD’s loyal love keeps showing up in creation, redemption, and preservation, and in Jeremiah 33:11 it points to God’s promise to restore His people after judgment, proving that His mercy is stronger than Israel’s sin and exile.

The Hebrew idea behind “mercy” here is often better understood as steadfast love, lovingkindness, or covenant faithfulness. It is not mere sentiment, but God’s committed love acting to save, forgive, and keep His people. That is why the refrain can be sung again and again, because every act of God’s goodness is another proof that He does not abandon those who belong to Him. Lamentations 3:22-23 says, “Because of the LORD’s loving devotion we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning.”

For us, this is a deep comfort. If you are in Christ, God’s mercy is not fragile or temporary, but secured by Jesus, who bore our sins on the cross and rose again for our justification. So the proper response is gratitude, repentance, and trust, not despair. Is the Church of God in Christ (COGIC) a good biblical church?

The Church of God in Christ is broadly a Christian, Bible-affirming denomination, but whether a specific local COGIC church is “good biblical” depends on whether it faithfully preaches the gospel, teaches the authority of Scripture, and lives in obedience to Christ. By its official doctrine, COGIC affirms the Trinity, the deity of Christ, salvation by grace through faith, and the necessity of holiness, which are all important orthodox Christian convictions.

That said, you should still test any church by Scripture, because not every church that uses Christian language is healthy or faithful. Look for clear preaching of Christ crucified and risen, repentance and faith, reverent worship, biblical church discipline, and leaders who submit to the Bible, not personality or tradition. What is the voice of one calling in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3; John 1:23)?

“The voice of one calling in the wilderness” is John the Baptist, whose ministry was to prepare the way for the Lord by calling people to repentance and pointing them to Jesus Christ (Isaiah 40:3; John 1:23). In Isaiah, the “wilderness” image speaks of making a highway for God’s coming, and John applies that prophecy to his own role as the forerunner of the Messiah.

This is more than a poetic title, it is a prophetic announcement that God Himself was coming to His people in the person of Christ. John’s message still matters: repent, for the King is near, and turn to Jesus, who died and rose again to save sinners (Mark 1:4; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

What is neonomianism?

Neonomianism is the teaching that the gospel is, in effect, a new, milder law, so that sinners are accepted by God partly on the basis of their faith and obedience rather than by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. In historic Christian terms, it is a serious distortion of justification, because it turns the gospel into a lower law instead of good news for guilty sinners.

Biblically, Scripture says we are “justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” and “a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:24, 28). The law shows our sin, but Christ alone fulfills what we cannot and saves by His finished work, not by a softened covenant of works.

A related warning is in Galatians, where Paul rejects any message that adds human merit to Christ. “If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). That is why neonomianism must be rejected, even if it sounds morally serious or “balanced.”

What does it mean that neither height nor depth separates us from the love of God (Romans 8:39)?

Romans 8:39 means that no created power, no circumstance, and no spiritual force can tear believers away from God’s saving love in Christ Jesus. Paul’s point is that the love of God is secure because it rests on God’s sovereign grace, not on our strength, feelings, or changing circumstances, and it is part of the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints, rooted in Christ’s finished work and resurrection.

In context, Paul has just said that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, including “neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities” and then “neither height nor depth” (Romans 8:38-39). “Height” and “depth” were ways of speaking about the highest and lowest extremes, or even cosmic powers and the furthest reach imaginable, so Paul is piling up every possible boundary and saying none of them can overcome God’s love for His people.

This is wonderfully comforting for the believer who feels weak, afraid, or unsteady. Your grip on Christ may feel shaky, but His grip on you is stronger than every trial, every accusation, and every dark valley (John 10:28-29; Romans 8:1). That does not mean Christians never suffer, but it does mean suffering cannot cancel God’s covenant love.

If you are in Christ, rest in this promise today, and if you are not yet trusting Christ, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died for sinners and rose again for our justification (Romans 5:8; Romans 4:25).
What is the doctrine of preterition?

Preterition is the doctrine that God, in His sovereign election, passes over some sinners and leaves them in their sin, while graciously choosing others to salvation in Christ. In other words, election is God’s merciful saving choice, and preterition is His righteous decision not to grant saving grace to all, without making Him the author of sin.

Scripture speaks of God’s mercy and justice together: “So then, He has mercy on whom He desires to have mercy, and He hardens whom He desires to harden” (Romans 9:18); “What if God, desiring to show His wrath and to make His power known, endured with much patience the objects of His wrath prepared for destruction?” (Romans 9:22). This is a solemn doctrine, meant to humble us before God’s holiness and magnify grace in Christ.

A careful Christian should hold it with reverence, not speculation. The practical response is to run to Christ, trust Him fully, and proclaim the gospel to all people, because “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13).
Are there supposed to be any rituals in Christianity?

Yes, Christianity has ordinances or appointed practices, but not magical rituals that earn favor with God. The New Testament gives us baptism and the Lord’s Supper as Christ-instituted signs for the church, and we also see regular practices like prayer, Scripture reading, fasting, and gathered worship (Matthew 28:19; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26; Acts 2:42).

The key difference is this: Christians do not treat these as empty ceremonies or meritorious works. They are means of grace, acts of obedience, and expressions of faith in Christ, who alone saves by grace through faith, not by ritual performance (Ephesians 2:8-9; Titus 3:5).

What is the Presbyterian Church in America (PCA), and what do they believe?

The Presbyterian Church in America (PCA) is a conservative Reformed Protestant denomination that holds to Presbyterian church government, confessional Christianity, and the authority of Scripture. It was founded in 1973 and is broadly known for teaching salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, the sovereignty of God, covenant theology, and elder-led churches.

In brief, the PCA believes the Bible is the inspired, authoritative Word of God, God is Triune, Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, Christ died as a substitutionary sacrifice for sinners and rose bodily from the dead, and sinners are justified by faith apart from works, with the Holy Spirit sanctifying believers over time. Its official doctrinal standard is the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Westminster Larger and Shorter Catechisms, so it is strongly Calvinistic, paedobaptist, and Presbyterian in polity.

Practically, PCA churches usually practice infant baptism, celebrate the Lord’s Supper as a means of grace, and are governed by sessions, presbyteries, and a general assembly. On some secondary matters, there can be variation within the denomination, but those core Reformed convictions are what define it.

Where is God now? Where is God when it hurts?

God is not far away, and He has not abandoned you. The Bible says He is “near to the brokenhearted” and saves those who are crushed in spirit, and that He is the God who sees and hears the afflicted, even when pain makes Him feel hidden (Psalm 34:18; Exodus 3:7).

For those who trust in Christ, God is present by His Spirit, even in suffering, because Jesus Himself was pierced, rejected, and acquainted with grief, and He now reigns at the Father’s right hand as our sympathetic High Priest (John 14:16-18; Hebrews 4:14-16). That means your hurt is not proof that God is absent, but a place where He is able to sustain, uphold, and refine His people through trials that are real and grievous, yet not meaningless (Romans 8:28; 2 Corinthians 4:16-18).

What is the just war theory?

Just war theory is a Christian moral framework for judging when going to war may be morally permissible and how war must be conducted if it is undertaken. It is not a command to wage war, but a set of moral restraints meant to limit violence under God’s authority over life and justice.

Biblically, rulers may bear the sword as God’s servant to punish evil and protect the innocent, yet war is never treated lightly. Romans 13:1-4 shows civil authority as God’s servant for justice, while Proverbs 24:11-12 warns against passivity toward unjust bloodshed. Christians have often summarized the theory with ideas like just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, proportionality, and discrimination between combatants and noncombatants.

It is a secondary issue where faithful Christians disagree on details. Some emphasize that fallen governments can sometimes use force to restrain grave evil, while others stress a stricter pacifist reading of Jesus’ commands to love enemies. My view is that just war theory can reflect biblical principles when it is tightly constrained by justice, humility, and the protection of the innocent, but it must never become a permission slip for aggression or revenge.

What does it mean that women should have a gentle and quiet spirit (1 Peter 3:4)?

In 1 Peter 3:4, a “gentle and quiet spirit” means a humble, peaceable, inward beauty that trusts God rather than trying to control others through strife, and Peter says this is “of great worth in God’s sight” (1 Peter 3:4). It is not a call for women to be mute, fearful, or without influence, but for the heart to be marked by meekness, self-control, and reverence for the Lord.

In context, Peter is speaking to Christian wives, especially in situations where a husband may not obey the word, and he points them to conduct that adorns the gospel more than outward appearance does (1 Peter 3:1-6). The same Bible that calls women to this beauty also shows godly women speaking boldly, serving faithfully, and exercising wisdom, so this is about the posture of the heart, not erasing voice or dignity.

A helpful biblical word here is meekness, which is strength under God’s control, not weakness. Proverbs 31 and 1 Samuel 25 show that godly women can be both strong and gentle at the same time.

What does it mean to be free from sin?

To be free from sin means that, in Christ, you are no longer under sin’s ruling power, guilt, and final condemnation, even though you still fight against sin’s presence in this life. The Bible teaches that believers have been set free from sin to become slaves of righteousness, and that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, see Romans 6:6-7, Romans 6:14, Romans 8:1.

This freedom is not sinless perfection yet. It is real liberation: the dominion of sin is broken, your old master has been dethroned, and the Holy Spirit now enables a new life of repentance, obedience, and holiness, see John 8:34-36; Galatians 5:16-17. Is God man-made? Did man create the idea of God?

No, the Bible teaches that God is not man-made. Rather, God is the eternal Creator who made man in His image, and human beings are accountable to Him, not the other way around (Genesis 1:1; Genesis 1:26-27; Romans 1:20-25).

What is the significance of the statement “God is within her; she will not fall” in Psalm 46:5?

In Psalm 46:5, “God is within her; she will not fall” means that God’s presence is the security of His people, so the city He dwells with cannot be finally overthrown. In context, “her” points to Zion, Jerusalem, the place of God’s covenant presence, and the verse declares His protecting nearness, not a promise that believers will never suffer trouble, but that they will not be ultimately shaken because “God is within her” and “God will help her at break of day” (Psalm 46:5).

The Psalm goes on to say, “Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts,” yet “The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (Psalm 46:6-7). The main point is God’s sovereign presence, His faithfulness to His covenant people, and the stability He gives in the midst of chaos.

For Christians, this beautifully points us to the greater reality fulfilled in Christ, God dwelling among His people and never forsaking them. If you want, I can also explain how this verse is applied to the church today.
What does the Bible say about worship?

The Bible says worship is the fitting response of God’s people to who He is, what He has done, and what He is worth. It is not just singing, but the whole-hearted honoring of God with reverence, obedience, gratitude, and joyful praise, offered through Jesus Christ, who is the only mediator between God and man, and by the Holy Spirit. Worship centers on God’s glory, not our preferences, and it must be done “in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23-24; 1 Timothy 2:5).

Scripture shows that worship includes praise, prayer, reading and hearing God’s Word, confession, thanksgiving, giving, fellowship, the Lord’s Supper, and a life of obedience. The true worshiper offers his whole life to God as a “living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1-2; Colossians 3:16-17; Hebrews 12:28-29).

A few clear biblical truths stand out:
- God alone is worthy of worship, because He is Creator and Lord (Revelation 4:11).
- Worship must not be idolatrous, because no created thing may replace God (Exodus 20:3-5).
- External actions without a sincere heart are empty, because God desires truth in the inward being (Isaiah 29:13; Psalm 51:16-17).
- In the church, believers gather to edify one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, while keeping Christ central (Ephesians 5:18-20; Hebrews 10:24-25).

The practical call is simple: come before God with humility, repent of any divided heart, and seek to worship Him in a way shaped by Scripture rather than by mere taste or tradition.

If you want, I can also give you a short biblical overview of worship in the Old Testament, the New Testament, or in gathered church worship.
What is more important, the death of Christ or His resurrection?

Both are essential, but if you are asking which is more directly tied to our forgiveness, Christ’s death is the sacrifice for our sins, while His resurrection is God’s vindication of that sacrifice and the proof of His victory over death. The Bible joins them tightly: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

His death answers the problem of guilt before a holy God, because Jesus bore sin in our place, which is the heart of substitutionary atonement, “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). His resurrection declares that the payment was accepted and that He is Lord, “He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

So, the death of Christ is the atoning basis of salvation, and the resurrection is the triumphant confirmation and completion of that saving work. You should not separate what God has joined together. If you want, I can also explain how the New Testament presents the cross and resurrection as one unified gospel message.
What is the emerging / emergent church movement?

The emerging or emergent church movement is a broad, loosely connected stream of Christians who sought to rethink church practice and language for a postmodern culture, often emphasizing conversation, community, authenticity, and mission over traditional forms and structures.

A charitable summary of the main appeal is that many participants wanted to reach people who were alienated by shallow Christianity, and they rightly wanted the church to be more honest, relational, and culturally understandable.

My concern is that the movement often became unclear about doctrine and biblical authority, and in some expressions it treated truth as overly flexible, which can drift from the apostolic faith once delivered to the saints, where Scripture is the final authority and Christ is proclaimed plainly, not merely reimagined for each culture, 2 Timothy 3:16-17; Jude 3.

In other words, the best parts of the movement are not new, since every generation should call people to authentic discipleship, but the danger is when “conversation” replaces conviction and the Gospel is softened. A faithful church must be both compassionate and clear: sinners need not only community but repentance, faith in Christ, His death for our sins, and His bodily resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

If you want, I can also give you a brief history of the movement or compare it with evangelical Christianity.
What does the Bible say about underage drinking?

The Bible does not give a direct law about “underage drinking” as a modern legal category, but it clearly forbids drunkenness and commands wisdom, self-control, and respect for governing authorities. Scripture says, “Do not get drunk on wine” (Ephesians 5:18), and “It is not for kings, O Lemuel, not for kings to drink wine” when it leads to blurred judgment (Proverbs 31:4-5).

In principle, that means a young person should not use alcohol in a way that violates conscience, parents’ authority, civil law, or self-control. Romans 13:1-2 teaches believers to submit to governing authorities, so if the law forbids it, Christians should obey. More importantly, 1 Corinthians 6:12 reminds us that not everything permitted is beneficial, and 1 Peter 5:8 calls us to be sober-minded and watchful.

If you’re asking because this is a real situation for you, the wise next step is to ask, “Will this honor Christ, keep my conscience clear, and help me walk in holiness?” If you want, I can also help you think through what the Bible says about drinking alcohol more generally, not just underage drinking.
Will there be a great apostasy / falling away during the end times?

Yes, Scripture teaches that there will be a significant falling away before Christ’s return, though faithful Christians differ on how some end-time details unfold. Jesus warned that “many will fall away” and that “the love of many will grow cold” because of increased lawlessness, and Paul spoke of “the apostasy” and the revealing of “the man of lawlessness” in 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4; Matthew 24:10-12.

One main historic Christian view is that this refers to a climactic end-times rebellion, while another sees these warnings as describing the whole church age with a final intensified expression near the end. I lean toward a final, intensified apostasy before Christ’s return, because the language in 2 Thessalonians 2 and Matthew 24 seems to point to a concentrated crisis, but Scripture is clear that the exact timetable is hidden from us.

The comfort for believers is this, true sheep will be kept by Christ, even in dark days, because “no one will snatch them out of My hand” and God will preserve His people to the end, John 10:28-29; Philippians 1:6. So the call is not to panic, but to remain steadfast, rooted in the Word, and vigilant in prayer, Hebrews 10:23-25.

If you want, I can also explain whether “the apostasy” in 2 Thessalonians 2 refers to the church, the world, or both.
Should all pronouns referring to God be capitalized?

No, not all Christians treat that as a binding rule. Capitalizing pronouns for God is a reverent English convention, not a biblical command, and faithful Christians differ on whether to use it consistently or at all.

The main argument for capitalization is that it can show honor and distinguish God from human beings, which fits reverence like that in Psalm 95:6 and Isaiah 6:3. The main argument against making it mandatory is that Scripture itself was written in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek without English capitalization, so this is a matter of style, not doctrine.

My view is that it is a good and reverent practice when your audience expects it, but it should never be treated as spiritually required or as the measure of orthodoxy. If you want, I can also tell you how different Bible publishers and churches usually handle it.
What is Kabbalah?

Kabbalah is a mystical Jewish tradition that seeks hidden meanings about God, creation, and the spiritual world through symbolic interpretation of Scripture and other writings. In its classical forms, it is not part of biblical Christianity, because it goes beyond the plain teaching of Scripture, which calls us to trust what God has revealed, not to seek secret knowledge (Deuteronomy 29:29; Colossians 2:8).

Christians should remember that God has spoken clearly in His Word, and His saving truth is centered in Jesus Christ, in whom are “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). If you are asking because you are exploring spirituality or truth, the better question is not, “What hidden code can I uncover?” but, “Has God revealed Himself in Christ?” The Bible says He has, and salvation is found by repenting and trusting in Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose bodily from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).
Should a Christian be a prepper or in any way involved with doomsday prepping?

A Christian may prepare wisely for ordinary hardships, but should not live in fear or adopt a doom-driven mindset. Scripture commends prudence, not panic, as in Proverbs 21:20 and Proverbs 27:12, while also warning us not to be anxious about tomorrow, Matthew 6:34.

So the question is not, “Can I make reasonable preparations?” but, “Am I trusting God or trying to secure my own safety apart from Him?” A believer can keep some supplies, save wisely, and plan for disasters as an act of stewardship, but doomsday prepping can easily become fear, control, or practical unbelief if it is driven by anxiety rather than wisdom.

The Christian posture is watchfulness with peace, not obsession with catastrophe. Jesus calls us to seek first the kingdom of God, Matthew 6:33, and to remember that our life is in His hands, James 4:13-15.

If you want a simple guideline: prepare reasonably for likely needs, keep your heart free from fear, and stay generous and ready to help others if trouble comes. Also ask yourself in prayer, “Lord, am I storing out of wisdom, or out of distrust?”

What is the church?

The church is the people Jesus Christ has called out of the world to belong to Him, confess Him as Lord, and gather as His body for worship, teaching, fellowship, prayer, and the ordinances. The Bible pictures the church as Christ’s body and bride, with Christ Himself as the head, not as a building or merely a religious organization, but as a living people redeemed by His blood, called to holiness and mission (Matthew 16:18; Ephesians 1:22-23; Ephesians 5:25-27; 1 Peter 2:9-10).

In the New Testament, the local church is the visible gathering of believers under the Word, while the universal church includes all true believers in Christ across time and place. That means church is both a shared spiritual reality and a concrete, gathered life with elders, discipleship, discipline, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper (Acts 2:42; 1 Corinthians 12:12-13; Hebrews 10:24-25).

If you want, I can also explain the difference between the universal church and the local church, or what marks a healthy church.
Does a cashless society have anything to do with the end times?

A cashless society is not, by itself, proof that the end times have arrived. Christians disagree on how Revelation and related passages map onto modern economics, but the Bible does warn that a future system of buying and selling may be tied to allegiance to the beast, as in Revelation 13:16-17.

The key issue is not cash versus digital payment, but worship, loyalty, and control. Scripture says the beast will cause people to receive a mark so that no one can buy or sell unless they belong to him, and that points to a real end-times test of allegiance, not merely a payment technology. Revelation 13:16-17; Revelation 14:9-11

So I would not say every move toward digital money is the fulfillment of prophecy. But I would say Christians should stay alert, because technology can be used for good or for coercion, and the Bible prepares us to expect pressure to compromise in the last days.

I am a former Catholic. Should I continue to go to Catholic Church so I can reach people for Christ?

Yes, you may lovingly reach Catholics for Christ, but you should not stay in a place that teaches a false gospel as though it were a healthy church home. The Bible says the gospel is that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, and we are justified by grace through faith in Christ alone, not by works or sacramental merit, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9; Galatians 1:6-9.

If you are asking whether to attend as a visitor for evangelistic conversations, that can be wise in some cases. But if you mean making a Catholic parish your regular spiritual home, that is another matter, because you need shepherding in the truth, and believers are called to be joined to a faithful local church that proclaims the whole counsel of God, Acts 2:42; Hebrews 10:24-25.

What does the Bible say about world missions?

The Bible teaches that world missions are God’s heart, Christ’s command, and the church’s joyful calling to make disciples of all nations. Jesus said, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” in Matthew 28:19-20, and He also said the gospel must be preached “to all nations” before the end in Mark 13:10.

From the beginning, God promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham, which points forward to the nations being reached through Christ, Genesis 12:3. The Psalms and the prophets also look ahead to the nations worshiping the true God, Psalm 67:1-4; Isaiah 49:6. In the New Testament, the risen Christ sends His people outward by the power of the Holy Spirit, Acts 1:8, and Paul says faith comes by hearing the word of Christ, Romans 10:14-17.

So missions is not a side project, it is part of the church’s identity. We proclaim Christ crucified and risen, call people everywhere to repent and believe, and make disciples by baptizing them and teaching them to obey all that Jesus commanded, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Acts 17:30-31.

A simple next step is to pray regularly for the nations, your church’s missionaries, and for boldness in your own witness. If you want, I can also show you how to pray for missions, or give you a short Bible study on missions from Genesis to Revelation.
How should we live our lives in light of our identity in Christ?

In light of our identity in Christ, we should live as people who have been made new, walking in holiness, love, humility, and obedience by the power of the Holy Spirit, not to earn God’s favor, but because we already have it in Christ Jesus. “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17), and “walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received” (Ephesians 4:1).

The Bible teaches that our identity is rooted first in union with Christ. We are forgiven, adopted, justified, and set apart for God’s purposes (Romans 8:1; Ephesians 1:5-7). That means our lives should increasingly reflect the character of our Savior, putting off the old self and putting on the new self (Ephesians 4:22-24).

Practically, that means:
- abiding in Christ through His Word and prayer, because apart from Him we can do nothing (John 15:5)
- loving fellow believers with sincere, sacrificial love (John 13:34-35)
- resisting sin and pursuing holiness, because we belong to God (1 Peter 1:14-16)
- serving others humbly, following the example of Christ (Philippians 2:3-8)
- shining as witnesses in the world, speaking and living the gospel with grace and truth (Matthew 5:16; Colossians 4:5-6)

If you belong to Christ, your life is not aimless. God is shaping you to look more like Jesus, and He will finish what He started (Philippians 1:6). A good next step is to ask, “What would it look like today for me to live as someone who is already loved, forgiven, and sent by Christ?”
How do I know the Bible is not just mythology?

You can know the Bible is not “just mythology” because it presents itself as public, historical truth, and its central claims are anchored in real people, places, and events, especially the life, death, and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ (Luke 1:1-4; 1 Corinthians 15:3-8).

A few reasons matter here:

The Bible names kings, cities, rulers, and timelines, not “once upon a time” language. Luke says he investigated eyewitness testimony carefully so Theophilus could know the “certainty” of what had been taught (Luke 1:1-4).

The Old Testament and New Testament repeatedly treat their events as real history, and the New Testament authors argue from witnesses, not private spiritual insight. Paul says the resurrection was seen by many, including more than 500 brothers at one time, and he ties Christianity to a claim that could be checked against witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).

Jesus Himself treated Scripture as God’s Word and as trustworthy, not as mythology. He said, “Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35), and He grounded His identity and mission in the written Word (Matthew 5:17-18).

Most importantly, Christianity rises or falls on a historical claim: that Jesus died for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. If Christ has not been raised, then the faith is empty, but Paul says He has been raised, and that changes everything (1 Corinthians 15:14-17).

Of course, someone may say, “All ancient religious texts make truth claims,” or “Miracles sound unlikely.” That is understandable. But the Bible does not ask for blind myth-belief, it calls you to examine the evidence and the message. Its coherence, manuscript preservation, fulfilled prophecy, and the testimony of eyewitnesses all point to something far greater than legend.

The deeper issue is not only whether the Bible is historical, but whether its holy God is speaking through it. Scripture teaches that we are sinners and need rescue, and that rescue is found in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for forgiveness and new life (Romans 3:23-24; Romans 10:9-13).

If you are open, I would encourage you to read one Gospel, especially Luke or John, asking God to show you whether Jesus is who He claims to be. What part of the Bible feels most myth-like to you?
What does it mean that the Bible is infallible? What is biblical infallibility?

Biblical infallibility means that Scripture is entirely trustworthy and never fails to accomplish God’s truth and purpose, so it does not deceive, mislead, or err in all that it affirms. In other words, the Bible is a sure, unfailing Word from God, and therefore perfectly reliable for faith and practice, as Jesus says, “Your word is truth” (John 17:17; 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

This is closely related to biblical inerrancy, which says the Bible is without error in the original writings, because God cannot lie and He breathed out His Word through human authors (Titus 1:2; 2 Peter 1:20-21). The practical result is that when Scripture speaks on doctrine, morality, history, or the meaning of salvation, it speaks with divine authority, not merely human opinion.

A simple way to remember it is: infallible means the Bible cannot fail; therefore you can safely build your life on it. If you want, I can also explain the difference between infallibility, inerrancy, and inspiration in a very simple chart.
What does the Bible mean when it says something is unclean?

In the Bible, **“unclean” usually means something is ritually or ceremonially defiled, not necessarily morally sinful in every case**. In the Old Testament, many things could make a person temporarily unclean for worship, such as touching a corpse, certain bodily discharges, skin disease, or eating foods God had marked off as unclean for Israel, and that state meant they were unfit to approach the tabernacle until cleansing was done, as in Leviticus 11, Leviticus 13–15, and Numbers 19.

That ceremonial uncleanness pointed to a deeper truth: **God is holy, and sinful people need cleansing to come near Him**. The New Testament shows the fulfillment in Christ, who is the one who truly cleanses us from sin, and it also teaches that many of the old ceremonial distinctions were shadows that found their reality in Him, as in Mark 7:18–23, Acts 10:15, and Hebrews 9:13–14.

So the key distinction is this, **unclean** can mean **ritually defiled** in a ceremonial sense, while **sinful** means **morally guilty before God**. Some things were unclean by God’s law without being sinful in themselves, but sin is always a deeper matter of the heart and conduct before God.

A simple application: when you read “unclean,” ask whether the text is talking about **ceremonial purity, moral impurity, or both**. If you want, I can also explain how the categories of clean and unclean relate to Jesus’ teaching in the Gospels.
What is the meaning of life?

The meaning of life is to know God, love Him, and glorify Him forever through Jesus Christ. Scripture says humanity was made in God’s image for His praise, but sin has broken our fellowship with Him, and only Christ can restore us to God, because He died for our sins and rose again bodily from the dead, and through faith in Him we receive forgiveness and new life, not by works (Genesis 1:27; Isaiah 43:7; Romans 3:23-24; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9).

That means life is not finally about self-creation, success, pleasure, or even just being “a good person.” It is about being reconciled to the living God and walking with Him now, then enjoying Him forever in the new creation. Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6).

If you want the true meaning of life, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you. Would you like me to explain how the Bible answers this in a little more depth?
How can there be subordination in the Trinity?

Christians have historically distinguished between the Trinity’s **equal deity** and an **order of relations**. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in essence, equal in glory and power, yet Scripture shows the Son willingly submitting to the Father in the work of redemption, without implying He is less God (John 1:1; John 5:18; Philippians 2:6-8; 1 Corinthians 15:28).

So there is no inequality of being, only an eternal distinction of persons and a voluntary, economic subordination in Christ’s saving mission. The Son is not a lesser god, and the Spirit is not a lesser spirit, because the Bible teaches one divine essence and full deity for each Person, while also showing ordered relations in sending, obeying, and glorifying (Matthew 28:19; John 14:16-17; John 17:1-5).

The careful orthodox way to say it is: **the Trinity is ontologically equal, but economically ordered**. That protects both truths, God’s oneness and the real personal distinctions within the Godhead.

If you want, I can also explain the difference between **eternal subordination** and **economic subordination**, and why many Christians are cautious about the first term.
Why are there so many religions? Do all religions lead to God?

There are many religions because human beings are religious by nature, yet sin bends our search for God into countless false starts, false gods, and man-made systems. The Bible teaches that God has made Himself known in creation and conscience, but people suppress that truth and exchange it for idols and lies, so the result is spiritual confusion rather than one clear path to God. Romans 1:18-25.

No, all religions do not lead to God. Jesus Christ said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” John 14:6, and the apostles preached that “there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” Acts 4:12.

Christianity is not mainly a human attempt to climb up to God, but God coming down to save sinners. We are separated from God by sin, but Jesus, who is truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by religious effort or sincerity. Ephesians 2:8-9; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

If you are wondering whether God can be known personally, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and eternal life. If you’d like, I can also explain why Christianity claims to be uniquely true without being arrogant.
Do Mormons believe in the Trinity?

No. Latter-day Saints, commonly called Mormons, do not believe in the historic Christian Trinity. They teach that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three distinct beings or personages, not one God eternally existing in three persons, which is what Scripture teaches, for example Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14.

That matters because the Trinity is not a minor detail, it is part of the identity of the true God. The Father is God, the Son is fully God, and the Holy Spirit is fully God, yet there is one God, not three gods, and not one God who merely appears in three roles.

If you want, I can also explain the main differences between Mormon teaching and historic Christianity in a simple side-by-side chart.
Where is the moral law summarily comprehended?

The moral law is summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments, given by God at Sinai, and they are reflected in the great commandments to love God and love your neighbor, as Jesus teaches in Matthew 22:37-40 and as summarized in Romans 13:8-10.

In other words, the Ten Commandments give a concise summary of God’s moral will for human life. The first table teaches love for God, and the second table teaches love for neighbor. This is why the law is holy and good, and why it still exposes sin and guides believers in grateful obedience, even though we are justified by faith alone in Christ alone, not by works.
What does it mean to be contrite? What is contrition?

To be **contrite** means to be **deeply broken over your sin**, humbled before God, and turned away from it with a sincere desire for mercy and change. **Contrition** is that inward sorrow and humility before the Lord, especially in light of His holiness and our guilt.

Scripture speaks this way often: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17). God looks with favor on the one who “is humble and contrite in spirit, and trembles at My word” (Isaiah 66:2). This is not mere regret over consequences, but real repentance, a heart that grieves sin because it is against God.

Contrition is not the same as despair. A contrite heart does not hide from God, it runs to Him for mercy through Christ. For every sinner, the hope is the gospel: Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again, and those who repent and believe in Him are forgiven and made new (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 1 John 1:9).

If you want, I can also show you the difference between **contrition, repentance, and remorse**.
What does it mean that “at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11)?

Psalm 16:11 means that true, lasting joy is found in God’s presence, and that fellowship with Him is the believer’s greatest good, now and forever. In Scripture, God’s “right hand” often pictures favor, power, and nearness, so “pleasures forevermore” speaks of the unending delight of being with the Lord, not fleeting earthly happiness.

In the immediate context, David is saying that God Himself is his portion, his refuge, and his life, and that God will not abandon him to the grave. For Christians, this points forward to Christ, who entered death and rose again so that all who trust in Him may enjoy the fullness of God’s presence forever, not by works but by grace through faith, with resurrection hope and eternal joy in Him.

This verse also reminds us that the world’s pleasures are temporary, but God’s pleasure is holy, satisfying, and eternal, as Psalm 73:25-26 and John 17:3 also show. If you want, I can explain how this verse points specifically to Jesus and the resurrection.
What is divine providence?

Divine providence is God’s sovereign, wise, and loving rule over all creation, by which He preserves, governs, and directs everything toward His holy purposes. Scripture says He “works out everything according to the counsel of His will” and that in Him “all things hold together” (Ephesians 1:11; Colossians 1:17).

This means nothing is outside God’s control, yet He is never the author of sin. He ordains and overrules events in a way that is perfectly holy, wise, and good, even when we cannot trace His hand in suffering or delay (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20).

For believers, providence is a great comfort, because our lives are not random, and our Father is actively caring for us. It should lead us to trust Him, pray faithfully, and obey Him in the ordinary things of life (Matthew 6:26-33; Proverbs 3:5-6).

If you want, I can also explain how providence differs from fate, or give a simple Reformed definition.
In what ways is the Christian life like the Olympics?

The Christian life is like the Olympics in that it calls for disciplined training, focused effort, and endurance toward a worthy goal, but the goal is not earthly glory, it is faithfulness to Christ and the eternal prize of His calling, as in 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 and Hebrews 12:1-2.

Christians, like athletes, must run with perseverance, lay aside hindrances, and keep their eyes fixed on the finish line. Yet unlike Olympic runners, we do not strive to earn God’s love or justification by works. We run because we have already been saved by grace through faith in Christ, who died for our sins and rose again, and the Spirit strengthens us for sanctification, endurance, and obedience.

A few helpful parallels:
- Training matters, just as prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and self-denial matter for growth in holiness.
- Focus matters, because distractions can slow a runner, and sin can entangle the believer.
- Endurance matters, because the Christian race is often long and costly.
- A crown is promised, but it is an imperishable one from the Lord, not human applause.

The difference is just as important: the Christian life is not a self-salvation project. We do not run to become God’s children, we run because in Christ we already are. If you want, I can also give you a short sermon-style version or a youth-group illustration.
What should be the Christian perspective on nudity in art?

Christianity does not treat nudity in art as automatically sinful or automatically innocent. The key questions are purpose, context, modesty, and whether the work honors God or stirs lust, because Scripture warns that lust is sin while also showing that the human body is part of God’s good creation, though now affected by the fall, Genesis 1:27, Genesis 3:7, Matthew 5:28.

Faithful Christians have often distinguished between artistic depiction of the body and sensual display designed to provoke desire. A painting, sculpture, or drawing may study the beauty and dignity of the human form, but if it is presented in a way that tempts the viewer to lust, it crosses a moral line, Proverbs 4:23; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5.

So my view is that nudity in art can be morally permissible in some settings, but it must be approached with great caution, sobriety, and discernment. Christians should ask whether the artwork promotes what is noble and pure, or whether it normalizes immodesty and feeds the flesh, Philippians 4:8; Romans 13:14.

A practical guide is to avoid art that would reasonably lead you, or others, into lust, and to choose what can be received with a clean conscience before the Lord. If you are unsure, pray, seek wise counsel from mature believers, and let love for holiness govern your viewing, 1 Corinthians 10:31; Romans 14:23.

If you want, I can also help you think through this from the standpoint of museums, private collection, or Christian artists.
Should we allow false teachers into our home?

Scripture warns us not to receive false teachers in a way that shares in their evil works, so as a general rule, we should not give them a platform of support or spiritual endorsement in our homes (2 John 1:10-11; Romans 16:17-18).

The best charitable argument for wider hospitality is that Christians should be known for kindness and openness, and not every person with error is equally dangerous in every setting. But the New Testament is especially sober about those who persist in denying Christ or spreading destructive doctrine, and love sometimes means refusing access rather than offering a seat at the table.

My view is that we should not host false teachers as teachers, guests of honor, or spiritual influencers, though ordinary kindness and a call to repentance are still fitting when possible. If the issue is a specific person or situation, I can help you think through it biblically.
How is God’s Word a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105)?

God’s Word is a lamp to your feet because it gives enough light for your next step, showing what is true, what is sin, and how to walk in wisdom before God, even when the road ahead is still dark (Psalm 119:105; Psalm 119:130). In the psalm’s setting, “lamp” and “light” picture God’s covenant instruction guiding a believer through real-life decisions, not merely offering religious ideas.

Practically, Scripture guides your conscience, corrects your path, and keeps you from stumbling into folly. It is also a means God uses to sanctify His people, as Jesus prayed, “Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth” (John 17:17). When you do not know the whole future, God usually gives enough light for obedience today.

A good next step is to read a short passage each day, ask, “What does this show me about God, sin, and obedience?”, and then obey the clearest thing you see.

Why were the people guilty for a priest’s sin?

In the Old Testament, the priest was a representative head for the people, so his sin brought guilt on the whole covenant community because he stood before God on their behalf. Leviticus 4:3 says, “If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people,” and that principle shows how seriously God treats representative leadership.

This does not mean every person was equally personally guilty for the priest’s private sin, but it does mean the whole nation could be affected by the failure of one appointed mediator. The priest’s office pointed forward to Christ, the perfect High Priest who never sinned and whose sacrifice truly removes guilt, not merely covers it for a time, as Hebrews 7:26-27 and Hebrews 9:11-14 teach.

The lesson is sobering: sin in spiritual leadership is never private, because God holds leaders accountable and their failure can wound many. It also comforts believers, because Jesus does not share in that guilt, He bears our guilt and gives us a flawless mediator before the Father. What is spiritual mapping?

Spiritual mapping is a practice within some Christian circles that tries to identify the spiritual strongholds, histories, or territorial powers believed to influence a city, region, or people group, often with the goal of targeted prayer and evangelism. It is not a clearly taught doctrine in Scripture, and Christians differ on how much of it is biblically grounded.

The strongest biblical case for a cautious version is that Scripture does speak of spiritual warfare and unseen powers, such as Ephesians 6:12 and Daniel 10:13, and believers should pray intentionally for places and people. The main concern is that spiritual mapping can go beyond what Scripture explicitly teaches and can drift into speculation, giving too much attention to alleged spiritual “geography” rather than to the ordinary means God has given, like prayer, the Word, repentance, and gospel proclamation.

My view is that Christians may pray strategically for specific communities, but we should be careful not to treat spiritual mapping as a required or authoritative method. Keep the focus where Scripture places it, on the holiness of God, the reality of sin, the authority of Christ, and the spread of the gospel through prayerful witness, not secret knowledge. If you want, I can also explain how spiritual mapping compares with biblical spiritual warfare.
What is God’s design for marriage?

God designed marriage as a covenant union between one man and one woman for life, meant to display faithful love, mutual help, and the covenant relationship between Christ and His church. Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6; Ephesians 5:31-32 show that marriage is not merely a human arrangement, but God’s good creation for companionship, holiness, and a visible picture of the gospel.

In Genesis 2:18, God says it is not good for the man to be alone, so He provides a suitable helper, and the “one flesh” union in Genesis 2:24 teaches real, exclusive, lifelong covenantal commitment. Jesus confirms this design, and Paul shows that marriage is meant to reflect Christ’s sacrificial love and the church’s loving response, which is why the marriage covenant should be marked by fidelity, humility, and self-giving love.

Practically, this means husbands are called to love their wives as Christ loved the church, and wives are called to respect their husbands, with both pursuing faithfulness, forgiveness, and shared discipleship under God’s Word. What is the value of group Bible study?

Group Bible study is valuable because God uses the gathered church to help believers hear, understand, obey, and encourage one another in His Word, not just to learn privately but to grow together in faith and love. Scripture says, “And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds, not forsaking our own assembling together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching” (Hebrews 10:24-25).

It also helps with biblical interpretation, because mature believers can sharpen one another, correct blind spots, and keep us anchored in the plain meaning of Scripture (Acts 17:11; Proverbs 27:17). In the New Testament, the church is a body, so group study supports mutual edification, accountability, and practical application of sanctification in everyday life (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 4:11-16).

How can I overcome a feeling of spiritual emptiness?

Spiritual emptiness often comes when our hearts are looking to lesser things to do what only God can do, and the Lord is gracious to meet us there. Jesus says, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst” (John 6:35).

If you belong to Christ, this emptiness is not proof that God has abandoned you. It may be a call to return to the ordinary means of grace, because God often strengthens His people through His Word, prayer, and fellowship with His church, not through constant emotional highs (Acts 2:42; Hebrews 10:24-25).

A few helpful next steps:
- Open the Psalms and pray them honestly, especially Psalm 42 and Psalm 63.
- Read one passage of Scripture each day and ask, “What does this show me about God, Christ, and my own heart?”
- Pray directly to God about your emptiness, your distractions, and any known sin.
- Reconnect with a faithful local church and a mature believer who can walk with you.
- If there is unconfessed sin, repent quickly, because sin numbs the soul, but God is merciful to restore the repentant (1 John 1:9).

All of us are sinners in need of grace, and Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose bodily from the dead so that sinners can be forgiven and brought near to God. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

I understand why that question matters so deeply. If paradise is real, you want more than guesses, you want certainty.

The Bible teaches that no one can earn assurance of heaven by enough good deeds, because all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and sin separates us from the holy God who will judge the world in righteousness (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2; Hebrews 9:27). But God has provided one Savior, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 3:18).

So the way to assurance is not to trust in your own works, but to repent and believe in Jesus Christ alone, receiving His forgiveness as a gift of grace, not something earned (Ephesians 2:8-9; John 3:16; John 14:6). The Bible says, “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36).

What is the spiritual gift of miracles?

The spiritual gift of miracles is a God-given ability, given by the Holy Spirit, to perform extraordinary signs that visibly confirm God’s message and authority. In the New Testament, miracles often accompanied the apostles and the giving of revelation, showing that God was powerfully at work through them, such as in 2 Corinthians 12:12 and Hebrews 2:3-4.

Christians differ on whether this gift continues today. Cessationists believe the miraculous sign gifts were unique to the apostolic era, while continuationists believe God may still grant such gifts, though always under Scripture’s authority and never as a replacement for it. My view is that the gift of miracles was a special sign gift tied to the apostolic foundation of the church, because its main purpose was to authenticate the gospel message, not to become the ordinary pattern for all ages.

Either way, the greatest miracle is not signs and wonders, but the new birth, when God gives a sinner new life in Christ, because salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Jesus Christ alone. If you want, I can also explain how this gift relates to healing, tongues, and prophecy.
What does it mean that God is merciful?

God’s mercy means that He does not give sinners the full punishment they deserve, and instead He compassionately helps, forgives, and restores those who turn to Him. Scripture says, “The LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (Psalm 103:8), and “because of the LORD’s loving devotion we are not consumed” (Lamentations 3:22).

In the Bible, mercy is not God ignoring sin. He is holy and just, so mercy is meaningful because judgment is real. At the cross, God’s mercy and justice meet: Jesus Christ bore the penalty for sin, so that God can remain just and still justify the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25-26). That is the heart of the Gospel, Christ’s saving work for sinners.

For you, this means you can come honestly to God with your guilt, weakness, and need. If you are burdened by sin, turn from it and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for your forgiveness and new life.

Who is the head of the church, biblically speaking?

Biblically speaking, Jesus Christ is the head of the church, not any pope, pastor, or council. The church is His body, and He rules it with sovereign authority and loving care, as seen in Ephesians 1:22-23, Colossians 1:18, and Ephesians 5:23.

This means the church belongs to Christ, is governed by His Word, and is accountable to Him. Human leaders are real and important, but they are servants and under-shepherds, not the head. See also Colossians 2:19 and 1 Peter 5:2-4.

Who is the ancient serpent of Revelation 12:9?

The ancient serpent in Revelation 12:9 is Satan, the devil, the same deceiver who appeared in Genesis as the serpent in the garden. Revelation itself identifies him as “the great dragon,” “that ancient serpent,” “the one called the devil and Satan,” who deceives the whole world, and this fits the Bible’s unified storyline of spiritual rebellion against God (Genesis 3:1-15; Revelation 12:9).

This matters because Scripture presents Satan as a real personal enemy, not a symbol of evil in general, and Christ came to destroy the works of the devil through His cross and resurrection (Hebrews 2:14-15; 1 John 3:8). Book of 1 John - Bible Survey

1 John is a pastoral letter from the apostle John that gives believers assurance of eternal life, calls them to walk in the light, and tests false teaching by the truth about Jesus Christ. It strongly emphasizes that true fellowship with God produces obedience, love, and ongoing repentance, not sinless perfection, while also warning that denial of Christ’s true person is antichrist error.

John writes against confusion in the church by giving clear tests of genuine faith, especially right doctrine, righteous living, and brotherly love, with key themes in 1 John 1:5-10, 1 John 2:3-6, 1 John 2:18-23, 1 John 3:11-18, and 1 John 5:11-13. The book is deeply comforting because it shows that believers can know they have eternal life in Christ, not by self-confidence but by God’s promise and the witness of the Spirit.

A brief survey:

- **Author:** The apostle John, traditionally understood as the same John who wrote the Gospel of John.
- **Audience:** Believers facing false teaching and spiritual uncertainty.
- **Purpose:** “so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13, BSB).
- **Major themes:** light and darkness, truth and deception, obedience, love, assurance, confession of sin, Christ’s deity and incarnation, and victory over the world.
- **Key doctrinal emphasis:** Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, and His atoning work is central to salvation, which connects directly to the doctrine of the incarnation and the sufficiency of Christ’s saving work.
- **Tone:** pastoral, urgent, affectionate, and firm.

Simple chapter flow:
- **Chapter 1:** God is light, believers confess sin and walk in fellowship.
- **Chapter 2:** Obedience, love, warnings about antichrists, and confidence in Christ.
- **Chapter 3:** Children of God are marked by righteousness and love.
- **Chapter 4:** Test the spirits, confess the incarnation, and love because God first loved us.
- **Chapter 5:** Faith in the Son gives eternal life, and believers can have assurance and prayerful confidence.

The book is especially helpful for anyone asking, “How can I know I really belong to Christ?” John answers with both truth and comfort, pointing us to the Son of God who came in the flesh, died for our sins, and gives eternal life to all who believe. What happens at the final judgment?

At the final judgment, Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily, the dead will be raised, and every person will stand before Him to give an account, with eternal life for those in Christ and righteous condemnation for those who remain in unbelief, according to the Bible (Matthew 25:31-46; John 5:28-29; Revelation 20:11-15).

Scripture teaches that this will be a true public judgment, not a vague spiritual idea. The books are opened, deeds are revealed as evidence of the heart, and God’s justice will be shown to be perfectly right, while His mercy in Christ will also be magnified (Ecclesiastes 12:14; Romans 2:5-11; 2 Corinthians 5:10). For believers, this is not a judgment for condemnation, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, but it is still a real evaluation of life and service before the Lord (Romans 8:1; 1 Corinthians 3:12-15).

The good news is that if you belong to Christ by faith, His cross and resurrection are your only ground of acceptance before God, not your works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for forgiveness and life. In what ways is becoming a Christian becoming an entirely new man / woman?

Becoming a Christian means God gives you a new heart, a new identity, and a new direction in Christ. The Bible says that anyone in Christ is a “new creation,” old things have passed away, and new things have come, which is the language of regeneration and union with Christ, not mere self-improvement. 2 Corinthians 5:17; Ezekiel 36:26-27.

This newness includes:
- a new standing before God, justified by grace through faith, no longer condemned in Christ, Romans 5:1; Romans 8:1
- a new nature, born again by the Holy Spirit, John 3:3-8
- a new Master, since you now belong to Jesus Christ, Romans 6:17-18
- a new family, adopted as God’s child, Galatians 4:4-7
- a new way of life, with real repentance and growing sanctification, Ephesians 4:22-24; Colossians 3:9-10

This does not mean the Christian becomes instantly sinless, but it does mean sin no longer rules as your identity or authority. The believer is being transformed into the likeness of Christ day by day by the Spirit’s power, 2 Corinthians 3:18.

What are the Pauline epistles?

The Pauline epistles are the New Testament letters written by the apostle Paul to churches and individuals, including Romans through Philemon. They teach core Christian doctrine, such as justification by faith, sanctification, the church, and the Christian life.

In the New Testament, these letters are usually grouped as Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. Paul wrote them to address real needs in the early church, and the Holy Spirit used them to instruct all believers, not only the original readers.

They are important because they explain the gospel clearly, especially that sinners are made right with God by grace through faith in Christ, not by works, as seen in Romans 3:28 and Ephesians 2:8-9. If you want, I can also give you a simple summary of each Pauline letter.
How can I be sure I am praying according to the will of God?

You can be sure you are praying according to God’s will when your prayers are shaped by God’s revealed Word, centered on Christ, and submitted to the Father’s wise purposes, not merely your own desires. Scripture says, “If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” and “if we know that He hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have what we have asked of Him” (1 John 5:14-15).

A few biblical tests help here. First, pray in line with Scripture, because God will not answer prayers that contradict His commands or character, such as prayers fueled by selfishness or sin (James 4:3; Psalm 66:18). Second, ask for what honors Christ and advances His kingdom, like holiness, wisdom, repentance, endurance, and love, which are all plainly God’s will (Matthew 6:9-10; 1 Thessalonians 4:3; Colossians 1:9-10). Third, hold your requests with humility, saying in effect, “not my will, but Yours” as Jesus did in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42). That is not unbelief, but trust.

Practically, when you pray, open the Bible first and let the passage shape what you ask for. Then pray specifically for what God has already promised, and leave the outcome to His fatherly wisdom. If you are uncertain, pray for wisdom itself, because “if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God” (James 1:5).

A helpful question to ask is, “Will this request help me obey Christ, love others, and glorify God?” If you want, I can also show you how to test a specific prayer you’re wrestling with.
What does the Bible say about busyness / being too busy?

The Bible warns that busyness can easily crowd out what is most important, especially hearing God’s word, seeking His kingdom, and resting in Him. It does not praise frantic, distracted living, but calls God’s people to wisdom, priorities, and peace, such as in Luke 10:38-42, where Martha was “distracted by much serving,” while Mary chose “the good portion.”

Scripture shows at least two dangers with being too busy. First, busyness can make us anxious and divided in heart, like Martha, whereas Jesus says, “Only one thing is necessary” and commends sitting at His feet, listening to His word (Luke 10:41-42). Second, constant labor can become unbelief if we live as though everything depends on us rather than on the Lord, who says, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

The Bible also teaches wise diligence. Work is good, and the Proverbs commend hard work, but not restless overwork. “It is in vain that you rise early and stay up late” if the Lord does not build the house (Psalm 127:1-2). Jesus Himself withdrew to pray, showing that even faithful ministry needs rhythms of communion with the Father (Mark 1:35; Luke 5:16).

If busyness is ruling your life, a good next step is to ask, “What am I doing that is good, but not necessary?” Then set aside protected time each day for Scripture and prayer, and seek to rearrange your week around worship, rest, and obedience rather than constant activity. What are the seven baptisms mentioned in the Bible, and what do they mean?

The Bible does not give one official list called “the seven baptisms,” but Christians sometimes use that phrase to summarize seven major baptism-related washings and baptisms found in Scripture. The clearest and most important are John’s baptism, Jesus’ baptism, Christian baptism, Spirit baptism, baptism into Christ’s death, baptism by suffering, and the Old Testament washings that pointed forward to cleansing.  

John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance, preparing Israel for the coming Messiah, as in Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:4. It signified turning from sin and getting ready for the Lord.  

Jesus’ baptism marked the beginning of His public ministry and identified Him with sinful humanity, though He Himself had no sin, as in Matthew 3:13-17. It also revealed the Trinity, the Father speaking, the Son being baptized, and the Spirit descending, showing the one God in three persons.  

Christian baptism is the ordinance given to Christ’s disciples after His resurrection, commanded in Matthew 28:19. It is an outward sign of union with Christ, a public confession of faith, and a picture of cleansing from sin, death to the old life, and rising to new life, as in Romans 6:3-4; Acts 2:38.  

Spirit baptism is the work of the Holy Spirit by which believers are placed into the body of Christ, as in 1 Corinthians 12:13. This is not a separate water ceremony, but God’s inward saving work that unites the believer to Christ and His church.  

Baptism into Christ’s death is the spiritual reality described in Romans 6:3-4 and Colossians 2:12. Paul means that believers are united to Christ in His death and resurrection, so sin no longer has mastery over them. This is the doctrine of union with Christ.  

Baptism by suffering refers to the hard trials and death Jesus spoke of when He said, “I have a baptism to undergo” in Luke 12:50, and also in Mark 10:38-39. Here “baptism” means being overwhelmed by suffering, especially the cross.  

The Old Testament washings and ceremonial baptisms pointed forward to the need for cleansing and the greater cleansing Christ would bring, as in Hebrews 9:10 and Mark 7:4. These rituals taught that sin makes us unclean and that only God can truly purify the heart.  

The main thing to see is that all these point in different ways to cleansing, identification, repentance, union with Christ, or judgment through suffering. The center of it all is Jesus Christ, who saves sinners by His death and bodily resurrection, and the New Testament baptism that matters most is the one that points us to Him in faith. What do you think about the Bible codes? Is there any validity to them?

The so-called “Bible codes” have no solid biblical basis, and Christians should not treat them as a reliable way to find hidden prophecy or secret messages. Scripture is clear, sufficient, and meant to be read in context, not mined for encrypted predictions, and it warns us against speculative pursuits that pull us away from the plain meaning of God’s Word, such as 2 Timothy 3:16-17 and Deuteronomy 29:29.

Some people are drawn to Bible codes because they want proof that the Bible is supernatural, or because hidden patterns feel exciting and mysterious. But the problem is that these claims usually depend on selective word-spaces, flexible search methods, and patterns that can be found in many long texts if you look hard enough.

My view is that Bible codes are not a trustworthy doctrine or a sound method of interpretation. The Bible itself teaches that God has spoken openly and clearly in Scripture, and the proper Christian task is to read, believe, and obey what is written, not chase secret code systems. A better next step is to study the plain meaning of a passage in context and ask how it reveals Christ and calls you to faith and obedience.

How can I see the hand of God moving in my life?

You can see the hand of God moving in your life most clearly by looking for His faithful work through His Word, His providence, His conviction, and His sanctifying grace. God is often moving not mainly in spectacular signs, but in steady ways that conform you to Christ, because “He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6).

Start by asking, “Is God drawing me to Christ, exposing sin, strengthening faith, and producing obedience?” That is often the clearest evidence of His hand, since the Holy Spirit convicts, guides, and transforms believers (John 16:8; Romans 8:28-29). Sometimes His leading looks like open and closed doors, but even more often it looks like patience in trial, growth in holiness, a deeper love for Scripture, and a greater dependence on prayer.

A simple way to look for Him is this: read Scripture daily, pray honestly for wisdom, and keep a short journal of answered prayers, providential timing, and moments of conviction or comfort. Over time, patterns become clearer, and you can begin to trace God’s fatherly care in both joy and suffering, as Psalm 23 and Romans 8 remind us.

Are we to love the sinner but hate the sin?

Yes, as a general Christian principle, we are to love people made in God’s image while hating evil and sin, because God Himself is holy and opposes sin, yet shows mercy to sinners in Christ (Psalm 5:4-6; Romans 5:8). That said, the phrase can be too vague if it is used to avoid naming sin clearly or to sound like mere tolerance instead of biblical love.

Scripture calls us to speak the truth in love, to love our neighbor, and to warn against sin without hatred toward the person, because every one of us is a sinner in need of grace (Ephesians 4:15; Leviticus 19:18; Romans 3:23). Real love does not affirm what destroys people, but points them to repentance and to Jesus Christ, who died and rose again to save sinners (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Luke 5:32).

So yes, love the sinner, hate the sin, but make sure your love is truthful, compassionate, and willing to call sin what God calls it. A good next step is to ask, “Am I speaking with Christ’s gentleness, and also with His truth?”
Is the Buddhist concept of Zen compatible with the Christian faith?

Zen is not compatible with historic Christian faith if it is treated as a spiritual path to enlightenment apart from Christ, because the Bible teaches that salvation, peace with God, and true life come through Jesus Christ alone, not through an impersonal awakening or self-emptying method. Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6), and there is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

The deepest issue is worship and authority: Zen seeks a kind of transcendence or liberation through its own framework, while Christianity calls us to repent, believe the gospel, and know the living God through the death and resurrection of His Son. The Bible does commend quietness, self-control, and meditation on God’s word (Psalm 1:1-2; Philippians 4:6-8), but Christian meditation is not emptying the mind into a spiritual neutrality, it is filling the mind with God’s truth and submitting to Christ.

If you mean “Can a Christian use some calming practices associated with Zen, like silence or focused breathing?” then some outward practices may be morally neutral, but only if they are detached from Zen’s religious meaning and kept under Christ’s lordship. A Christian should never seek spiritual guidance, identity, or ultimate peace from Zen, because true peace with God is found only in Christ, who died for our sins and rose again (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

What is the Wailing Wall / Western Wall?

The Wailing Wall, more properly called the Western Wall, is a retaining wall of the ancient Temple Mount in Jerusalem, and it is the holiest accessible site in Judaism because it is the closest place to the former location of the Jewish Temple. It is not part of the Temple itself, but a surviving structure from the temple complex built in Herod’s day.

Historically, the First and Second Temples stood on the Temple Mount, and the Second Temple was destroyed by the Romans in AD 70, fulfilling Jesus’ warning that not one stone would be left upon another there (Matthew 24:1-2). The Western Wall remains as a powerful reminder of Jerusalem’s history and of the sorrow and hope bound up with God’s dealings with Israel.

For Christians, the wall is significant as part of the biblical setting of redemptive history, but our access to God is not through a physical site. Jesus Christ is the true and final meeting place between God and sinners, our great High Priest and mediator, and through His death and resurrection we come near to God by grace through faith (John 14:6; Hebrews 4:14-16; Ephesians 2:13-18).

What is Taizé worship, and is it biblical?

Taizé worship is a simple, contemplative style of Christian worship that uses short repeated chants, silence, candles, and Scripture reading, originating with the ecumenical community in Taizé, France. It can include sincere devotion to Christ, but as a worship form it is a tertiary matter, so faithful Christians may differ on whether it is a wise or helpful expression of worship.

A fair case for it is that repetition, silence, and meditative singing can help believers “be still” before God and pray with focus, and Scripture does include repeated praise and reflective meditation, such as Psalm 1:2 and Psalm 46:10. The caution is that worship should be governed by truth and reverence, so any form, including Taizé, must not drift into vague spirituality, empty repetition, or an atmosphere that downplays the gospel of Christ crucified and risen, since Jesus says true worshipers worship the Father in spirit and truth, and Paul warns against merely human religion in Colossians 2:8.

My view is that Taizé can be biblically acceptable as a worship aid in some settings if its content is sound, Christ-centered, and ordered by Scripture, but it should not replace clear preaching, congregational edification, and the ordinary means of grace, because the church is built up by the Word, prayer, and the gathered body in a way that is not merely contemplative but also doctrinally robust, as in Colossians 3:16 and 2 Timothy 4:2.

Does the Old Testament truly predict a second advent of the Messiah?

Yes, the Old Testament gives real grounds for expecting both the Messiah’s suffering and a later, glorious coming in judgment and kingdom power. Passages like Daniel 7:13-14, Zechariah 12:10, Zechariah 14:3-5, Isaiah 9:6-7, and Psalm 110:1 point to a ruler who is not only rejected and afflicted, but also exalted, reigning, and bringing final justice.

The strongest case is that the prophets often place the Messiah’s humiliation and triumph side by side without spelling out the long gap between them. Christians believe Jesus fulfilled the first coming in His incarnation, cross, burial, and resurrection, and that His promised return completes what the Old Testament anticipated in fuller form, especially in Daniel 7:13-14 and Zechariah 14:4-9. This is not a modern invention, but a faithful reading of the text in light of Christ.
