Contemporary Christian music - is it honoring to God? Should it be used in church services?

Contemporary Christian music can honor God if the lyrics are biblically faithful, the heart is sincere, and the congregation is truly aided in praising Christ. Whether it should be used in church services is a tertiary matter where faithful Christians may disagree, because Scripture does not command one musical style for gathered worship, but it does command that worship be orderly, edifying, and centered on God’s truth, not on performance or entertainment, see Colossians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 14:26; 1 Corinthians 14:40.

One strong Christian view says contemporary music can serve the church well because it helps believers sing Scripture, remember truth, and participate with understanding in worship. Another strong Christian view cautions that some modern styles can easily drift toward emotional manipulation, performance, or vague theology, so churches should prefer forms that are more reverent, congregational, and text-rich.

My view is that it may be used in church if it is doctrinally sound, congregationally singable, and intentionally ordered to magnify Christ rather than the musicians, because the issue is not “old versus new” but whether the church is faithfully letting “the word of Christ dwell in you richly” and worshiping “in spirit and truth,” Colossians 3:16; John 4:24.

A simple test is this: do the lyrics clearly confess the holiness of God, the sinfulness of man, the cross and resurrection of Jesus Christ, and the call to faith and obedience? If not, it may be emotionally moving but not spiritually nourishing.

What does it mean to test the spirits?

To “test the spirits” means to discern whether a teaching, impression, or spiritual claim comes from the Holy Spirit or from a false spirit, because not every religious message is from God (1 John 4:1). John gives the test plainly: confessing the true Jesus Christ, the Son of God come in the flesh, is essential to sound doctrine, and denying Him is not of God (1 John 4:2-3).

In context, John was guarding the church against false prophets, so this is not vague intuition, but careful comparison with apostolic truth and Scripture. The Bible also says to examine everything and hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and the Bereans were commended because they tested teaching by the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11).

Practically, test a message by asking: Does it agree with the Bible? Does it honor the true Christ? Does it produce holiness, humility, and obedience rather than confusion and rebellion? The Holy Spirit never leads contrary to the Word He inspired.

Why should I get married?

Marriage is a God-given covenant, not just a social contract, and Scripture presents it as a wise and honorable good when entered in rightly, especially for companionship, purity, and a picture of Christ and the church. Yet it is not required for every believer, because both marriage and singleness are gifts from God (Genesis 2:18; Matthew 19:4-6; 1 Corinthians 7:7; Ephesians 5:31-32).

A strong biblical reason to marry is companionship, because God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Marriage also provides a proper covenantal context for sexual intimacy and helps guard against sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 7:2, 9). And for Christians, marriage is meant to display something greater, the faithful love of Christ for His bride, the church (Ephesians 5:25-27).

At the same time, the Bible is clear that singleness can also be a good and fruitful calling. Paul says the unmarried person may have undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:32-35). So the question is not, “Must I get married to live faithfully?” but, “Has God given me this calling, and would marriage help me serve Him well?”

If you are asking personally, it is worth praying over your motives, your readiness for covenant faithfulness, and whether you desire marriage for holiness, companionship, and service, not merely loneliness, pressure, or romance. A good next step is to talk with a mature pastor or trusted Christian couple about your situation and ask God for wisdom from James 1:5.

Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath?

Christians have differed on this, because it is a secondary doctrine, but Sunday is commonly called the Lord’s Day, and many believers see it as the Christian Sabbath principle carried into the first day of the week, while others say the Sabbath command was uniquely tied to the seventh day under the Mosaic covenant. The strongest case for Sunday worship is that Jesus rose on the first day, the church gathered on the first day, and the apostles recognized that day in a special way, for example John 20:1, Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2, Revelation 1:10.

My view is that the moral principle of one day in seven for rest and worship still stands, fulfilled and reshaped in Christ, so Sunday is the Christian Sabbath for many faithful churches, though I would not treat every orthodox believer who disagrees as outside the faith. Exodus 20:8-11 grounds the Sabbath in creation, while Hebrews 4:9-10 points to a deeper Sabbath rest found in Christ, which is why Christians should set apart the Lord’s Day for worship, rest, and mercy.

If this matters for your conscience or church practice, I’d encourage you to pray over Scripture, speak with your pastors, and aim to honor the Lord’s Day with joy rather than legalism.
What does it mean that those who humble themselves will be exalted (Matthew 23:12)?

In Matthew 23:12, Jesus means that God opposes proud self-exaltation but gives honor to those who repent of pride and take the low place before Him, because “the greatest among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 23:11-12; James 4:6). In context, Jesus is warning the scribes and Pharisees, who loved status, and He is teaching that true greatness in the kingdom comes through humble service, not self-promotion.

This is not a promise that every humble person will immediately gain worldly success, but that God Himself will ultimately lift up the humble in His time, both now in His grace and finally in His kingdom. Scripture echoes this pattern: “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you” (James 4:10; 1 Peter 5:6).

For us, that means we should stop striving to make ourselves impressive and instead seek to serve Christ faithfully where He has placed us. A good next step is to ask the Lord to expose any pride in your heart and then deliberately choose one hidden act of service this week.
How should poetry in the Bible be interpreted?

Biblical poetry should be interpreted by its plain meaning in context, with careful attention to imagery, parallelism, and genre, not as if every line is meant to be literal prose. Poetry in Scripture is real truth spoken in elevated language, so we ask what the author is saying through the image, not whether the image itself is a report of ordinary events.

A few biblical patterns help: Hebrew poetry often uses parallelism, where one line echoes, expands, or contrasts another, as in Psalm 19:1 and Proverbs 10:1; it also uses metaphor, hyperbole, and vivid pictures to press truth into the heart. For example, when Psalm 18:2 says, “The LORD is my rock,” it does not mean God is a stone, but that He is strong, steady, and protective. The Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Song of Songs, and much of the Prophets should be read with that in mind.

The key is to interpret poetry in light of the immediate context, the whole book, and the rest of Scripture. Scripture interprets Scripture, and poetic language never contradicts doctrinal truth, because the Bible is God’s Word, and God does not lie. This fits with the truth that God is spoken of in human language for our understanding, while His character remains holy, sovereign, and faithful.

A good first step is to read a poetic passage twice, then ask, “What is the main claim or burden here, and what picture is used to express it?” If you want, I can also show you how to interpret a specific psalm or proverb step by step.
What is the significance of the statement in Romans 1:22 that “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools”?

Romans 1:22 means that when sinful people claim the status of wisdom while rejecting God’s truth, their thinking is exposed as spiritual folly and moral rebellion. In context, Paul is describing humanity’s downward spiral: though God has made Himself known, people suppress the truth, exchange the glory of the Creator for idols, and then their minds become darkened and distorted, which is why “wisdom” apart from God ends in foolishness, not enlightenment, Romans 1:18-23.

The phrase is significant because it shows that unbelief is not merely an intellectual problem but a worship problem. In biblical terms, true wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, Proverbs 1:7, so when people refuse God, they do not become more free or more advanced, they become enslaved to sin and self-deception. This is a sober reminder that human pride cannot save us, and it points us to Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” Colossians 2:3.

What does it mean that sin is lawlessness?

Sin is lawlessness means sin is not just weakness or mistake, it is rebellion against God’s righteous rule. “Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness” (1 John 3:4), which shows that sin is a violation of God’s holy command, not merely a flaw in human behavior.

In Scripture, God’s law reflects His character, so to break His law is to oppose His authority and goodness. That is why sin is serious, and why we all need Christ, who obeyed God perfectly and bore our guilt on the cross, died, and rose again for our justification (Romans 3:23-24; 1 Peter 2:24; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

This also means the answer to lawlessness is not self-improvement, but repentance and faith in Jesus Christ alone. Turn from sin and trust in the Savior who forgives, cleanses, and makes sinners new.

Has anyone ever seen God?

No one has ever seen God in His fullness as He is in Himself, because He is invisible and holy, yet God has made Himself known truly and savingly. The Bible says, “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18); it also says, “God, whom no man has seen or can see” (1 Timothy 6:16).

At the same time, people in Scripture did see manifestations of God’s presence, such as Abraham, Moses, and Isaiah, but not a complete sight of the divine essence. The Son, Jesus Christ, is the perfect revelation of God, because He is “the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3).

If you are asking because you want to know what God is like, look to Jesus Christ. He revealed the Father, died for sinners, and rose bodily from the dead so that we may know God by grace through faith. Turn from sin and trust in Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

Are books such as 90 minutes in Heaven and 23 minutes in Hell biblically based?

They are not biblically authoritative, and Christians should not treat them as binding doctrine. The Bible is sufficient for what God has chosen to reveal about death, judgment, heaven, hell, and salvation, and it gives us clear ground to test all such claims, “to the law and to the testimony” (Isaiah 8:20; 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

The Bible does teach that there is a real heaven and a real hell, that people will face judgment, and that Christ alone saves sinners, but it does not give us permission to build doctrine from private visions or near-death experiences. We are warned not to go beyond what is written, and even spiritual experiences must be tested carefully (Deuteronomy 29:29; 1 John 4:1; Colossians 2:18-19).

So, books like these may contain some elements that sound biblical, but they are not “biblically based” in the sense of being reliable sources for doctrine. The safer Christian approach is to read them, if at all, with caution and always subordinate them to Scripture.

Why does God not seem to care about the millions of starving children in the world?

I’m sorry, that pain is real, and it is right to grieve over starving children. The Bible does not teach that God is indifferent, but that He is holy, compassionate, and just, even when His providence is hard for us to understand.

You may be wondering, if God is good and powerful, why He permits such suffering. Christians ask that too. Scripture says God “is righteous in all His ways and gracious in all His works” (Psalm 145:17), and it also says that human sin has brought misery and brokenness into the world (Genesis 3:17-19; Romans 8:20-22). That does not make starvation feel smaller, but it does tell us the world is not as God originally made it.

The clearest sign that God does care is Jesus Christ. He entered our suffering, fed the hungry, had compassion on the crowds, and then went to the cross to bear sin and its curse for sinners (Matthew 14:14; Mark 8:2-3; Isaiah 53:4-6; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He was buried and rose bodily from the dead, proving He is Lord and that evil and death will not have the last word (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 6:9).

That means God’s care is not vague sentiment, but saving action in Christ and a coming judgment and renewal when all wrongs will be set right (Revelation 21:4-5). In the meantime, He calls His people to mercy, generosity, and practical help for the needy, not indifference (James 2:15-17; 1 John 3:17-18).

If this question is personal for you, bring that grief honestly to God in prayer, open Psalm 13 or Psalm 10, and talk with a faithful local pastor or church elder about it. And if you are asking whether you can know this God, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.
What is postmodern therapy, and is it biblical?

Postmodern therapy is a broad family of counseling approaches that focuses less on “objective truth” and more on language, personal stories, social power, and the meanings people give to their experiences. Biblically, it is not a sufficient foundation for the soul, because Scripture presents God’s truth as real and authoritative, not merely as one narrative among many, though some of its listening skills can be useful when rightly submitted to Christ.

A major strength of postmodern therapy is that it often helps people feel heard and noticed, especially where shame, trauma, or harmful narratives have shaped them. But its weakness is that it can drift into relativism, making identity and morality depend mainly on personal interpretation rather than on God’s created order and Word, which is why Christians must test every counsel by Scripture, not by cultural assumptions alone, 2 Timothy 3:16-17; Romans 12:2.

The Bible teaches that human beings are not mainly problems to be deconstructed, but sinners who need forgiveness, new hearts, and sanctification in Christ, Jeremiah 17:9; 2 Corinthians 5:17. That means any therapy that denies sin, avoids repentance, or treats God’s truth as optional is not biblical. Still, if a counselor listens carefully, speaks truth gently, and helps a person move toward repentance, wisdom, and hope in Christ, those parts can fit under a Christian framework.

So, the best Christian judgment is this: postmodern therapy as a philosophy is not biblical, but certain practices like careful listening, attention to suffering, and awareness of harmful narratives can be used in a Christ-submitted way. The goal is not just self-expression, but transformation by the renewing of the mind and reconciliation to God through Jesus Christ, Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 5:18-20.

If you’re asking because you’re considering counseling, look for a pastor or licensed counselor who openly honors Scripture, human sin, repentance, and the lordship of Christ.
I am a Christian who is addicted to smoking. How can I quit?

I’m sorry you’re in this struggle. Addictions can feel stubborn, but in Christ you are not without hope, and God is patient with His children as He sanctifies them.

Smoking is not merely a habit if it is enslaving you, it is something that can master you, while Scripture says, “I will not be mastered by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Your body belongs to the Lord, and He calls you to glorify Him with it, because you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

A wise, concrete way forward is to combine repentance, practical help, and accountability:
- Tell the Lord plainly that you want freedom, and ask Him for strength to obey Him today.
- Remove cigarettes, lighters, and triggers where possible.
- Tell one mature believer or your pastor this week and ask them to check in on you.
- Consider proven cessation help, such as nicotine replacement or a stop-smoking program, alongside prayer and discipline.
- Replace the habit with another response, like short walks, water, Scripture meditation, or deep breathing when cravings hit.

If you have tried before and failed, do not despair. Sanctification is often a fight, and the Lord who began a good work in you will carry it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Also, if smoking is tied to stress, loneliness, or grief, bring those burdens to Christ honestly, because He invites the weary to come to Him (Matthew 11:28-30).

Keep your eyes on the Gospel: Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again bodily, and He is able not only to forgive you but also to change you. Turn from this sin and trust Him for both mercy and power.

What is mortification of sin / the flesh?

Mortification of sin, or “putting the flesh to death,” means the Spirit-empowered, ongoing killing of sinful desires and habits in the believer’s life, not by self-reliance but by union with Christ and obedience to God’s Word. The Bible says, “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13), and “put to death, then, the members of your earthly nature” (Colossians 3:5).

In Scripture, “the flesh” often means our fallen, sinful nature that resists God, not our physical body itself. So mortification is not hating your body, but crucifying sinful impulses like lust, pride, anger, greed, bitterness, and unbelief, so that holiness grows in their place.

This is part of sanctification, the lifelong work of the Holy Spirit in believers. We do not earn salvation by mortifying sin, but those who are truly in Christ will fight sin because they belong to Him. As Galatians 5:24 says, “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”

Practically, this means:
- confessing sin quickly to God,
- cutting off temptations that feed it,
- filling your mind with Scripture,
- praying for the Spirit’s help,
- and staying close to a faithful local church.

Is God’s love reckless?

No, God’s love is not reckless. His love is holy, purposeful, and wise, because God does not act in confusion or folly, but in perfect wisdom and steadfast mercy, “For God is not a God of disorder but of peace” and “He works all things according to the counsel of His will” (1 Corinthians 14:33; Ephesians 1:11).

The Bible shows God’s love as covenant love, not careless emotion: “The LORD, the LORD God, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). His love is not reckless because the cross was not a rash impulse, but a deliberate saving plan, where Christ “was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge” and died for sinners, then rose bodily from the dead (Acts 2:23-24; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

If by “reckless” you mean that God’s love pursues sinners who do not deserve it, that part is true in a wonderful sense, because His grace is astonishing and relentless. But we should be careful not to call God foolish or unstable. His love is not reckless, it is sovereign, sacrificial, and perfectly wise.

Does the Bible teach that there is a gift of celibacy?

Yes, the Bible does teach that some people are given a special grace for celibacy, especially in the context of remaining unmarried for the sake of undivided devotion to the Lord. Jesus says, “not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given” and speaks of those who are “eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:11-12); Paul also says that he wishes all were as he is, yet “each has his own gift from God” (1 Corinthians 7:7; 1 Corinthians 7:32-35).

This is not a command for all believers, but a gift some receive for a particular calling, and it should be honored without making marriage seem lesser. Paul treats both marriage and singleness as good gifts from God, with different callings and different responsibilities, and the aim is holiness and faithful service to Christ.

What did it mean that Satan wanted to be like the Most High in Isaiah 14:14?

In Isaiah 14:14, “I will make myself like the Most High” means proud, rebellious self-exaltation, Satan’s desire to take God’s place in authority and glory, not merely to be “similar” to God. The context of Isaiah 14 is a taunt against the king of Babylon, but the language also fits the deeper reality of Satan’s pride and fall, which is consistent with passages like Ezekiel 28:12-17 and 1 Timothy 3:6.

The key issue is not innocence or imitation, but **usurpation**. “The Most High” is God’s supreme title, so Satan’s heart was to dethrone God, seize worship, and rule on his own terms. That is the essence of sin, pride set against the holiness and sovereignty of God.

This is a warning to us too, because the same pattern still tempts human hearts, self-rule instead of submission to God. The remedy is humility before Christ, who did not grasp at exaltation but humbled Himself and was exalted by the Father, Philippians 2:5-11.

What does the Bible say about the hornet?

The Bible mentions the hornet as an instrument God uses to drive out Israel’s enemies and prepare the land for His people, not as a random creature acting on its own. Key passages are Exodus 23:28, Deuteronomy 7:20, and Joshua 24:12.

In context, the hornet picture shows God’s sovereign power: He can use even small or feared creatures to accomplish His purposes. Whether the term refers to literal hornets, a swarm, or a divinely sent terror is debated, but the point is clear, God fights for His covenant people and gives victory by His hand. That fits the broader biblical theme of divine judgment and deliverance.

What were the key events in the life of Jesus Christ?

The key events in Jesus Christ’s life are His virgin conception by the Holy Spirit, His birth in Bethlehem, His baptism by John, His ministry of preaching, healing, teaching, and calling disciples, His transfiguration, His suffering and crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, His burial, His bodily resurrection on the third day, His appearances to the disciples, His ascension into heaven, and His promised return. These are the great gospel events by which God reveals the incarnate Son, our Savior, and Lord, and they are central to Christian faith, not just inspirational memories, but real acts of redemption, fulfillment, and victory over sin and death, as seen in Matthew 1:18-25, Luke 2:1-20, Matthew 3:13-17, Matthew 4:23-25, Matthew 17:1-8, Luke 23:33-56, Luke 24:1-12, Acts 1:1-11.

Do Christians need a day of rest?

Yes, Christians should practice regular rest and worship, though the New Testament does not bind believers to Old Covenant Sabbath-keeping as a covenant sign in the same way Israel was under Moses. The principle of one day set apart for rest and worship remains wise and biblical, and many Christians see the Lord’s Day, Sunday, as the fitting day for that pattern, while others differ on how strictly that should be applied.

The Old Testament Sabbath was a holy sign for Israel, grounded in creation and the covenant law, “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8-11). In the New Testament, believers are told not to be judged over a Sabbath regulation, because these things pointed to Christ, who gives the true rest of the soul (Colossians 2:16-17; Matthew 11:28-30; Hebrews 4:9-10). That means Christians are not saved by Sabbath-keeping, but by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

So the wise Christian response is to receive rest as a gift, set aside time for worship, prayer, and ceasing from ordinary labor, and guard against both legalism and laziness. A practical step would be to choose a weekly rhythm where you gather with your local church, worship, and intentionally rest in the Lord.

How can I be a good Christian?

To be a good Christian, begin with Christ Himself, not with self-improvement. A good Christian is one who has been saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, then learns to obey Him out of love, not to earn God’s favor, because “by grace you have been saved through faith” and “not by works” (Ephesians 2:8-10).

The heart of Christian life is this: repent of sin, trust in Jesus Christ who died for your sins and rose again bodily, and follow Him as Lord. Jesus said, “If anyone would come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me” (Matthew 16:24), and “If you love Me, you will keep My commandments” (John 14:15).

Practically, a good Christian:
- reads and obeys Scripture regularly, because God’s Word is your guide (2 Timothy 3:16-17),
- prays honestly and often,
- stays connected to a healthy local church,
- loves other believers,
- turns quickly from sin and seeks forgiveness,
- and grows in holiness by the Spirit’s help (Galatians 5:16-25).

Do not measure yourself by perfection, but by a growing pattern of repentance, faith, and obedience. “He who began a good work in you will continue to perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6).

What does the Bible say about lawsuits / suing?

The Bible does not forbid every civil lawsuit, but it strongly warns believers against rushing into court with fellow Christians, especially over ordinary disputes, and it calls us to pursue reconciliation and fairness first. Jesus taught, “If anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:40), and Paul rebuked Corinthian believers for taking one another before unbelievers instead of settling matters within the church (1 Corinthians 6:1-8).

The main New Testament principle is this: Christians should prefer brotherly reconciliation, wise mediation, and church discipline over litigation when possible. Paul’s concern in 1 Corinthians 6 is not that all courts are always unlawful, but that believers were shaming the church by turning minor, personal conflicts into public lawsuits before unbelieving judges. For a Christian, “why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?” is a hard but holy question (1 Corinthians 6:7).

At the same time, Scripture recognizes that governing authorities exist to punish wrongdoers and uphold justice (Romans 13:1-4). So if there is serious harm, criminal wrongdoing, abuse, fraud, or a matter that must be addressed for protection and justice, involving civil authorities can be appropriate. The issue is not “court ever” versus “court never,” but whether you are acting from love, justice, humility, and a desire for peace.

Practically, if you are facing a dispute, start by seeking direct reconciliation, prayer, wise counsel from mature believers, and, if needed, help from your church leaders. If you want, I can also help you think through a specific situation biblically.
What is kingdom now teaching?

“Kingdom now” teaching is the view that the promises of God’s kingdom are being realized in fullness or near-fullness in the present age, so that the church’s mission, spiritual authority, or even social transformation is treated as the present manifestation of the kingdom in a strong way. Scripture does teach that Christ’s kingdom has truly begun, but not yet in its final, visible, consummated form, because Jesus still says, “My kingdom is not of this world” and we still wait for His return and the renewal of all things, according to John 18:36; Acts 1:6-11.

The concern with some versions of “kingdom now” teaching is that they can blur the Bible’s already and not yet tension, sometimes overstating human authority, victory, or dominion in this age. The New Testament teaches that believers are citizens of the kingdom now, but we still groan, suffer, and hope for the future appearing of Christ and the final kingdom, as seen in Romans 8:18-25; 1 Corinthians 15:24-28; Philippians 3:20-21.

My view is that the kingdom is already inaugurated in Christ’s first coming, but it is not yet consummated until His return. That keeps us grounded in real present blessings, like new birth and Christ’s reign, while also guarding us from triumphalism and reminding us to live by faith, not by false claims of final victory before the King returns.

What is The Infinite Way?

“The Infinite Way” is a spiritual teaching movement founded by Joel S. Goldsmith in the mid-20th century. It teaches a kind of “New Thought” mysticism, emphasizing inner divine consciousness, healing through spiritual realization, and the idea that God is present within rather than salvation through Christ alone.

From a biblical Christian perspective, it is not orthodox Christianity, because it does not uphold the Bible’s teaching on the holiness of God, human sin, and the exclusive saving work of Jesus Christ, who said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6, BSB). Scripture teaches that we are reconciled to God not by awakening divine consciousness, but by grace through faith in Christ’s death and resurrection for our sins, “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, BSB).

Does God have favorites?

God shows no partiality in the sense of unjust favoritism, and yet He does choose and set His special love on His people by grace, not because they were better or more deserving. The Bible says, “God does not show favoritism” in His righteous judgment, while also teaching that He “has chosen us in Him before the foundation of the world” (Deuteronomy 10:17; Ephesians 1:4-5).

So the answer depends on what you mean by “favorites.” If you mean sinful preference, no, God is perfectly just and impartial (Romans 2:11). If you mean covenant love and gracious election, yes, God freely sets His saving love on His own people in Christ, and that is pure mercy, not unfairness (Romans 9:15-16).

This should humble us, not make us proud. None of us deserves God’s grace, but anyone who repents and trusts in Jesus Christ is welcomed by Him. How can I live a holy life?

A holy life begins with belonging to a holy God. Scripture says, “As He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do” (1 Peter 1:15-16), and true holiness flows from union with Christ, not mere rule-keeping.

The Bible teaches that we are made holy by God’s grace through faith in Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again, and then we grow in practical holiness by the Holy Spirit through repentance, Scripture, prayer, and obedience (1 Thessalonians 4:3; Romans 12:1-2; John 17:17).

Here is the path in plain terms:
- Trust Christ daily, because without Him we can do nothing of lasting spiritual good.
- Confess sin quickly and turn from it, since holiness and repentance belong together.
- Feed your mind with Scripture, because God’s Word renews and sanctifies.
- Pray for the Spirit’s help, especially where temptation is strong.
- Stay close to a faithful local church for worship, accountability, and the means of grace.
- Practice obedience in ordinary life, in speech, purity, honesty, forgiveness, and love.

Holiness is not sinless perfection in this life, but a real and growing conformity to Christ. “He who began a good work in you will continue to perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6).

One helpful next step is to choose one area of sin or weakness, bring it honestly before God today, and ask a mature Christian to help keep you accountable in it.

What is the sinner's prayer?

The “sinner’s prayer” is a simple prayer of repentance and faith where a person turns from sin and asks Jesus Christ to save them. It is not a magic formula, and the Bible does not present it as the thing that saves, rather, salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 10:9-10).

Scripture’s emphasis is that sinners must repent and believe the gospel, because all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day (Romans 3:23; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Mark 1:15). A prayer can express that faith, but the saving power is in Christ Himself, not in the exact words.

If you are asking because you want to come to Christ, turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for your forgiveness and new life. If you want, I can also show you what the Bible says about repentance and faith in a very simple way.
How can a Christian avoid being a doormat for other people?

A Christian avoids being a doormat by practicing meekness without surrendering truth, by loving others without enabling sin or abuse, and by learning to set wise, biblical boundaries. Jesus was gentle, but He was never spineless, and He often withdrew from hostile people when needed, because He did not entrust Himself to everyone (John 2:24-25; Matthew 10:16).

The Bible calls us to be kind and forgiving, but it also commands us to speak the truth in love and to guard our hearts (Ephesians 4:15; Proverbs 4:23). Jesus said, “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16). That means you do not have to answer every demand, absorb every insult, or keep giving access to people who repeatedly misuse your trust.

A few practical ways to do this:
- Learn to say “no” plainly and calmly without overexplaining.
- Set limits on time, money, emotional labor, and access.
- If someone is manipulative, ask for clarity and put their words back on them.
- In serious cases, step back and involve mature believers, elders, or authorities if there is abuse.
- Pray for courage and wisdom, then act on what is right, not what merely keeps the peace.

This is not selfishness. It is stewardship. You are a servant of Christ first, not a slave to human approval (Galatians 1:10). And when you are weak, remember that God does not call you to passivity, but to faithful, courageous love. If you want, I can help you think through a specific situation and suggest a Christ-honoring boundary.
What does it mean that the workers are few (Matthew 9:37)?

Jesus means that there are many people ready to hear and be gathered into God’s kingdom, but too few faithful messengers and shepherds to bring them the gospel, pray for them, and disciple them, as He says in Matthew 9:37-38. In the immediate context, He had compassion on the crowds because they were “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd,” so the problem was not lack of need, but lack of workers.

This is a call to pray for God to send laborers, and also a call for believers to be willing laborers themselves, because the harvest is the Lord’s and the work is urgent. If you want, I can also explain how Matthew 9:37 connects to evangelism and church ministry today.
What was the purpose of the Levitical Law?

The Levitical Law was given to reveal God’s holiness, expose human sin, govern Israel as His covenant people, and point forward to Christ, the true sacrifice and perfect High Priest, who fulfills the law on our behalf, Romans 3:19-20; Galatians 3:24; Hebrews 10:1-14.

In its immediate context, the law set Israel apart from the nations, teaching them how to live before a holy God in worship, justice, and purity, Leviticus 19:2. It also showed that sin brings guilt and that atonement is needed, especially through the sacrificial system, which anticipated the once-for-all work of Jesus, Hebrews 9:11-12.

So the law was never given as a ladder for sinners to climb into righteousness by their own effort. It functioned as a tutor, a mirror, and a shadow, driving us to Christ and showing our need for grace, Romans 7:7; Galatians 3:19-25.

What does the Bible say about confession of sin to a priest?

The Bible does not teach that Christians must confess sins to a priest in order to receive forgiveness. Scripture teaches that we confess our sins to God, and that Christ alone is our mediator, as in 1 John 1:9 and 1 Timothy 2:5.

A priestly system for absolving sin is not the New Testament pattern, because Jesus is our great High Priest and has already offered the sufficient sacrifice for sin, Hebrews 4:14-16; Hebrews 10:19-22. James 5:16 does encourage believers to confess sins to one another for prayer and accountability, but that is different from a sacramental confession required for forgiveness.

So the biblical pattern is this: confess your sin honestly to God, repent, trust in Christ’s finished work, and seek help from mature believers and your church for prayer and restoration. If you want, I can also show how Catholics and Protestants each argue from Scripture on this question.
Should Christians go to nightclubs? Is clubbing a sin?

Going to a nightclub is not automatically a sin, but for many Christians it is a place of strong temptation where sobriety, modesty, and wise self-control are often hard to maintain. Scripture calls believers to live wisely, avoid drunkenness and sexual immorality, and not let themselves be shaped by the world’s patterns, but to be transformed by renewing the mind, Romans 12:1-2; Ephesians 5:15-18; 1 Corinthians 6:18-20.

The question is usually not, “Is the building itself sinful?” but, “Will this setting help me love Christ and walk in holiness?” A nightclub often centers on drunkenness, lust, sensual dancing, and worldly conformity, so for many Christians the wise answer is to avoid it, Proverbs 4:14-15; 1 Thessalonians 5:6-8.

If a Christian goes, they should be able to do so with a clear conscience before God, without compromising holiness, and without putting themselves in a place where sin is likely to flourish, 1 Corinthians 10:23-24, 31; Romans 14:23. My pastoral counsel is to ask, “Can I be there as salt and light without being pulled into sin?” If the honest answer is no, then it is better to stay away.

If clubbing has become part of a sinful pattern in your life, the call is not merely to manage it, but to repent and turn to Christ, who died and rose again to forgive sinners and give new life, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 1 John 1:9. Does the statue outside the United Nations have any connection to the beast of the end times?

Christians should be cautious about assigning prophetic meaning to every modern statue or international symbol, because Scripture does not tell us to read end-times prophecy through speculation, but through the text itself, especially Daniel, Matthew 24, 2 Thessalonians 2, and Revelation 13.

The statue outside the United Nations is not identified in the Bible as “the beast,” and there is no clear biblical basis to say it is a direct fulfillment. Revelation 13 describes a beastly world power and a false prophet who leads people into idolatry and deception, while 2 Thessalonians 2 speaks of the man of lawlessness exalting himself against God. Those are real future realities, but the Bible does not give us warrant to label a particular statue as that fulfillment unless the text clearly fits.

A wise Christian approach is to avoid sensationalism and stay grounded in Scripture, because many things throughout history have been wrongly declared the final sign. If you are interested, I can help you compare the statue to the actual biblical descriptions in Revelation 13 and Daniel 7.
What is the sign of Jonah?

The “sign of Jonah” is Jesus’ reference to Jonah’s three days in the fish as a picture of His own burial and resurrection, and also Jonah’s preaching to a sinful generation as a warning of coming judgment. Jesus says, “For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” in Matthew 12:40, and He rebukes those who wanted a spectacle instead of believing His word in Matthew 12:39; Matthew 16:4.

In context, the sign is not a vague miracle request, but the decisive proof of Jesus’ identity, especially His death, burial, and bodily resurrection. Jonah was a real prophet, and his experience pointed forward to Christ in a typological way, which is a historic Christian reading of Scripture.

The lesson is sobering: if people reject Christ after the clearest sign has been given, they remain accountable. Jonah’s preaching led Nineveh to repentance, but Jesus is greater than Jonah, and His resurrection calls you to repent and trust in Him for forgiveness and life.

What does it mean to walk worthy?

To “walk worthy” means to live in a way that matches the calling you have received from Christ, showing a life that fits the Gospel. Paul uses that phrase in Ephesians 4:1, and he connects it to humility, gentleness, patience, and love, and in Colossians 1:10 he says it includes bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God.

It does not mean earning God’s favor, because we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, but it does mean that genuine faith produces a transformed life, a sanctified life that increasingly reflects Christ. A simple way to apply this is to ask, “Does my speech, choices, and attitude look like someone who belongs to Jesus?” and then bring one area into obedience today.

What is a divine appointment?

A divine appointment is an event, meeting, or opportunity that God has sovereignly arranged for a purpose, often to encourage, correct, warn, or lead someone to Christ. The idea fits passages like Proverbs 16:9, “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps,” and Acts 8:26-39, where God directed Philip to the Ethiopian eunuch at exactly the right time.

In the Bible, these moments are never random, they are part of God’s providence. A divine appointment may be as simple as a conversation, a chance encounter, or an interruption that becomes a means of grace.

Practically, you can treat unexpected opportunities with prayerful attention, asking, “Lord, how do You want me to love, speak, or serve here?” If you want, I can also show you a few biblical examples of divine appointments.
What is the Qur’an?

The Qur’an is the central sacred text of Islam, regarded by Muslims as the word of God revealed to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over about 23 years. Christians should understand it respectfully as an important religious text, while also remembering that it is not the inspired Word of God in the biblical sense, because the Bible alone is God-breathed and final for faith and practice, 2 Timothy 3:16-17.

Historically, it is written in Arabic and organized into 114 chapters called surahs, covering theology, law, morality, prayer, and stories of earlier figures such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Muslims deeply revere it, but its teaching differs sharply from Scripture on key doctrines like the Trinity, the deity of Christ, and the saving work of the cross.

What would have happened “if the Lord had not been on our side” (Psalm 124:2)?

Psalm 124:2 means that without the Lord’s protection, Israel would have been utterly overwhelmed by their enemies. The psalm immediately explains it: they would have been swallowed alive, swept away like water, and trapped like prey in a hunter’s snare, because human strength alone could not have saved them.

This is a testimony to God’s providence, not merely ancient luck. The people of God survive because the Lord is for them, as Psalm 124:8 says, “Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.” That same truth reaches us today: apart from God’s mercy, we are helpless in sin, but in Christ we have a stronger deliverance, because Jesus has conquered sin and death through His cross and resurrection.

What did Jesus mean when He said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to get into heaven?

Jesus meant that riches can be a profound spiritual obstacle because they tempt people to trust in wealth instead of God, so that humanly speaking it is impossible for a rich person to save himself, but not impossible for God. He explains this right after the disciples are astonished, saying, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:23-26; Mark 10:23-27; Luke 18:24-27).

In the immediate context, a rich young ruler walked away from Jesus because he loved his possessions more than Christ, and Jesus exposed the deeper issue, not that money is automatically evil, but that the heart can be enslaved by treasure. Scripture warns, “You cannot serve God and money” (Matthew 6:24), and “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10).

So the warning is not, “No rich person can be saved,” but, “No one is saved by wealth, status, or self-reliance.” Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. If you have riches, the right response is humble repentance, open hands, generosity, and trust in Christ rather than in what you own.

How do we decide which books belong in the Bible since the Bible does not say which books belong in the Bible?

We recognize the books of the Bible by God’s providence, not by giving the church authority over God’s Word. Scripture itself shows that God’s word is recognized as His word, for example when Jesus says, “Scripture cannot be broken” in John 10:35, and when He affirms the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms as the written testimony about Him in Luke 24:44.

The church did not create the canon, it received it. The main tests used historically were apostolic origin or prophetic authority, consistency with the rest of Scripture, and widespread recognition among God’s people, but those are marks of recognition, not the final basis of authority. The deeper answer is that the Holy Spirit bears witness to the voice of God in Scripture, so believers receive the books God inspired rather than voting them into authority, just as “the sheep hear His voice” in John 10:27.

So while the Bible does not contain a single table of contents verse, it does give us enough to trust that God has spoken, and the church can discern which writings are truly His Word by their divine qualities and apostolic connection. A helpful next step is to read 2 Peter 1:19-21 and 2 Timothy 3:16-17, then pray for humility and clarity as you study how the canon was recognized.
What does it mean to walk by the Spirit (Galatians 5:16)?

To walk by the Spirit means to live each day under the Holy Spirit’s leading, relying on His power rather than the desires of the flesh, so that your life increasingly bears the fruit of holiness. In Galatians 5:16-25, Paul contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit, showing that Spirit-led living is the path of progressive sanctification.

In context, Paul is not talking about a mystical feeling, but an ongoing pattern of obedience shaped by the Spirit through God’s Word. The Spirit does not lead us away from Scripture, but into greater conformity to Christ, producing love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control, against which there is no law (Galatians 5:22-23).

Practically, walking by the Spirit means:
- setting your mind on God’s truth each day,
- confessing sin quickly,
- depending on the Spirit in prayer,
- and choosing obedience in concrete situations, especially when the flesh pulls the other way.

A simple way to begin is to read Galatians 5 slowly, ask God to expose one area of the flesh, and then obey Him in that specific area today.

What does the Bible mean when it says "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'"?

Psalm 14:1 says, “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” In its context, this is not mainly a statement about intelligence, but about moral rebellion, a settled refusal to acknowledge God’s rule. The psalm goes on to describe corruption and sin flowing from that inward denial, because when a person excludes God, they also reject His authority and holiness.

The “heart” in Scripture is the inner person, the seat of thought, desire, and will. So this is not just an argument with the lips, but a posture of life, living as if God does not see, judge, or matter. Proverbs 1:7 says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge,” and Romans 1:21-22 shows that people can suppress the truth about God even when they know enough to be accountable.

This does not mean every honest struggler or doubter is a “fool” in the same sense. The Bible is condemning proud, stubborn unbelief, not humble questions asked in search of truth. The warning is serious, but it is also merciful, because it calls us to repent of self-rule and turn to the living God.

If this verse is pressing on your conscience, a good next step is to read Psalm 14 slowly alongside Romans 1:18-25 and ask God to show you where you may be resisting Him. And if you want, I can also explain how this verse applies to atheism, doubt, or self-sufficiency today.
What is onanism? Is onanism a sin?

Onanism originally refers to the sin of Onan in Genesis 38:9-10, where he refused his duty to provide offspring for his deceased brother and deliberately spilled his seed on the ground. In the Bible, the issue is not merely the physical act, but his rebellious refusal to obey God and his selfishness before the Lord.

Yes, onanism is sin in the biblical sense of Onan’s act, because Genesis says, “what he did was evil in the sight of the LORD, and He put him to death also” Genesis 38:10. The broader principle is that God condemns sexual immorality and selfish misuse of sexuality, and He calls us to holiness, not self-indulgence, in 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5 and 1 Corinthians 6:18-20.

If you mean masturbation by “onanism,” Scripture does not directly use that word, but it does call believers to flee lust, impurity, and sexual sin. The question, then, is not only “Is it technically named in a verse?” but “Does this honor God with my body?” 1 Corinthians 6:19-20.

If this is personal for you, bring it honestly to the Lord in repentance and ask Him to renew your mind, help you turn from lust, and walk in purity. If you want, I can also explain the Genesis passage and how Christians have understood it.
Is Israel and the church the same thing? Does God still have a plan for Israel?

Israel and the church are not exactly the same thing, and yes, God still has a real plan for ethnic Israel. The New Testament shows both distinction and continuity, and faithful Christians differ on the details of how the promises to Israel are fulfilled.

The strongest case for distinction is that Paul speaks of Israel and the church as related but not identical, and he says, “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” regarding Israel in Romans 11:28-29; Romans 11:25-26 also speaks of a future mercy toward Israel. At the same time, the church is made up of Jews and Gentiles united in Christ by faith, the true people of God in the new covenant, as seen in Ephesians 2:11-22 and Galatians 3:28-29.

So I would say this: God has not abandoned Israel, and He will keep every promise He intends to keep. Some Christians believe the Old Testament promises to Israel are fulfilled in the church in a spiritual or expanded sense, while others believe there remains a future national turning of ethnic Israel to Christ, and Romans 11 gives strong reason for that hope. My own view is that Paul teaches a future mercy for Israel, while the church already shares in the blessings of the Messiah through faith.

The key issue is this, both Jews and Gentiles are saved the same way, by grace alone through faith alone in Jesus Christ alone, who died for sins and rose bodily from the dead. If you want, I can also show you how Romans 9 to 11, Ephesians 2, and the promises to Abraham fit together.
Are Catholic beliefs and practices biblical?

Some Catholic beliefs are biblical and shared by all orthodox Christians, but several distinctively Catholic doctrines and practices are not clearly taught in Scripture and are therefore not binding on Christians. Scripture is the final authority, so we test every tradition by God’s Word, not the other way around, as in Acts 17:11 and 2 Timothy 3:16-17.

At the core, Catholics affirm many essential truths: the Trinity, Christ’s deity and humanity, the virgin birth, the cross, and the resurrection. But there are significant differences on issues like the authority of the pope, Mary’s sinlessness and assumption, prayers to saints, indulgences, and the Mass as a repeated sacrifice. From a biblical Protestant view, those teachings go beyond, or sometimes conflict with, the plain teaching of Scripture, especially texts like 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 9:25-28, and Colossians 2:18-19.

So the careful answer is, not everything in Catholicism is unbiblical, but not everything in Catholicism is biblical either. A true Christian should hold fast to the Gospel of justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, because we are saved by Christ’s finished work, not by sacramental works or human merit, as taught in Ephesians 2:8-9 and Romans 3:28.

What should we learn from the tribe of Simeon?

The tribe of Simeon teaches us that sin has consequences, but God’s mercy still reaches repentant people. Simeon was one of the sons of Jacob, yet his tribe is often remembered for instability, violence, and eventual fading within Israel, which warns us that unfaithfulness can lead to real loss, even among God’s covenant people, Genesis 49:5-7; Numbers 25:14-15.

At the same time, Simeon reminds us that God does not cast off every sinner who turns to Him. Their inheritance was folded within Judah’s territory, showing both judgment and providence, Joshua 19:1-9. That points us to the greater hope of the Gospel, because in Christ there is forgiveness, a new name, and a secure inheritance for all who repent and believe, Ephesians 1:11-14.

So the lesson is: do not treat sin lightly, but do not despair if you have failed. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again for our salvation, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

What is the hypostatic union?

The hypostatic union is the biblical truth that Jesus Christ is one Person, the eternal Son of God, with two complete natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion, change, division, or separation. The Son did not stop being God when He became man, and He did not merely appear human, but truly took on human nature in the virgin birth and lived among us, as John 1:1, John 1:14, and Colossians 2:9 teach.

This matters because only One who is fully God and fully man can be the perfect mediator and Savior, since He can reveal God to us and also bear our sin in our place, as 1 Timothy 2:5 and Hebrews 2:14-17 show. In practical terms, this means your hope rests not in a mere teacher or prophet, but in the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, who can truly save to the uttermost.

Doubting God — how can I overcome doubt in my relationship with God?

Doubt can be painful, but it does not mean God has abandoned you. The Bible shows that faith often grows through honest struggle, like the man who cried, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” in Mark 9:24.

You overcome doubt by bringing it into the light of God’s Word, prayer, and the fellowship of believers, not by pretending it is not there. Scripture says, “So then faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” in Romans 10:17, and God invites His people to draw near with confidence because Christ is our merciful High Priest, in Hebrews 4:14-16.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.

Did God create other people in addition to Adam and Eve?

Yes. The Bible presents Adam and Eve as the first human pair, but it also shows that God gave them children and that humanity spread from them, so all other people descend from Adam and Eve, not from a separate creation of other humans (Genesis 1:27-28; Genesis 4:1, 25; Acts 17:26).

A key biblical point is that all humans share one common origin, which matters for the doctrine of sin, since “sin entered the world through one man” and death through sin, and also for the gospel, because Christ is the last Adam who saves those who trust in Him (Romans 5:12-19; 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49).

What does the Bible say about self-discipline?

The Bible teaches that self-discipline is a fruit of the Spirit and a mark of mature Christian growth, not mere self-improvement. It is the Spirit-enabled ability to govern our desires, thoughts, words, and actions under the lordship of Christ, with passages like 2 Timothy 1:7, Galatians 5:22-23, and 1 Corinthians 9:24-27 showing that disciplined living is part of the Christian life.

Scripture presents self-discipline as practical holiness. Proverbs warns that a person without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls, vulnerable and exposed, while Peter calls believers to “make every effort” to add self-control to their faith and other virtues, because growth in godliness is intentional (Proverbs 25:28; 2 Peter 1:5-8).

It is also connected to spiritual warfare and endurance. Paul speaks of training like an athlete, disciplining his body so that he will not be disqualified, and he tells Titus that God’s grace trains us to deny ungodliness and live uprightly in this present age (1 Corinthians 9:24-27; Titus 2:11-12). In other words, grace does not make us passive, it teaches us to say no to sin and yes to righteousness.

Practically, this means Christians should build habits that help them obey Christ, such as regular prayer, Scripture reading, wise limits on temptations, and accountability in a local church. What is original sin?

Original sin is the inherited fallen condition and guilt that all people receive from Adam, so that we are born inclined toward sin and in need of God’s grace. Scripture teaches that “through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and in this way death came to all men, because all sinned” (Romans 5:12), and that we are “by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3).

In Adam, humanity fell into real rebellion, not merely bad habits, and this is why every person is born spiritually dead and unable to save himself. This doctrine helps explain why we do not merely commit sins, but are sinners by nature, which is why we need regeneration, justification, and new birth in Christ.

The good news is that where Adam brought ruin, Christ brings life, because “as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). If you want, I can also explain how original sin relates to personal guilt, free will, or infant salvation in historic Christian teaching.
Are intrusive thoughts sin? Are spontaneous violent, sexual, or blasphemous thoughts sin?

Intrusive thoughts are not automatically sin, because temptation or a sinful thought can come uninvited before you choose to dwell on it, consent to it, or act on it. Jesus was tempted in every way yet without sin, and Scripture shows that sin involves the heart’s agreement and pursuit, not merely the sudden appearance of a thought, as in Matthew 4:1-11; James 1:14-15.

Spontaneous violent, sexual, or blasphemous thoughts are deeply unsettling, but the mere intrusion of them is not the same as choosing them. The Bible warns us that sinful desire, entertained lust, hatred, or irreverence are real sins of the heart, but unwanted thoughts that you hate and resist should not be treated as if you have committed the same sin simply by experiencing them, as in Matthew 5:27-28; 1 John 3:15; Psalm 19:12.

What matters is what you do with the thought, do you reject it, confess it, and turn to Christ, or do you nurse it and make it yours? Take every thought captive to obey Christ, and if a thought comes, answer it quickly with truth from Scripture and prayer, as in 2 Corinthians 10:5; Philippians 4:8.

If these thoughts are frequent, distressing, or feel uncontrollable, speak with a trusted pastor or mature believer, and if they are tied to anxiety or compulsions, consider also a qualified mental health professional, since many believers need help with both conscience and body. Pray honestly to the Lord about the fear and shame, and ask Him to renew your mind and give you peace in Christ, as in Romans 12:2; Hebrews 4:15-16.

Book of 1 Corinthians - Bible Survey

1 Corinthians is Paul’s inspired letter to a troubled church in Corinth, written to correct divisions, sexual immorality, confusion about worship, and errors about the resurrection. Its main theme is that Christ crucified shapes the holiness, unity, and order of the church, because “we preach Christ crucified” and “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23-24).

Paul wrote to believers who were gifted but immature, reminding them that the church is God’s temple and that their bodies belong to the Lord, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; 1 Corinthians 6:19-20). He answers questions about marriage, meat offered to idols, spiritual gifts, the Lord’s Supper, love, and the resurrection, showing how the gospel governs both doctrine and daily life.

The clearest practical takeaway is this: a healthy church is not one that merely has gifts, knowledge, or freedom, but one that is governed by the cross of Christ in love, purity, humility, and hope. If you want, I can also give you a chapter-by-chapter outline of 1 Corinthians.
How do I identify my spiritual gift?

A good way to identify your spiritual gift is to look for where the Lord is already bearing fruit through you, then confirm it through Scripture, prayer, and the counsel of mature believers. Spiritual gifts are given by the Holy Spirit for the common good, so they are meant to edify the church, not merely to express personality (1 Corinthians 12:4-7; 1 Peter 4:10).

Start by serving faithfully in ordinary ways, because gifts are often recognized in motion, not in isolation. Ask, “Where do I see unusual burden, joy, effectiveness, and blessing from others?” and then test that with the body of Christ, since “by their fruit” we know what is genuine (Matthew 7:16; Romans 12:4-8).

A simple process is:
- Pray for wisdom and willingness to serve, not for status.
- Read the main gift passages: Romans 12:3-8; 1 Corinthians 12:4-11; Ephesians 4:11-13; 1 Peter 4:10-11.

What is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Colossians 1:24)?

Nothing is lacking in Christ’s atoning suffering for our salvation, because His sacrifice was once for all and fully sufficient, but in Colossians 1:24 Paul is speaking of the remaining sufferings that Christ’s body, the church, must endure as the gospel is carried forward. In that sense, what is “lacking” is not redemption, but the appointed share of afflictions that believers, united to Christ, still experience for the sake of His body, the church.

Paul says, “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions, for the sake of His body, which is the church” (Colossians 1:24). How can I get my prayers answered by God?

What is the more excellent way (1 Corinthians 12:31)?

What is the open heaven concept?

The phrase “open heaven” is not a single technical doctrine in Scripture, but it usually refers to a season or moment of special divine revelation, blessing, or access to God’s presence, as seen in passages like Genesis 28:12-17, Ezekiel 1:1, Matthew 3:16, and Acts 7:55-56.

In the Bible, an “open heaven” can mean God granting unusual revelation or confirming His work, but it does not mean humans can control God’s presence like a formula. Jacob saw the ladder, Ezekiel saw visions, Jesus was baptized and the heavens were opened, and Stephen saw the glory of God, all of which show God sovereignly revealing Himself, not people unlocking Him by technique.

So, biblically speaking, the idea is best understood as God’s gracious self-disclosure and nearness, not a guarantee of constant extraordinary experiences. What is the origin of baptism?

Baptism did not begin with the church as a human invention, but the Bible shows its roots in God’s saving work and in the ministry of John the Baptist, who called Israel to repentance in preparation for the Messiah. John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance, and Jesus later commanded His disciples to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, giving baptism its full New Covenant meaning. Matthew 3:1-6; Matthew 28:19-20.

Historically, baptism also fits the Bible’s larger cleansing pattern, where water symbolized purification, judgment, and new life, as in the flood, the Red Sea, and Old Covenant washings. In the New Testament, baptism becomes the outward sign that points to union with Christ in His death and resurrection, burial of the old life, and walking in newness of life, a beautiful picture of regeneration and discipleship. Romans 6:3-4; Colossians 2:12.

What is historical criticism?

Historical criticism is a method of studying the Bible that asks how a text was formed, what its original historical setting was, and what sources, editors, or traditions may stand behind it. In its modern form, it often treats the biblical text like any other ancient document, sometimes approaching it with skepticism about supernatural events.

Christians can value careful historical and literary study, because Scripture was written in real history to real people, but we should not let any method sit above the Bible itself. The Bible is God’s inspired Word, and it interprets history truthfully, not merely as human religious reflection, so historical study must be servant to Scripture, not judge over it, 2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21.

In practice, historical criticism includes things like source criticism, form criticism, and redaction criticism. These can sometimes help with background questions, but they become dangerous when they deny the plain claims of Scripture, such as prophecy, miracles, or the resurrection of Jesus, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

Matthew is careful here: the birth of Christ fulfills both names, because in Jesus, God truly came near to save His people from their sins. What is the lust of the eyes?

The lust of the eyes is the sinful desire to covet, crave, or obsess over what you see, especially things God has not given you. Scripture warns that “the lust of the eyes” is one of the chief ways temptation works, alongside “the lust of the flesh” and “the pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

Eve saw that the fruit was “desirable” and took it (Genesis 3:6), Achan saw what was forbidden and coveted it (Joshua 7:21), and David saw Bathsheba and sinned (2 Samuel 11:2-4).

What is the Hindu caste system?

The Hindu caste system is a traditional social hierarchy in South Asian society that divided people into hereditary groups, with one’s birth often determining occupation, social status, and marriage prospects. What does the Bible say about rest and relaxation?

The Bible teaches that rest is good, gift-like, and necessary, but it is rest under God, not escape from Him. God Himself rested after creation, and He commands His people to rest, trust, and worship, not merely to keep working endlessly (Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:8-11).

There are at least three clear biblical themes here. First, physical rest is part of wise stewardship of our bodies and limits, as seen in the Sabbath principle and in Jesus inviting the weary to come to Him for rest (Exodus 23:12; Matthew 11:28-30). Second, true rest is deeper than a nap or vacation, because our souls rest in Christ, who gives peace with God through His finished work, the cross, burial, and bodily resurrection, received by grace through faith alone (Hebrews 4:9-10; Romans 5:1; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Third, rest should lead us back into faithful obedience, not laziness or self-indulgence, because Scripture warns against sloth while also commending peace and contentment (Proverbs 6:6-11; 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12).

So yes, relaxation can be a good and God-honoring gift when it is thankful, moderate, and restorative. Malachi 2:16 means that God strongly opposes covenant-breaking in marriage, because marriage is meant to be a faithful, lifelong union before Him, not something discarded lightly. In context, Israelite men were treacherously divorcing their wives and covering their sin with religious language, so God is condemning the violence and unfaithfulness behind that hardness of heart, not celebrating divorce as morally neutral, and Jesus later confirms marriage’s seriousness in Matthew 19:3-9.

How transparent should church finances be?

Church finances should be **open, orderly, and accountable**, because Scripture consistently treats stewardship as something done before God and with integrity before people, not hidden in secrecy. A healthy church should let its members know how money is received and spent, with wise safeguards for privacy where needed, especially in matters like staff compensation, giving records, or sensitive counseling support.

The Bible praises faithfulness in handling money and warns against even the appearance of wrongdoing: “For we are taking pains to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men” (2 Corinthians 8:20-21). That principle fits church finances well. Elders are stewards, not owners, and should model trustworthy oversight (1 Peter 5:2-3). Congregations should also be able to see whether giving is being used for gospel ministry, mercy, missions, and ordinary needs in a way that matches the church’s stated priorities (Acts 4:34-35; Philippians 4:15-18).

At minimum, a church should usually provide:
- regular budget reports,
- annual income and expense summaries,
- clear categories for major spending,
- approval and oversight processes,
- independent review or an outside audit when feasible,
- and a clear policy for handling designated gifts.

Transparency does not mean publicizing every private detail to everyone. Wise confidentiality can protect people, but it should never become a cover for mismanagement. If leaders refuse ordinary accountability, that is a serious warning sign.

A practical next step is to ask your church leaders for the budget, financial policy, and reporting schedule, and then evaluate whether the church is honoring both **good stewardship** and **2 Corinthians 8:21**.

Is it wise for Christian teens to be dating?

Dating is not commanded or forbidden in Scripture, so it is a matter of wisdom, maturity, and purpose rather than a universal rule. For Christian teens, it can be unwise if it is mainly driven by romance, emotional dependency, or temptation, but it can be appropriate if it is ordered toward purity, accountability, and honoring Christ.

It also teaches that our relationships should help us walk wisely, not pull us into sin, because “bad company corrupts good character” (1 Corinthians 15:33). A wise approach is to ask whether both teens are mature enough to keep clear boundaries, whether their parents or guardians are involved, whether the relationship has a serious and God-honoring purpose, and whether they would be comfortable bringing it into the light before Christ. Why does God allow us to go through trials and tribulations?

God allows trials and tribulations to refine His people, expose what we truly trust, and produce perseverance, maturity, and hope. Scripture says, “the testing of your faith produces perseverance” and that this can lead us to be “mature and complete, not lacking anything” (James 1:2-4; Romans 5:3-5).

The Bible also shows that suffering is not random for the believer. God uses it to discipline us in fatherly love, to make us share in Christ’s holiness, to wean us from self-reliance, and to deepen our comfort so we can comfort others (Hebrews 12:5-11; 2 Corinthians 1:3-5). In all of it, He is not absent. He is near to the brokenhearted, and He promises to work even hard things for the good of those who love Him (Psalm 34:18; Romans 8:28).

At the center of this is Jesus Himself. The sinless Son of God suffered, died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. That means our pain is never proof that God has abandoned us, because Christ has already walked the path of suffering and conquered sin and death. Salvation is not earned by enduring trials, but received by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

What day is the Sabbath, Saturday or Sunday?

The Sabbath in the Old Testament was the seventh day, Saturday, because God rested on the seventh day after creation and commanded Israel to keep that day holy. See Genesis 2:2-3 and Exodus 20:8-11.

The New Testament shows believers gathering on the first day of the week, Sunday, in celebration of Christ’s resurrection, but it does not command Christians to keep Sunday as the Sabbath in the same way Israel kept the seventh day. See Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2.

So, if you mean the biblical Sabbath command, it is Saturday. If you mean the Christian day of worship and resurrection celebration, many churches meet on Sunday.

Why did God punish Pharaoh for Abram’s lie (Genesis 12:17)?

God did not punish Pharaoh for Abram’s lie in a way that excuses Abram, but Genesis 12 shows that God intervened against Pharaoh’s house because Sarai was being taken, and because God was preserving the promise He had made to Abram. Abram’s deception was still sin, and the chapter quietly exposes it by showing that fear led him to compromise.

In context, Abram had left the land of promise and feared for his life, so he told Sarai to say she was his sister, which was a half-truth used to mislead. Pharaoh then took Sarai into his house, and “the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with severe plagues because of Abram’s wife Sarai” (Genesis 12:17, BSB). That does not mean Pharaoh was morally innocent in every sense, but the text places the immediate divine judgment on Pharaoh’s household because of the injustice done to Sarai, while Abram remains culpable for his deception.

This is one of Scripture’s honest moments, it does not flatter the patriarchs. Abram is still chosen by grace, yet he is still responsible for sin. That fits the broader biblical pattern: God’s covenant faithfulness is greater than human failure, and He preserves His purposes even when His people act badly.

The lesson is sobering and hopeful. Sobering, because lying and fear-driven compromise have real consequences. Hopeful, because God is merciful to sinners and keeps His promises despite our failures. What is Kemetic spirituality / Kemetism?

Kemetic spirituality, or Kemetism, is a modern revival or reconstruction of the ancient Egyptian religion, centered on the worship of the gods of ancient Egypt and on practices inspired by pharaonic culture. “Kemet” was the ancient name for Egypt, meaning “the black land,” and Kemetists typically seek to honor deities such as Ra, Osiris, Isis, and others through ritual, prayer, offerings, and reverence for ma’at, or cosmic order.

From a biblical Christian perspective, Kemetism is a form of idolatry, because the living God alone is worthy of worship, and He forbids the worship of created beings or false gods (Exodus 20:3-5; Isaiah 45:5). The Bible teaches that there is one God, and salvation is found only in Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose bodily from the dead, so the call to anyone in any religion is to repent and trust in Him alone for forgiveness and new life (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

What is the false cause fallacy?

The false cause fallacy is the mistake of assuming that because one thing happened after another, the first thing caused the second. In logic, it is often called “post hoc ergo propter hoc,” meaning “after this, therefore because of this.”

For example, if someone says, “I wore my lucky shirt and then my team won, so my shirt caused the win,” that is a false cause. The Bible warns us to be careful in judgment and not jump to conclusions without solid evidence, because “the first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him” (Proverbs 18:17).

In everyday life, this fallacy can show up when people blame a medicine, event, or policy for something just because it happened before the result. A wiser approach is to ask whether there is real evidence of causation, not just timing.

What does the Bible say about Christian fathers?

The Bible calls Christian fathers to lead their homes with loving, sober, Christ-like authority, to nurture their children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord, and to model faith in daily life. Fathers are not to provoke their children to anger, but to raise them with gentle firmness and spiritual care, as images of God’s own fatherly goodness, discipline, and mercy.

Colossians 3:21 adds, “Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged,” which shows that a father’s words and tone matter, not just his rules.

The Bible also presents fathers as teachers and examples. In the New Testament, fatherhood is meant to reflect the Fatherhood of God, who is holy and compassionate. What was the process of deciding on the Old Testament canon?

The Old Testament canon was not decided by a single late vote, but recognized over time by God’s covenant people as the Spirit-inspired Scriptures already given through His prophets. In other words, the church of Israel did not create the canon, it received it.

In the Old Testament itself, God’s written words were treated as authoritative from the start, and later books were measured by that standard, especially the Law of Moses and the prophetic writings (Deuteronomy 31:24-26; Joshua 1:7-8; Isaiah 8:20). The books were recognized because they came through divinely appointed prophets, were received by God’s people, and were consistent with the existing Word of God.

By the time of Jesus, the Jewish Scriptures were already broadly recognized as the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings. Jesus affirmed this threefold collection when He spoke of “the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44). He also treated those Scriptures as fully authoritative and unbreakable (Matthew 5:17-18; John 10:35).

So the process was really one of recognition, not invention. The key marks were prophetic authorship, covenantal use among God’s people, doctrinal consistency, and long-standing reception. Christians believe this canon was providentially preserved by God, and the New Testament confirms the authority of the Old Testament as Scripture.
