Do unbelievers immediately go to hell when they die?

The Bible teaches that when unbelievers die, they immediately enter a state of conscious judgment and separation from God, often called Hades or Sheol, and they await the final resurrection and final judgment, after which they will be cast into the lake of fire. Jesus’ parable of the rich man and Lazarus shows immediate conscious torment after death for the unbelieving man, and Hebrews says, “It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Luke 16:19-31; Hebrews 9:27).

So, in a careful Christian sense, they do not yet experience the final hell at the moment of death, but they do go immediately into terrible punishment apart from Christ, awaiting the last judgment. The final state is described in Revelation 20:11-15 as the lake of fire, which is the second death.

How did Satan and other angels sin if heaven is sinless?

Heaven is sinless because God is perfectly holy, but angels were created moral beings, not robots, so they were able to obey or rebel. What is a Bible Baptist Church, and what do Bible Baptists believe?

A Bible Baptist Church is a Baptist church that emphasizes the Bible as its final authority and usually holds to believer’s baptism, local church autonomy, and a simple, Scripture-centered ministry. Bible Baptists are not a separate denomination in the same way as, say, Roman Catholicism, but rather a stream within Baptist life that aims to be governed by Scripture alone.

In general, Bible Baptists believe the core Christian doctrines: the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, His virgin birth, His sinless life, His substitutionary death, His bodily resurrection, salvation by grace through faith alone, and Christ’s return and final judgment. They also usually affirm baptism only for professing believers, congregational church government, the Lord’s Supper as an ordinance of the church, and a strong emphasis on evangelism and personal holiness, with 2 Timothy 3:16-17 and Matthew 28:19-20 often serving as key texts.

There is some variety among Bible Baptist churches on secondary matters such as end-times views, church style, and spiritual gifts, so not every Bible Baptist church will look exactly the same. If you want, I can also explain how Bible Baptists differ from Southern Baptists, Independent Baptists, or Reformed Baptists.
What is sexual ethics?

Sexual ethics is the moral teaching about how God calls people to use their bodies, desires, and relationships in purity and love. In the Bible, sexual intimacy is reserved for the covenant of marriage between one man and one woman, and anything outside that pattern is sin, even though God offers forgiveness and new life through Jesus Christ.

Scripture presents sex as a good gift with a holy purpose, not as something to define on our own terms. “Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4), and God’s will is “your sanctification: that you should abstain from sexual immorality” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Jesus also taught that sexual sin flows from the heart and must be taken seriously (Matthew 5:27-28).

If you’re asking because of personal struggle or confusion, the Christian answer is not shame but repentance and grace: turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again for forgiveness and new life. What is spiritual sickness? What does it mean to be spiritually sick?

Spiritual sickness is the condition of the soul under sin, when a person is separated from God, dulled to His truth, and in need of His healing grace. In Scripture, this is not merely weakness, but a real moral and spiritual corruption that affects the heart, mind, and will, as seen in passages like Isaiah 1:5-6 and Mark 2:17.

To be spiritually sick means to be wounded by sin, unable to fix yourself, and needing the Great Physician, Jesus Christ, who came not for the self-righteous but for sinners: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). The Bible teaches that sin brings death and separation from God, but Christ came to save, forgive, and make us whole through His cross and resurrection, which is why the proper response is repentance and faith in Him alone.

If you mean this in a personal way, the hopeful answer is that God does not merely expose our sickness, He heals it. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died for our sins and rose again for your salvation. What makes you ask about spiritual sickness?
What is fellowship with God?

Fellowship with God is a real, living relationship of shared communion with Him through Jesus Christ, by the Holy Spirit, where we walk in the light, know His love, and enjoy His presence. Scripture says, “our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ” and that “if we walk in the light, as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another” (1 John 1:3; 1 John 1:7).

It means more than religious activity. It includes being reconciled to God by grace through faith, having our sins forgiven by Christ’s blood, and then growing in daily communion with Him through prayer, His Word, obedience, and repentance. This is the fruit of justification and sanctification, not the basis of our acceptance before God.

A simple way to think of it: fellowship with God is “with God,” not merely “about God.” It is enjoyed because Christ has opened the way for sinners through His atoning death and bodily resurrection.

What does Jesus mean when He says, “Verily, verily” or “Truly, truly,” in the gospels?

When Jesus says “Verily, verily” or “Truly, truly,” He is emphasizing that what follows is especially solemn and certain, like saying, “I am telling you the truth with full authority.” In the Gospels, this often introduces a weighty declaration about God, salvation, or His own identity, as in John 3:3 and John 5:19.

In the original setting, this double affirmation is not casual speech. It marks Jesus’ words as utterly trustworthy and calls the hearer to pay close attention, because the Son of God is speaking with divine authority, not merely offering opinion. That fits the Gospel of John’s repeated emphasis on Jesus as the Word made flesh, and it supports the truth of His deity and authority.

A helpful way to read it is: “Listen carefully, this is certain.” If you want, I can also show you a few of the most important “truly, truly” sayings and what each one means.
What should we learn from the tribe of Asher?

The tribe of Asher teaches us God’s faithfulness to bless His people, even when their place in history seems quiet, and it warns us not to let comfort replace wholehearted devotion to God. Jacob said Asher would have “rich food” and “royal delicacies” (Genesis 49:20), Moses said Asher would be “most blessed of sons” and “dip his foot in oil” (Deuteronomy 33:24), yet Asher’s later story reminds us that material blessing can coexist with spiritual compromise.

A few lessons stand out:

- **God keeps His promises.** Asher received a good inheritance in the land, showing that the Lord is faithful to bless as He wills, according to His covenant purpose.
- **Comfort can become a danger.** Asher settled in a fertile region, but Joshua 19 and Judges 1 show that Israel often failed to drive out the Canaanites fully, a reminder that ease can dull zeal.
- **Quiet faithfulness matters.** Asher is not one of the most prominent tribes, but God still recorded them, counted them, and used them. In Scripture, hidden service is never wasted.
- **Blessing is meant to lead to obedience.** The true aim of God’s gifts is not self-satisfaction but worship and holiness.

If you are asking personally, the application is simple: thank God for every mercy, and ask Him to keep your heart from settling for comfort when He calls you to faithfulness. You might meditate on Deuteronomy 33:24-25 and pray that the Lord would make you spiritually fruitful, not merely outwardly comfortable.

Why does the Bible speak against braided hair?

The Bible is not forbidding every braid or hairstyle. In 1 Timothy 2:9 and 1 Peter 3:3, the warning is against ornate, attention-seeking display, especially in a context of vanity and luxury, not against simple grooming or all braided hair.

In the first-century world, elaborate hairstyles and costly adornment could signal pride, sensuality, and social status. Paul and Peter are urging modesty, humility, and a beauty that comes from godly character, not outward show, which is why 1 Peter 3:4 contrasts outward adornment with “the hidden person of the heart.” This is a matter of modesty and Christian testimony, not a blanket ban on braids.

So the principle is: do not use your appearance to boast or distract, but let your life reflect Christ. A helpful question to ask is, “Am I dressing and styling myself to honor God and serve others, or to draw attention to myself?”

What is the difference between a covenant and a contract?

A contract is a mutual agreement between parties, usually based on exchange, terms, and legal enforcement; a covenant is a binding relationship sworn with promises, often sealed by oath, and in the Bible it is usually initiated by a greater party and rooted in faithfulness rather than mere exchange.

In Scripture, a covenant is much deeper than a business deal. God makes covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel, David, and finally the new covenant in Christ, where He binds Himself to save, bless, and keep His people by grace (Genesis 9:9-17; Genesis 15:18; Exodus 24:7-8; 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6-13). A contract can be broken when terms are missed, but a covenant emphasizes personal loyalty, solemn commitment, and relationship.

The clearest Christian hope is that God keeps His covenant by sending Jesus, who fulfills the law, bears sin on the cross, rises bodily from the dead, and secures forgiveness for all who repent and trust in Him alone. If Jesus was God, why did He say "No one is good but God alone"?

Jesus was not denying His deity there, He was exposing the man’s shallow use of the word “good” and pressing him to think carefully about who Jesus is. In the context of Mark 10:17-18, the man called Jesus “Good Teacher,” and Jesus answered, “Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone,” which confronts the man with the implication: if Jesus is truly good in the absolute sense, then He is claiming a goodness that belongs to God alone.

The Bible elsewhere clearly teaches that Jesus is fully God, yet truly man, without sin, and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. For example, John 1:1, John 1:14, Colossians 2:9, and Hebrews 4:15 show both His deity and His sinlessness. So this statement is not a denial of the Trinity or the hypostatic union, but a challenge to the rich young ruler, forcing him to ask whether he really recognizes Jesus for who He is.

In other words, Jesus was not saying, “I am not good,” but “Do you understand what you are saying when you call Me good?” That is a searching question for all of us. If you are willing, I can also walk you through the passage in Mark 10 verse by verse.
What does it mean that God will reveal the hidden things (Daniel 2:22 and 28)?

In Daniel 2:22 and 28, it means that God knows what human beings cannot know on their own, and He can disclose hidden realities, including the king’s dream and its meaning, because He is the God who reveals mysteries. Daniel says, “He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him” and “there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries” (Daniel 2:22; Daniel 2:28).

In context, this is not just about secret information, but about God’s sovereignty over history, kings, and kingdoms. Babylon’s wise men could not uncover the dream, but the Lord showed Daniel so that Nebuchadnezzar would know the Most High rules over all. That points us to God’s omniscience, His providence, and His power to make known what He wills.

For believers, the comfort is that nothing is hidden from God, and He is able to bring truth to light in His time. If this passage is stirring your heart, a good next step is to read Daniel 2 slowly and pray for humility, asking God to make His truth clear through His Word.
What items should be included in a church constitution?

A church constitution should clearly state the church’s doctrine, membership, leadership, ordinances, discipline, meetings, finances, and how the document can be amended. In other words, it should protect the church’s life together so everything is done decently and in order, as Scripture calls us to do, “for God is not a God of disorder, but of peace” and “all things should be done in a proper and orderly manner” (1 Corinthians 14:33; 1 Corinthians 14:40).

Common items to include are:

- Name and purpose of the church
- Statement of faith, especially the core doctrines of the gospel
- Membership requirements, admission, and removal
- Church authority and governance, such as elder-led, congregational, or other biblical structure
- Qualifications and duties of pastors, elders, deacons, and officers
- Ordinances, meaning baptism and the Lord’s Supper
- Church discipline and restoration process, based on passages like Matthew 18:15–17
- Meetings of the church, including member meetings and voting procedures
- Selection, removal, and terms of leaders
- Finances, stewardship, and approval of budgets or spending
- Property ownership and legal matters
- Conflict resolution within the church
- Amendment process for the constitution
- Dissolution clause, if the church ever closes

A good constitution should not replace Scripture, but serve Scripture by making the church’s convictions and procedures clear. Since the church is the household of God, order matters for peace, accountability, and faithful witness (1 Timothy 3:15).

What is topical preaching? Should a pastor preach topically?

Topical preaching is when the preacher chooses a subject, then gathers and explains Scripture passages related to that subject. It can be very helpful when it is done carefully and under the authority of the text, not by forcing verses to say what they do not say.

A pastor should preach topically at times, because Scripture itself addresses many themes across many books, and that can help a congregation see the whole counsel of God, but he should not make topical sermons his main diet if it means regularly drifting away from careful, expository preaching of the Bible in context. Paul’s charge to preach the word and the example of teaching through whole passages point us toward exposition as the normal pattern, while topical messages can serve as occasional, useful applications or doctrinal studies, Acts 20:27; 2 Timothy 4:2; Nehemiah 8:8.

The best topical preaching is still Bible-bound: one theme, many texts, and each text handled honestly in its own context. Poor topical preaching can become proof-texting, where verses are stitched together to support a favorite idea rather than letting Scripture govern the sermon.

If you are thinking as a church member, a healthy pattern is usually a steady diet of expository preaching with occasional topical series on doctrines or practical issues, like prayer, suffering, marriage, or stewardship.
What are tribulation saints?

Tribulation saints are people who come to faith in Jesus Christ during the future period of tribulation, after the church has been gathered and before Christ returns in glory. The clearest biblical picture is of believers who are saved during intense end-time persecution, many of whom are martyred for refusing the beast and remaining faithful to Jesus, as seen in Revelation 7:9-14; Revelation 13:7-10; Revelation 20:4.

Christians who hold a premillennial, pretribulational reading of Revelation usually use that term for those believers, while other faithful Christians may understand the tribulation passages differently. My view is that the phrase is a helpful biblical shorthand for those who are converted during that final time of trial, because Revelation plainly shows saints present in that period and standing before God by the blood of the Lamb.

Who are the Black Hebrews / Black Israelites?

“Black Hebrews” or “Black Israelites” usually refers to a range of groups, some of which are culturally or religiously Jewish-adjacent, and some of which are more accurately called Hebrew Israelite movements. They are diverse, but many claim that Black people are the true descendants of the ancient Israelites.

It is important to distinguish them from biblical Israel in the text of Scripture. The Bible teaches that ethnic Israel was chosen by God in history, but membership in God’s covenant people is ultimately fulfilled in Christ, so that Jews and Gentiles are reconciled together through faith in Jesus, not by ethnicity alone, “There is neither Jew nor Greek... for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:13-16).

Historically, some Black Hebrew identity movements arose among Black Americans in response to slavery, racism, and a search for dignity and heritage. That pain is real and understandable. But when these movements deny the deity of Christ, the Trinity, or salvation by grace through faith, they depart from historic Christianity. The true hope for any people group is not a new ethnic claim, but the Gospel: all have sinned, Christ died for our sins and rose again, and forgiveness is offered to all who repent and trust in Him (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 3:23-24).

What does the Bible say about church-hopping?

The Bible does not use the phrase “church-hopping,” but it clearly calls believers to committed fellowship, shepherding, and accountable membership in a local church, not a consumer mindset that keeps drifting from one body to another, **Hebrews 10:24-25; Acts 2:42; Hebrews 13:17**.

Christians may sometimes change churches for good reasons, such as moving, doctrinal error, serious sin in leadership, or a healthy search for a faithful congregation, but a pattern of leaving whenever preferences are unmet often reflects immaturity and hinders growth in **sanctification** and service, **Ephesians 4:11-16; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27**.

If you are considering a change, talk honestly with your current elders or pastors, pray for humility, and seek a church where the Word is preached, the ordinances are rightly observed, and you can lovingly submit and serve.
Dance in worship - what does the Bible say?

The Bible shows that dance can appear as an expression of joyful worship, but it does not command dance as a required part of gathered church worship. In Scripture, dancing is associated with celebration before the Lord, such as Miriam after the Red Sea (Exodus 15:20), David before the ark (2 Samuel 6:14), and praise language that includes dancing in the Psalms (Psalm 149:3; Psalm 150:4).

At the same time, New Testament worship is emphasized more through Word-centered gathering, prayer, singing, thanksgiving, and orderly edification, not through a prescribed dance practice (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19; 1 Corinthians 14:26, 40). So dance is a matter of Christian liberty, but it should never distract from reverence, modesty, and the aim of building up the church.

A wise guiding principle is this: if dance is used, it should be fitting, modest, orderly, and clearly serving worship rather than performance. If you want, I can also help you think through whether dance is appropriate in a local church service or in personal worship.
What is secular humanism?

Secular humanism is a worldview that says human reason, ethics, and meaning can be grounded without reference to God or divine revelation, and that human beings are the highest source of moral authority. In practice, it tends to place confidence in science, autonomy, and human progress while rejecting the Bible’s claim that God is Creator and final judge.

Christians would say it is a serious rival to biblical faith because Scripture teaches that true wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, not autonomous self-rule, and that apart from God we are morally lost, not morally self-sufficient, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" Proverbs 1:7; "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'" Psalm 14:1. The Bible also teaches that human beings bear God’s image and have real dignity, but that dignity does not make us our own savior or standard of truth, for "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" Romans 3:23.

Christians have understood this as a serious prophecy, though faithful believers differ on questions of timing and whether it had an initial fulfillment in history or awaits fuller fulfillment. What is not in doubt is that Scripture teaches God judges proud nations and cities, and His word does not fail.

What does it mean to watch and pray?

To “watch and pray” means to stay spiritually alert and dependent on God, especially in temptation and trial. Jesus said this to His disciples in the garden: “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak” (Matthew 26:41).

In context, “watch” means to be awake, sober-minded, and ready for what is coming, not drifting spiritually or assuming you are strong enough on your own. “Pray” means to bring your weakness to God, asking for help, protection, wisdom, and perseverance. Together, the command calls us to vigilance and prayerful dependence, which is part of sanctification, the Spirit’s ongoing work in believers.

This applies very practically: watch for places, habits, or relationships that expose you to temptation, and pray before, during, and after those moments. If you’re facing a specific struggle, tell God plainly about it and ask a trusted mature believer or your local church to pray with you, since “the prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5:16).

How is eternity in Hell a fair punishment for sin?

Hell is fair because sin is not measured only by the outward act, but by the holy God against whom it is committed. Scripture teaches that God is perfectly holy and just, and that our sin deserves real judgment, not because God is harsh, but because He is righteous, and evil must be answered, not ignored, Romans 3:23-26; Revelation 20:11-15.

A few truths help here. First, the seriousness of an offense is tied in part to the one offended. To sin against the infinitely holy Creator is not a small thing. Second, Hell is not a random overreaction, but God’s just and final sentence on unrepentant sin, Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:8-9. Third, the Bible presents Hell as the terrifyingly deserved outcome of refusing God’s mercy, not as a mistake in God’s character.

At the same time, the heart of the Gospel is that God has provided a way of escape. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4. His cross is the place where God’s justice and mercy meet, Romans 3:25-26. Whoever repents and trusts in Christ is forgiven and receives eternal life, John 3:16, 18.

So yes, Hell is fair in light of God’s holiness and our sin, but the wonder is that mercy is offered in Christ. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life. If you want, I can also explain why “eternal” punishment fits the nature of sin and God’s justice.
How is Satan god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4)?

In 2 Corinthians 4:4, Satan is called “the god of this age” because, by God’s allowance, he exercises real but limited influence over fallen humanity, especially by blinding unbelievers to the gospel of Christ. This does not mean Satan is equal to the true God, but that he is the ruler of a rebellious world system under God’s sovereign control, as seen also in John 12:31 and Ephesians 2:2.

Paul’s point is that Satan’s power is mainly deceptive and spiritual, not ultimate. He darkens minds so people “cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4), which is why salvation requires God to shine light into the heart by grace.

The phrase fits the Bible’s larger teaching that the whole world lies in the power of the evil one in its fallen condition (1 John 5:19), yet Satan is still a creature on a leash, not a rival deity. Christ has already triumphed over him through the cross and resurrection, and one day Satan will be fully judged and removed forever.

Is faith intellectual assent?

No. In Scripture, faith includes intellectual assent, but it is more than that, it is personal trust in Christ, a resting in Him alone for salvation. Even demons have correct beliefs about God, yet they do not trust or submit to Him, which is why James says, “You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that and shudder” (James 2:19).

The Bible presents saving faith as receiving and resting on Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again, not merely agreeing that those facts are true (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; John 1:12). So faith has knowledge, agreement, and reliance, but the heart of it is trust in Christ as Lord and Savior.

What does it mean to be saved by grace?

To be saved by grace means that God gives sinners forgiveness, new life, and eternal salvation as an undeserved gift, not because we have earned it. The Bible says, “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Grace means God’s favor toward the guilty, not the reward of the deserving. We are all sinners and spiritually unable to save ourselves, but Christ came, lived a sinless life, died on the cross for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is therefore by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.

This also means you cannot add your good works to make yourself right with God. Good works matter as the fruit of salvation, not the root of it, because “we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

What is the kalam cosmological argument for the existence of God?

The kalam cosmological argument is a philosophical argument for God that says, first, whatever begins to exist has a cause; second, the universe began to exist; therefore, the universe has a cause.

Christians often use it to point to the biblical Creator, because Scripture teaches that God made all things and existed before the universe, as in Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1-3. The argument does not by itself prove the Trinity or the gospel, but it can help show that the universe is not self-existent and that a transcendent, personal cause is reasonable.

Its usual form is:
1. Whatever begins to exist has a cause.
2. The universe began to exist.
3. Therefore, the universe has a cause.

Why is the virgin birth so important?

The virgin birth is important because it shows that Jesus is truly God’s Son, conceived by the Holy Spirit, not by human initiative, and it confirms both His sinless humanity and the miracle of the incarnation, where the eternal Son took on flesh (Luke 1:34-35; Matthew 1:18-23).

It matters because if Jesus were merely another man, He could not be the holy Savior we need. But Scripture presents Him as the promised Messiah, born of a woman, yet without the stain of Adamic sin, fully able to save sinners by His life, death, and resurrection, the heart of the Gospel (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

This doctrine also protects the truth of the Trinity and the deity of Christ: the Father sent the Son, the Holy Spirit conceived His human nature, and the Son truly became man without ceasing to be God. That is why the virgin birth is not a minor detail, but part of the wonder of the incarnation (John 1:14; Matthew 1:20).

How can I overcome disappointment with life?

Disappointment with life is heavy, and God does not ask you to pretend it is not real. He invites you to bring your grief honestly to Him, because He is near to the brokenhearted, and He is able to meet you there (Psalm 34:18; Matthew 11:28).

The first thing to remember is that this world is fallen, so disappointment is not a sign that God has failed, but that sin has touched everything. We long for what is good, lasting, and satisfying, yet apart from Christ we will always find life too small to bear the weight of our hopes. Scripture says, “the world is passing away” (1 John 2:17), and it also says God is working for His children’s good, even through painful things (Romans 8:28).

Then open Psalm 42 or Psalm 73 and read slowly, asking the Lord to show you where your heart has been looking for life apart from Him. Often disappointment grows when we place ultimate hopes on career, relationships, comfort, or success, rather than on Christ Himself.

The Gospel is our anchor here: you and I are sinners who need more than advice, we need a Savior. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, lived the perfect life we have not lived, died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. By grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, God forgives, reconciles, and gives a living hope that does not disappoint (Romans 5:1-5; 1 Peter 1:3). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

What is the Gemara?

The Gemara is the rabbinic commentary and discussion on the Mishnah, and together they form the core of the Talmud. It records later Jewish debates, explanations, and applications of the Mishnah’s laws.

Historically, the Mishnah is the earlier written collection of oral Jewish law, and the Gemara is the expansive analysis built around it, mainly from Jewish scholars in Palestine and Babylon. The word itself comes from an Aramaic root meaning “to complete” or “study.”

From a Christian perspective, it matters because it shows how post-Temple Judaism interpreted the law, but it is not Scripture and does not carry the authority of the inspired Word of God, which is the Bible (2 Timothy 3:16-17). How can I stop being a people-pleaser?

People-pleasing is a real snare, because it often means fearing people more than God, and Scripture says, “The fear of man is a snare” (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not becoming harsh or indifferent, but learning to seek the approval of Christ above the approval of others, because “If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

What is the golden chain of salvation?

The “golden chain of salvation” is Paul’s summary in Romans 8:29-30 of God’s saving work from beginning to end, showing that those God foreknew He predestined, called, justified, and glorified, all in an unbroken line of grace.

Romans 8:29-30 says, “For those God foreknew He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son... And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.” The point is not that human effort creates salvation, but that God sovereignly saves His people and brings them safely to the end.

In historic Christian theology, this supports the doctrines of election, effectual calling, justification by faith, and the perseverance of the saints. It is a comfort to believers: if God began your salvation, He will finish it, for “He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

Should Mark 16:9-20 be in the Bible?

Mark 16:9-20 is not in the earliest and strongest Greek manuscripts, so many faithful Christians conclude it was not originally part of Mark’s Gospel. At the same time, it has long been received in much of the church, and even those who question its originality usually note that its content largely echoes truths taught elsewhere in Scripture, such as the resurrection, the Great Commission, and the reality of signs accompanying the apostles’ witness, Matthew 28:18-20; Acts 1:8.

The best argument for including it is that the passage has an ancient and widespread ecclesial history, and some early Christians clearly treated it as part of Mark. The best argument against treating it as original is that the earliest manuscript evidence and the style/transition of the passage strongly suggest it was added later.

My view is that Mark 16:9-20 should be read with caution as a probable later ending, not used to build a doctrine that is not already taught clearly elsewhere. Christian faith does not stand or fall on this text, because the resurrection of Christ is firmly established in the rest of the New Testament, 1 Corinthians 15:3-8.
What is the difference between a sect and a cult?

A **sect** is usually a religious subgroup that has separated from a larger body, often over doctrine or practice, while a **cult** is typically a group that departs from historic Christian truth in a controlling, deceptive, or spiritually dangerous way. In Christian terms, a sect may still remain within the boundaries of orthodox faith, but a cult denies or distorts core doctrines like the Trinity, the deity of Christ, salvation by grace through faith, or the authority of Scripture.

Historically, “sect” can simply mean a distinct faction or movement, and the New Testament even uses the idea of “sects” for groups like the Pharisees and Sadducees in Acts 5:17; Acts 15:5. “Cult,” on the other hand, is not a formal biblical category, but Christians commonly use it for groups that reject the gospel and replace Christ’s lordship with false teaching and spiritual manipulation, such as “another gospel” in Galatians 1:8-9.

A simple way to remember it is this: a **sect** is a division, while a **cult** is a distortion. If you want, I can also give you a short Christian checklist for telling them apart biblically.
Is "name it claim it" teaching biblical?

No, “name it and claim it” teaching is not biblical. It turns faith into a technique for getting wealth, health, or success on demand, but Scripture teaches that God is sovereign, our requests must be submitted to His will, and believers are often called to suffering, not guaranteed earthly prosperity (James 4:13-15; Matthew 16:24; 1 Peter 4:12-13).

The best argument from its supporters is that God does answer prayer and delights to give good gifts to His children, so they emphasize passages about asking in faith and receiving from the Father (Matthew 7:7-11; Mark 11:24). But those texts are not a blank check for whatever we desire, because biblical faith trusts God’s wisdom and timing, and Jesus Himself prayed, “not My will, but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42; 1 John 5:14-15).

The Bible calls us to pray boldly, but humbly, asking for what honors Christ and trusting God with the outcome. A better pattern is, “Lord, if it is Your will, provide, heal, and guide me,” while resting in His grace whether He says yes, no, or wait.

What does the Bible say about cryonics or cryogenics?

The Bible does not mention cryonics or cryogenics directly, so Christians should judge the idea by biblical teaching about life, death, and God’s sovereignty. Scripture teaches that death is appointed to man once, and after that comes judgment, while God alone has authority over life and resurrection, not human technology (Hebrews 9:27; Deuteronomy 32:39; John 11:25).

Cryonics, the attempt to preserve a body after legal death in hope of future revival, rests on a hope the Bible does not give us. The Christian hope is not suspended animation or a second medical chance, but the bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ and, in Him, the resurrection of His people at His appointed time (1 Corinthians 15:20-23; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). That means Christians should not treat cryonics as a source of salvation, immortality, or ultimate security.

If someone is asking whether it is sinful to explore it, the key question is motive and faith. If it is pursued with humble honesty as a medical experiment, that is one thing, but if it becomes an expression of unbelief, or a practical denial that our times are in God’s hands, it is spiritually dangerous (Psalm 31:15; James 4:13-15). Our hope is to trust Christ, who died for our sins and rose bodily from the dead, and to repent and believe in Him for eternal life.

Why is solo Christo important?

Solus Christus, “Christ alone,” is important because the Bible teaches that Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and sinners, the only sufficient Savior, and the only way of salvation. “For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5; John 14:6; Acts 4:12).

Sin has separated us from Him, and no priest, saint, ritual, or human effort can pay for guilt or earn justification, but Christ’s sinless life, atoning death, burial, and bodily resurrection fully accomplish what we could never do ourselves. “He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 2:2; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

So “Christ alone” protects the Gospel: salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works. Does Genesis chapter 1 literally mean 24 hour days?

Genesis 1 presents the creation days as real, numbered days with “evening” and “morning” language, which is why many Christians understand them to be ordinary 24-hour days. Genesis 1:5, Genesis 1:8, Genesis 1:13, Genesis 1:19, Genesis 1:23, Genesis 1:31.

A charitable historic Christian alternative is that the “days” could be read as a literary framework or another non-literal sequence, because the Hebrew word for “day” can sometimes be used more broadly and the sun is not appointed until day 4. Even so, I think the strongest plain reading of the text is that Moses intended real sequential days, since the repeated pattern, numbering, and “evening and morning” formula naturally point that way, and Exodus 20:11 grounds the work week in God’s creation week. Genesis 1:1-31; Exodus 20:8-11.

This is not a core gospel issue, so faithful Christians should handle it with humility and charity. What is the power of the Holy Spirit?

The power of the Holy Spirit is God’s own active power at work in and through His people to give life, convict of sin, reveal Christ, empower holiness, and equip the church for witness and service. The Spirit is not an impersonal force, but the third Person of the Trinity, fully God, who applies the saving work of Christ to us.

How is the word to be read and heard, that it may become effectual to salvation?

The Word must be heard and read with reverence, diligence, faith, and a teachable heart, because Scripture is God’s living speech and the Spirit uses it to bring sinners to salvation and saints to growth, for “faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17; 2 Timothy 3:15-17).

What is millennialism?

Millennialism is the Christian belief about the “millennium,” the 1,000-year reign of Christ mentioned in Revelation 20:1-6. Faithful Christians disagree on whether that reign is future, present, literal, or symbolic, so it is a secondary doctrine where charity is needed.

The main historic views are amillennialism, premillennialism, and postmillennialism. Amillennialists see the “thousand years” as a symbolic description of Christ reigning now from heaven; premillennialists believe Christ will return before a future earthly reign; postmillennialists believe the gospel will increasingly triumph in history before Christ returns.

I lean premillennial, because Revelation 19–20 reads most naturally as Christ’s return followed by the millennium, but godly believers hold the other views from Scripture and should not divide over this. What does the Bible say about war?

The Bible treats war as a grievous result of living in a fallen world, not as something good in itself, yet it also shows that governing authorities may bear the sword to restrain evil and punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:1-4). Scripture does not glorify violence, but it does acknowledge times when nations, judges, or kings acted in warfare under God’s providence, while calling God’s people to seek peace, justice, and mercy (Ecclesiastes 3:8; Psalm 46:9).

In the Old Testament, Israel sometimes fought wars as part of God’s unique covenant dealings with that nation, and those commands are not a simple blank check for all nations in all times. In the New Testament, Christians are called above all to be peacemakers, to love their enemies, and to overcome evil with good, even while living under earthly governments that may use force for justice (Matthew 5:9; Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:17-21).

So the Bible’s overall witness is this: war is a tragic sign of human sin, sometimes permitted in a fallen world by God’s providence, but never something to celebrate lightly. For Christians, the call is to pray for peace, support just and lawful restraint of evil, and remember that the final and lasting peace comes only through the Prince of Peace, Jesus Christ (Isaiah 9:6; John 14:27).

What did Paul mean when he said, “I die daily” in 1 Corinthians 15:31?

Paul means that he faced continual, repeated exposure to danger and suffering for the sake of Christ, as though he were always under sentence of death, and he was willing to keep going because the resurrection was true. This is not mainly about a mystical habit of self-denial, though Christians do “die to sin” in another sense, Romans 6:11. Here Paul is speaking about his apostolic life, full of hardship, persecution, and mortal danger for Christ’s name, 2 Corinthians 4:10-12; 2 Corinthians 11:23-28.

What does the Bible say about motivation?

The Bible teaches that the best motivation for a believer is the fear of the Lord, love for Christ, and gratitude for His grace, not self-exaltation or mere outward performance. Scripture says, “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23), and “The love of Christ compels us” (2 Corinthians 5:14).

In biblical terms, motivation is not just about feelings, it is about the heart. God looks beneath the surface to the inward person, and He calls us to serve from faith, love, and a clear conscience, not from hypocrisy or empty religion (1 Samuel 16:7; Matthew 15:8).

A few key biblical motives are:
- **The glory of God**: “So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).
- **Love for Christ**: “If you love Me, you will keep My commandments” (John 14:15).
- **Gratitude for salvation**: We obey because we have been saved by grace, not to earn it (Ephesians 2:8-10).
- **Fear of the Lord**: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10).
- **Hope of reward and perseverance**: God does see faithful labor, even when others do not (Hebrews 6:10; Colossians 3:24).

The Bible also warns against wrong motives, such as wanting human praise (Matthew 6:1-6), greed (1 Timothy 6:9-10), or pride (Philippians 2:3). Those motives distort the heart and eventually poison the work.

What does it mean to put off the old man (Ephesians 4:22)?

To “put off the old man” means to renounce the old way of life that belonged to your former, fallen self, the life shaped by sin, deceit, and the desires that ignore God. - turning from lying, bitterness, impurity, greed, anger, and corrupt speech in the surrounding context of Ephesians 4,

What is/isn’t a Christian married couple allowed to do, sexually?

Within marriage, the Bible presents sex as a good gift from God for covenant love, mutual delight, and protection against sexual immorality, so a Christian husband and wife are free to enjoy one another with holiness and mutual consent, not selfishness or exploitation. Outside the boundaries of marriage, and wherever sex becomes coercive, degrading, adultery, pornography-driven, or contrary to the one-flesh covenant, Scripture forbids it, because marriage is meant to reflect faithful love, not lust or domination, see Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4; 1 Corinthians 7:3-5; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5.

What is allowed:
- Mutual intimacy between husband and wife as a gift, including affectionate physical pleasure within marriage, Song of Solomon 1:2; Proverbs 5:18-19.
- Regular sexual relations when both spouses consent, because Paul says not to deprive one another except by agreement for a limited time, 1 Corinthians 7:3-5.
- Variety in affectionate expression and positions are not specifically regulated by Scripture, so Christian liberty applies where the Bible is silent, provided the act remains loving, mutually consensual, and not sinful.

What is not allowed:
- Anything involving force, manipulation, or treating your spouse as an object rather than a person made in God’s image, Ephesians 5:25-29.
- Adultery, pornography, lustful use of another person, or bringing a third party into the marriage bed, Matthew 5:27-28; Hebrews 13:4.
- Any sexual practice that is intrinsically degrading, abusive, or contrary to the holiness of marriage, 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5.

A simple biblical test is this: does it honor God, honor your spouse, stay within the marriage covenant, and preserve mutual love and consent? If not, it should be avoided.

What does the Bible say about self-defense?

The Bible does not give a single slogan on self-defense, but it does teach both the value of preserving life and the call to love our neighbor, so Christians must think carefully, not selfishly, about protection and restraint. In Exodus 22:2-3, there is recognition that a home defender acting in the dark against a thief is not treated the same as murder, while in Romans 13:1-4 God gives civil authority the sword to punish evil, showing that force can be legitimate in a fallen world.

At the same time, Jesus forbids personal vengeance and commands love for enemies, Matthew 5:39-44, and believers are told not to repay evil for evil, Romans 12:17-21. So self-defense is not the same as revenge, and any use of force must be governed by love of neighbor, necessity, and a desire to stop harm rather than to “get even.”

What was the significance of Jesus being dead for three days?

Jesus being dead for three days was significant because it fulfilled Scripture, confirmed that His death was real, and set the stage for His bodily resurrection on the third day. The Bible says He died, was buried, and rose again “on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Luke 24:46).

A few key meanings stand out:

- **It fulfilled God’s plan and prophecy.** Jesus pointed to Jonah as a sign, saying the Son of Man would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights (Matthew 12:40). The third day pattern also echoes Old Testament deliverance themes.
- **It proved His death was genuine.** He was not merely unconscious or seeming dead. He truly died, was buried, and then was raised bodily, which protects the truth of the gospel.
- **It magnified the resurrection.** By remaining dead through part of three days, His rising was unmistakably God’s triumph over death, not a quick escape from suffering. His resurrection declares victory, vindicates His claims, and secures our hope (Romans 1:4; 1 Peter 1:3).
- **It aligned with the biblical “third day” pattern.** In Scripture, God often brings deliverance on the third day, showing His power to save and restore.

For believers, this means Christ’s work is finished and trustworthy. His death was sufficient for our sins, and His resurrection means sin and death do not get the last word.

How does the preservation of the Qur’an compare to the preservation of the Bible?

The Bible and the Qur’an have both been preserved with remarkable textual transmission, but they are preserved in different ways and with different kinds of historical evidence. Christians believe the Bible’s preservation is especially trustworthy because God gave His Word through many authors over many centuries, and the manuscript record lets us compare copies to recover the original text with great confidence, while the Qur’an also has a strong early manuscript tradition but a more centralized standardization history.

For the Bible, the Old Testament was copied carefully by scribes, and the New Testament has a very large manuscript base, so variants can be identified and evaluated in context, with no core Christian doctrine hanging on a disputed text, because the faith rests on the clear witness of Scripture, such as 2 Timothy 3:16-17 and 1 Peter 1:24-25. For the Qur’an, Muslims commonly emphasize preservation through memorization and early standardization under Uthman, and that is a real strength in their tradition, but historically there were also competing readings and the Uthmanic text had to be imposed as the standard.

A fair comparison is this, the Bible’s text is preserved through a broad manuscript tradition spread across many communities, which makes reconstruction possible with high confidence, while the Qur’an’s text is preserved through early canonical control and recitation traditions. The “gospel of inclusion” usually means the claim that God fully accepts people regardless of repentance, faith in Christ, or obedience to Scripture, often by redefining sin or denying Christ’s exclusive saving work. That is not the biblical gospel, because the true gospel says all have sinned, Christ died for sinners, and salvation comes through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ alone, not by self-acceptance or human worthiness, see Romans 3:23-24; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; John 14:6; Acts 4:12.

The Bible does show real welcome to all kinds of people, Jew and Gentile, male and female, slave and free, because the church is a people gathered by grace from every nation, but inclusion in Christ comes through union with Him, not apart from Him, see Galatians 3:28; Revelation 7:9-10. So the Christian message is wide in invitation but narrow in the way of salvation.

If you’re asking because you’ve heard that phrase used in church or culture, I can help you compare it with the biblical gospel more carefully.
What did Paul mean by the “Holy Scriptures” in 2 Timothy 3:15?

In 2 Timothy 3:15, Paul means the Old Testament Scriptures, the sacred writings Timothy had known from childhood, which were able to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. In Paul’s setting, “the Holy Scriptures” refers first to Israel’s Scriptures, not the New Testament, because those writings were already in Timothy’s hands and were being fulfilled in Christ (2 Timothy 3:14-15; Luke 24:27).

That matters because Paul is not contrasting the Old Testament with the gospel, but showing that the Old Testament points to the gospel. The same Scriptures that reveal God’s holiness and human sin also prepare us for Christ, the promised Messiah, and for salvation by grace through faith alone.

If you want, I can also explain how this verse supports the doctrine of Scripture’s authority and inspiration.
Is the priesthood of all believers biblical?

Yes, the priesthood of all believers is biblical. The New Testament teaches that all who are in Christ are part of a royal priesthood, with direct access to God through Jesus, the one true Mediator, not through a separate saving priest class, see 1 Peter 2:5, 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6; Hebrews 4:14-16; 1 Timothy 2:5.

The best historic Christian argument for a narrower priesthood is that the New Testament still recognizes ordained ministers and church elders for teaching, shepherding, and guarding doctrine, but that is a ministry office, not a mediating priesthood that stands between believers and God. I believe the Bible clearly teaches both the universal priesthood of believers and distinct pastoral offices, because all Christians offer spiritual sacrifices and proclaim God’s excellencies, while church officers serve under Christ’s headship, not in His place.

Practically, this means you do not need any human priest to come to the Father, but you do need Christ, and you are also called to serve, intercede, and witness as one of His people.
Why is there a curse associated with hanging on a tree?

In the Bible, hanging on a tree is associated with a curse because it signified being under God’s judgment, and Deuteronomy 21:22-23 says a man hung on a tree was “cursed by God.” Paul applies that text to Jesus in Galatians 3:13, showing that Christ bore the curse our sins deserved.

In Israel’s law, exposure on a tree or wooden stake was a public sign of shame and divine judgment, not a random superstition. The deeper point is theological: sin brings a real curse before a holy God, and the cross reveals both God’s justice and His mercy, because Jesus took that curse in our place, a truth Christians call substitutionary atonement. Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24.

That means the cross was not only a tragic death, but the place where Jesus suffered for sinners so that all who repent and trust in Him are redeemed from the curse of the law. If you want, I can also explain how Paul connects Deuteronomy 21 and the crucifixion in Galatians 3 step by step.
How can we learn to trust God like the prophet Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:17-19)?

Habakkuk teaches us to trust God by moving from questioning to worship, even when circumstances do not improve. In Habakkuk 3:17-19, he names real loss, “though the fig tree should not blossom,” and yet says, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD,” because his confidence is not in comfort, but in “the God of my salvation.”

We learn that same trust by doing three things. First, bring your honest grief and confusion to God, as Habakkuk did earlier in the book, instead of pretending faith means never struggling. Second, anchor your heart in who God is, holy, sovereign, and faithful, not merely in what He gives or withholds. Third, choose worship and obedience in the midst of uncertainty, trusting that “the LORD God is my strength” (Habakkuk 3:19).

This is not stoic optimism. It is faith resting in God’s character and promises, which is what true perseverance looks like. For believers today, that means praying through disappointment, staying close to Scripture, and keeping fellowship with other Christians so your eyes are trained on God rather than on loss.

A good next step is to read Habakkuk 1 through 3 slowly this week, and turn each honest fear into prayer before God. If you want, I can also help you turn Habakkuk 3:17-19 into a short personal prayer of trust.
Why are we supposed to give thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18)?

Because God is good and sovereign, and in Christ He is working even through hard things for the good of His people. 1 Thessalonians 5:18 says, “Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus,” which means thankfulness is not denial of pain, but trust that our Father remains wise, present, and faithful.

The Bible does not say we thank God for evil as though evil were good. Instead, we thank Him in the middle of trials because He is still Lord over them, He uses affliction to refine faith, and He has already given the greatest gift, His Son. Romans 8:28 says God works all things together for good for those who love Him, and James 1:2-4 teaches that trials produce steadfastness. In Christ, we have forgiveness, adoption, and an inheritance that suffering cannot cancel.

So gratitude is an act of faith. It says, “My circumstances are real, but God is more real still.” A practical next step is to name one hard thing today and thank God specifically for one way He has been faithful in it, while also bringing your grief honestly to Him in prayer.

If you want, I can also explain how this verse fits with lament and honest sorrow in the Psalms.
Why did Jesus refer to the temple as “my Father’s house” (John 2:16)?

Jesus called the temple “my Father’s house” to show His unique Sonship and His authority over the temple, because the temple was the place where God’s name dwelt among His covenant people, not a marketplace. In John 2:16, He is not speaking merely as a devout Jew, but as the Son who has the right to cleanse His Father’s house, which points to His deity and messianic authority.

In the Old Testament, the temple was the place of God’s special presence among Israel, so Jesus’ words are deeply loaded with covenant meaning. By calling God “my Father” in this setting, Jesus clearly distinguished His relationship to the Father from that of everyone else, and the Jews understood the implication of this claim. The New Testament later shows that Jesus is greater than the temple itself and is the true meeting place between God and man, the fulfillment of the temple’s purpose (John 2:19–21; Matthew 12:6). This fits the truth of the hypostatic union, that Jesus is truly God and truly man.

A helpful next step is to read John 2:13–22 slowly and ask, “What does Jesus’ zeal for His Father’s house teach me about worship, reverence, and the holiness of God?”
What does the Bible say about child abuse?

The Bible condemns child abuse as evil. Children are a gift from God and must be protected, not harmed, and God warns that severe judgment awaits those who cause little ones to stumble or be harmed (Psalm 127:3; Matthew 18:6; Colossians 3:21).

Scripture also shows God’s special concern for the vulnerable, the fatherless, and the oppressed, and He calls His people to defend them and do justice, not abuse power over them (Psalm 10:17-18; Proverbs 31:8-9; James 1:27). Abuse is a grievous sin because it violates love, justice, and the image of God in the child.

If this question is personal or close to home, the first step is to get the child to safety and tell a trusted pastor, church elder, or local authorities right away. I do not provide legal or medical advice, but if there is immediate danger, call emergency services now.

If you want, I can also help you think through what Scripture says about reporting abuse, forgiveness, and boundaries.
What is Christianophobia?

Christianophobia is hostility, fear, prejudice, or discrimination against Christians because they are Christians. In practice, it can show up as mocking the faith, excluding believers, pressuring them to deny Christ, or even violence and legal restriction.

Christians should not be surprised when the world hates Christ and those who belong to Him, because Jesus said, “If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first” (John 15:18, BSB). At the same time, Christians are called to respond without hatred, “always ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you” with “gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15, BSB).

If you mean this in a personal way, I’m sorry if you’re experiencing real opposition. A wise next step is to stay close to Scripture, pray for courage, and seek support from a faithful local church.
How can I know that my future sins are forgiven?

If you are in Christ, your future sins are forgiven because Jesus’ sacrifice was once for all, fully sufficient, and His blood cleanses from all sin, not only the sins you already remember. “He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” and “by one offering He has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 9:12; Hebrews 10:14), and “the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

The ground of your forgiveness is not the strength of your repentance or the quality of your memory, but Christ’s finished work, His death for our sins and His bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That does not make future sin harmless, because sin still grieves the Holy Spirit and can bring painful discipline, but it does mean that a true believer’s standing before God rests on justification by faith alone in Christ alone, not on perfect performance.

So how can you know? By looking to Christ, not inward to your own changing condition. If you have repented and trusted in Him, then God’s promise stands: “Everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name” (Acts 10:43). If you are worried because you hate your sin and want to be clean before God, that concern itself is often evidence of His work in you.

A good next step is to confess any known sin directly to God today, thank Him for the cross, and ask Him to keep you walking in repentance and faith. If you want, I can also show you how 1 John helps a believer distinguish between real assurance and false security.
Book of Malachi - Bible Survey

Malachi is the final book of the Old Testament, a prophetic call for covenant faithfulness after the exile. It exposes the people’s and priests’ spiritual negligence, then points forward to the coming of the Lord and His messenger, preparing the way for Christ, the true and final fulfillment of God’s covenant promises.

The book opens with God’s covenant love, “I have loved you,” yet Israel doubts it, showing a cold, cynical heart after return from exile (Malachi 1:2). Malachi rebukes corrupt priests, empty worship, unfaithfulness in marriage, injustice, and robbery of God through withholding tithes, because true worship must be reverent, obedient, and sincere (Malachi 1:6-14; Malachi 2:13-16; Malachi 3:8-10).

A major theme is the contrast between superficial religion and genuine fear of the Lord. The faithful are remembered by God, and He promises a coming day of refinement and judgment, when the arrogant will be burned like stubble but those who fear His name will rise with healing and joy (Malachi 3:16-18; Malachi 4:1-3). This is covenant lawsuit language, showing that God is not indifferent to sin, but holy, just, and patient.

Malachi also looks ahead to John the Baptist and to Christ. God says He will send “My messenger” to prepare the way, and then “the Lord” will suddenly come to His temple (Malachi 3:1). He also promises Elijah before the great and terrible day of the Lord, which the New Testament connects to John the Baptist’s ministry (Malachi 4:5-6; Matthew 11:10-14). In this way, Malachi is a bridge book, ending the Old Testament with promise and warning, and preparing the way for the Messiah.

The closing command is deeply practical: “Remember the law of My servant Moses,” and “fear My name” (Malachi 4:4-6). The book calls God’s people to repent from half-hearted religion and return to covenant loyalty, which in the fullest sense is found in Jesus Christ, who cleanses His people, judges evil, and calls for true worship in spirit and truth.

What are phylacteries?

Phylacteries are small leather boxes containing Scripture passages, worn by some Jewish men during prayer, especially on the forehead and arm, in obedience to the command to keep God’s words before them. The Bible calls for this practice in principle in Deuteronomy 6:8 and Deuteronomy 11:18, and Jesus mentions phylacteries in Matthew 23:5, where He rebukes their use for show.

In Jewish life, they are called tefillin, and they symbolize devotion to God’s law with mind and action. Jesus’ warning matters because outward religion without a humble heart is hypocrisy, and God desires truth in the inward being, not merely visible devotion.

If you want, I can also explain how phylacteries are different from mezuzahs.
Who are true worshipers (John 4:23)?

True worshipers are those who worship the Father through Jesus Christ by the Spirit, in sincerity and truth, not merely by outward religion or location. In John 4:23, Jesus is teaching that real worship is centered on God’s revealed truth and comes from hearts made alive to Him.

In context, Jesus is speaking to the Samaritan woman about the coming shift from worship tied to Mount Gerizim or Jerusalem to worship grounded in God’s saving revelation in Christ, because “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” and “the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him” (John 4:23-24). “In spirit” points to inward, Spirit-enabled worship, not empty ritual, and “in truth” points to worship according to God’s self-revelation, ultimately fulfilled in Jesus, who is the truth.

So true worshipers are believers who, by the Holy Spirit, approach the Father through the Son, with hearts shaped by Scripture, repentance, faith, and reverence. A practical step is to ask whether your worship is merely external, or whether you are coming to God with a sincere heart submitted to His Word.

If you want, I can also explain how John 4:23 connects to Old Testament worship and New Covenant worship.
Book of Obadiah - Bible Survey

Obadiah is a short prophetic book that condemns Edom for pride, violence against Judah, and gloating over Jerusalem’s fall, while promising that the LORD will bring justice and restore His people. It is a vivid reminder that God opposes proud nations and faithful vengeance belongs to Him, not us.

Obadiah likely speaks into the aftermath of Jerusalem’s invasion, when Edom stood aloof or even aided Judah’s enemies, and the book announces that Edom’s own downfall is certain because “the pride of your heart has deceived you” (Obadiah 1:3). The central message is that the day of the LORD is near for the nations, but deliverance and kingdom belong to the LORD alone: “The kingdom will belong to the LORD” (Obadiah 1:21).

A simple outline is:
- Obadiah 1:1-9, Edom’s judgment announced
- Obadiah 1:10-14, Edom’s violence against Jacob exposed
- Obadiah 1:15-21, the day of the LORD and Zion’s restoration

The book’s theological themes are God’s justice, pride’s downfall, covenant faithfulness, and the certainty of divine judgment. It also teaches that God sees hidden sins like smugness and indifference, not only open brutality.

For believers, Obadiah calls us to humble repentance, not pride or vengeance. A good next step is to read Obadiah alongside Psalm 137 and Romans 12:19, asking the Lord to search any hidden pride and to deepen trust in His righteous judgment.
What does it mean to gain the whole world but lose your soul?

Jesus is warning that all the wealth, success, status, and pleasure in the world are worth nothing if a person forfeits eternal life with God. “What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?” means that temporary gain cannot compensate for eternal loss, because the soul is of greater value than every earthly possession (Mark 8:36-37).

In context, Jesus is calling people to deny self, take up the cross, and follow Him, because true life is found in Him, not in the world’s applause. This is a call to repent and believe the Gospel, because sin separates us from God, and only Christ’s death and bodily resurrection can save us and restore us to God (Mark 8:34-35; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

So the question is not just, “What can I achieve?” but, “Where will I stand before God?” Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died for sinners and rose again for our salvation. If you want, I can also explain how this applies to money, career, or relationships.
Why did God send the flood when He knew sin would continue after the flood?

God sent the flood because human evil had become devastatingly widespread and because He was acting in holy judgment, even though He knew Noah’s descendants would still be sinners, too (Genesis 6:5-7, 11-13). The flood did not “fix” the human heart, but it did reveal God’s hatred of sin, preserve the line through which Christ would come, and display both judgment and mercy as Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord (Genesis 6:8; Genesis 8:21; Genesis 9:1).

Scripture shows that the real problem is deeper than one event of cleansing, it is the heart of man. After the flood, God said, “the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21), which means the flood was never meant as the final cure for sin. It was a severe, righteous warning that sin leads to death, and a fresh beginning for a world still in need of grace.

This also points us forward to Christ. The flood is a picture of judgment, but the gospel is God’s true rescue: Jesus bore judgment for sinners on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day so that all who repent and trust in Him are forgiven and made new (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8-9). If you want, I can also show how the flood fits into the larger Bible storyline from Genesis to Christ.
Should a church tithe 10% of the offerings it receives?

Tithing 10 percent from a church’s offerings is not a clear New Testament command, so faithful Christians may differ on whether a local church should set that as a rule. A strong case for it is that regular, intentional giving helps a church practice generosity and support ministry in an orderly way, while the main opposing view is that the New Covenant emphasizes cheerful, proportional, and sacrificial giving rather than a fixed percentage (2 Corinthians 9:6-7; 1 Corinthians 16:1-2).

My view is that a church may choose to designate a portion of its income for mercy, missions, or broader kingdom work, but it should not present “10 percent of offerings” as a binding biblical law for all churches. The New Testament pattern is to give generously, willingly, and purposefully for gospel work and the care of the needy, with the church’s leaders stewarding resources faithfully (Acts 4:34-35; 1 Timothy 5:17-18).
