Easter Bible reading plan

Here is a simple Easter reading plan that leads you from Jesus’ suffering to His resurrection and living hope.

Read one passage each day during Holy Week:

- Sunday: Matthew 21:1-11, Jesus enters Jerusalem as King.
- Monday: Isaiah 53, the suffering Servant who bears our sins.
- Tuesday: Luke 22:14-46, the Last Supper and Jesus in Gethsemane.
- Wednesday: John 13:1-38, Jesus washes the disciples’ feet and gives His new commandment.
- Thursday: John 18:1-40, Jesus is arrested and brought before Pilate.
- Friday: John 19:1-42, Jesus is crucified and buried.
- Saturday: Matthew 27:57-66, the tomb is sealed, and hope waits in silence.
- Sunday: Matthew 28:1-20, Jesus rises bodily from the dead and sends His disciples.

If you want a shorter version, read these four key texts: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, John 19, and John 20.

As you read, look for Christ’s substitutionary atonement, His obedience, and His victory over sin and death, because the gospel is that Jesus died for sinners and rose again on the third day, 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

A good next step is to read one passage each day, then write down one truth about Jesus and one thing to thank God for. Would you like a version for children, a family plan, or a 3-day plan?
What is ignosticism? What is an ignostic?

Ignosticism is the view that the question “Does God exist?” cannot be answered meaningfully until we first define what we mean by “God.” An ignostic is someone who holds that position.

Christians agree that words matter, and Scripture itself speaks clearly about the living God, who is not an abstract idea but the Creator, holy and personal, revealed in Jesus Christ, “For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). From a biblical standpoint, the issue is not that God is undefined in Himself, but that sinful humanity often distorts or rejects His self-revelation.

If you want, I can also explain how ignosticism differs from atheism, agnosticism, and apatheism.
What does it mean that Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath?

Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath means He has authority over the Sabbath because He is the Son of Man and the divine Lawgiver who established it, so He defines its true purpose rather than being controlled by human rules about it. In context, He said this after defending His disciples from Pharisaic accusations, teaching that “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” and “The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27-28; Matthew 12:8).

This shows at least three things. First, the Sabbath was a gift of rest and mercy, not a burden of man-made legalism. Second, Jesus is claiming authority that belongs to God alone, which fits His deity. Third, He reveals that the Sabbath finds its fulfillment in Him, because true rest is finally found in Christ, who gives rest to the weary soul (Matthew 11:28-30; Hebrews 4:9-10).

Practically, this means we should honor the Lord’s design for rest, worship, and mercy, while avoiding rule-making that burdens consciences beyond Scripture. If you want, I can also explain how this relates to the Christian Lord’s Day and whether believers are still obligated to keep the Sabbath.
What does it mean that Jesus Christ conquered death?

It means that Jesus truly died, was buried, and then bodily rose from the dead, so death did not have the final word over Him. The Bible says, “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day” and that through His resurrection He “has destroyed death and brought life and immortality to light” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 2 Timothy 1:10).

In the Bible, death is more than a biological event, it is the result of sin and the judgment on humanity. Jesus, however, was sinless, so death had no rightful claim on Him. By His cross and resurrection, He defeated sin, Satan, and the grave, and His victory means that all who trust in Him will also be raised. This is the great hope of the Gospel, Christ’s triumph over death secures forgiveness of sins, justification, and eternal life for His people.

If you belong to Christ, His victory means your death is not the end, and even now you can face suffering and grief with hope. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose again for you, for the forgiveness of sins and new life. Would you like me to explain how His resurrection gives believers assurance today?
What are the books of the Bible? What does it mean that the Bible is composed of different books?

The Bible is a single, unified Word of God made up of 66 distinct books, written by many human authors over many centuries, yet breathed out by the Holy Spirit and centered on Christ. “All Scripture is God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16), and the Bible’s unity shows one saving story, from creation and fall to redemption and new creation.

When we say the Bible is composed of different books, we mean it is not one long continuous scroll of the same kind of writing. It includes law, history, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, Gospels, letters, and apocalyptic writing, each with its own audience, purpose, and style, while still carrying one divine message. For example, Genesis tells beginnings, Psalms give worshipful song and prayer, the Gospels tell the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus, and Romans explains justification by faith.

The 66 books are:
- Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi
- New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude, Revelation

A helpful way to read the Bible is to remember that each book must be understood in its own context, but never isolated from the whole. One practical step is to begin reading one Gospel, such as Luke, so you can see how all the earlier books point to Jesus.

If you want, I can also give you a simple overview of what each Bible book is about.
What is the creation mandate / cultural mandate?

The creation mandate, also called the cultural mandate, is God’s original commission to humanity in Genesis to be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and exercise godly dominion over creation under His authority (Genesis 1:26-28; Genesis 2:15). It means people are to cultivate the world, build societies, work, govern, create, and steward the earth for God’s glory, not as autonomous owners but as His image-bearers.

In Scripture, this is not a license to exploit creation, but a call to responsible stewardship, wisdom, and obedient rule. After the fall, this calling remains, though now it is carried out in a world marked by sin and frustration, and it is ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the true Image of God, who restores what Adam lost (Colossians 1:15-20).

Practically, this means your work, family life, art, teaching, farming, building, science, and service can all be acts of worship when done under God’s Word. A helpful next step is to ask, “How can I do my ordinary responsibilities faithfully today as a steward for God’s glory?”

If you want, I can also explain how different Christians understand the cultural mandate in relation to evangelism and the Great Commission.
What does it mean that friendship with the world is enmity with God (James 4:4)?

James 4:4 means that to make peace with the sinful patterns, values, and desires of this fallen world is to set yourself against God, because the world in this sense is organized in rebellion against Him. James is warning believers not to love the world’s pride, lust, selfish ambition, and unbelief, because “the friendship of the world is enmity toward God” and “whoever wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God” (James 4:4; see also 1 John 2:15-17).

In context, James is confronting quarrels, selfish desires, and double-mindedness among believers, so this is not about avoiding all contact with unbelievers, but about refusing the world’s values. Christians are still called to love their neighbors and be salt and light, yet not to be conformed to this age but transformed by the renewing of the mind (Matthew 5:13-16; Romans 12:2).

The practical question is, whose approval do you want most, and whose way do you follow when they conflict? A good next step is to ask God to expose any area where you are compromising, then open James 4 and 1 John 2 and compare your desires with Christ’s.
Why did God harden Pharaoh’s heart?

God hardened Pharaoh’s heart to display His power, to make His name known, and to bring judgment on Egypt while rescuing His people, Israel, according to His sovereign purpose, not because God delights in evil. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it, showing real human responsibility under God’s righteous rule (Exodus 7:3-5; Exodus 9:12; Exodus 10:1-2; Exodus 14:4, 17-18).

The immediate context matters: Pharaoh had already repeatedly resisted the clear word of God, and then the Lord confirmed him in the path he had chosen, so that God’s justice and mercy would be displayed in the exodus. Paul uses Pharaoh as an example of God’s sovereignty in salvation and judgment, and he answers the “why” by saying God has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills, so that His purpose stands and His glory is shown (Romans 9:14-18; Romans 9:22-24).

This does not mean God is the author of sin. Pharaoh acted freely in his rebellion, and God’s hardening was judicial, a righteous handing over of a stubborn sinner to the hardness he wanted. That is a fearful warning, because persistent resistance to God can lead to deeper blindness, but it is also a comfort, because the Lord is able to save His people even through the schemes of tyrants.

If you want, I can also walk through the exact sequence of the hardening passages in Exodus and show how they fit together.
How should we treat our enemies according to Proverbs 25:21–22?

Proverbs 25:21–22 teaches that we should treat our enemies with practical kindness, not revenge, because God is the one who judges and can even use our mercy to shame evil and awaken repentance. “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink” (Proverbs 25:21-22); the New Testament echoes this same wisdom in Romans 12:20.

The point is not to pretend evil is good, but to overcome evil with good. This is hard, but it is Christlike, because Jesus Himself loved His enemies by going to the cross for sinners, and He calls His people to love, bless, and do good to those who hate them (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:21).

A helpful next step is to pray for one person who has wronged you, then look for one concrete act of quiet kindness you can do without seeking credit.
What does the Bible say about indecision / being indecisive?

The Bible does not praise indecision when it comes to obeying God, because divided loyalty and double-mindedness weaken faith and lead us away from wisdom. Scripture calls us to seek wisdom from God and then act in faith, not to remain stuck in wavering, as James 1:5-8 says, and it warns that “a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.”

At the same time, the Bible recognizes that wise decisions often require counsel, prayer, and patience, not rashness, so Proverbs 15:22 says, “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed,” and Proverbs 3:5-6 calls us to trust in the LORD with all our heart rather than leaning on our own understanding.

So biblically, indecision can be a symptom of fear, unbelief, or divided desires, but it can also be a sign that you need more wisdom, more counsel, or more time before acting. A good first step is to bring the choice before God in prayer, search the Scriptures for any clear command, and seek mature counsel from a faithful believer or elder in your local church.

If you want, I can also help you think through a specific decision in a biblical way.
What does it mean that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4)?

Revelation 21:4 means that in the new heaven and new earth, God will personally remove every sorrow, grief, pain, and regret from His people forever, because death and sin will be gone: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4).

In context, John is describing the final renewal of creation, not a temporary comfort. The picture is deeply personal, God Himself bending near to comfort His redeemed children, and the reason tears end is that the old order of sin and curse has passed away in Christ’s victorious kingdom (Revelation 21:1-5).

For believers, this is a promise of final restoration, not denial of present pain. It means every wound that sin caused, every grief you have carried, and every sorrow endured in faith will one day be answered by God’s own comforting presence, with no more death, mourning, crying, or pain.

If this verse is speaking to your own suffering, take it as an invitation to bring your grief honestly to the Lord now, trusting that the same God who promises the end of tears will also sustain you today.
What is the meaning of “there but for the grace of God go I”?

“ There but for the grace of God go I” means, “If it were not for God’s gracious restraint and mercy, I could be in that same fallen condition too.” It is a reminder of human sinfulness, humility, and dependence on God’s grace, not a statement that we are naturally better than others.

The Bible teaches that apart from God’s grace, all of us are spiritually helpless and deserving of judgment, because “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Salvation is not earned by superiority or moral effort, but by grace alone through faith in Christ alone, who died for sinners and rose again (Ephesians 2:8-9; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

So the phrase should produce humility and compassion, not pride. A Christian says it while remembering, “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

What does the Bible say about the ice age?

The Bible does not explicitly mention “the Ice Age” as a named historical period, but it does teach that God sovereignly governs the earth, including weather, seasons, and the shaping of creation (Genesis 8:22; Job 37:6-13; Psalm 104:5-9). So Christians can say the Bible is compatible with an ice age, but it does not give a detailed scientific timeline for it.

A careful biblical way to think about it is this: the flood in Noah’s day was a real global judgment, and many believers think events after the flood could have contributed to major climate changes, though Scripture does not spell out an ice-age mechanism (Genesis 7:11-12; Genesis 8:1-5). What the Bible does clearly say is that the created order is under God’s providence, not random fate.

What is the significance of the city of Nineveh in the Bible?

Nineveh is significant in the Bible as a great Assyrian city known for its wickedness, a place of God’s warning, mercy, and judgment, and the setting of Jonah’s famous mission. It stands as a powerful example that God is sovereign over the nations and merciful to repentant sinners, even Gentiles, while still judging unrepentant evil (Jonah 1:2; Jonah 3:5-10; Nahum 1:1-3).

Historically, Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, one of Israel’s most feared enemies. In Jonah, God sends the prophet to call Nineveh to repentance, and the people humble themselves, showing that God’s compassion extends beyond Israel to all peoples who turn from sin. Later, Nahum pronounces judgment on Nineveh because of its persistent violence, proving that God’s patience is real but not endless.

Its larger biblical significance is this: Nineveh reveals both the mercy and justice of God. That same message still stands today, because all people are sinners in need of repentance, and God calls us to turn from sin and trust in His saving mercy.
What is Epicureanism? What did Epicurus teach?

Epicureanism was a philosophy founded by Epicurus in ancient Greece that taught that the highest good was **pleasure**, understood mainly as the absence of pain and disturbance, not reckless indulgence. Epicurus taught that the gods, if they existed, were distant and uninvolved, and that death should not be feared because the soul perishes with the body.

In brief, Epicurus taught:
- **Pleasure is the goal of life**, especially calmness and freedom from fear.
- **The gods are not active in human affairs**, so people need not fear divine judgment.
- **Death is the end of consciousness**, so it should not be dreaded.
- **Virtue is valuable** mainly because it helps produce a peaceful life.

Historically, this matters because the New Testament explicitly mentions Epicureans in Acts 17:18, where they opposed Paul’s preaching of Christ and the resurrection. Biblically, their view of God and death is directly contradicted by the truth that God is personal, sovereign, and will judge the world through Jesus Christ, who died and rose bodily from the dead, proving that death is not the end. If you want, I can also compare Epicureanism with Stoicism and show how Paul answered both in Athens.
Book of Philippians - Bible Survey

Philippians is Paul’s joyful letter from prison, calling believers to live worthy of the gospel by rejoicing in Christ, humbly serving one another, and pressing on toward maturity in the Lord, even in suffering (Philippians 1:27; Philippians 2:5-11; Philippians 3:12-14).

Paul writes to a faithful church he loves dearly, thanking God for their partnership in the gospel and encouraging them that God will finish the work He began in them (Philippians 1:3-6). The letter is deeply pastoral, but it is also rich in theology: Christ’s humiliation and exaltation in Philippians 2:5-11 is one of the clearest passages on the incarnation, atonement, and lordship of Jesus Christ in all of Scripture.

The main themes are joy in the Lord, unity in the church, gospel partnership, humility, sanctification, and contentment. Paul repeatedly shows that Christian joy is not based on ease, but on Christ Himself, because “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). He also warns against confidence in the flesh and points believers to righteousness through faith in Christ alone, not through works of the law (Philippians 3:7-9).

A simple outline is:
- Philippians 1, gospel partnership and joyful perseverance in suffering
- Philippians 2, the mind of Christ, humility, and obedience
- Philippians 3, warning against false confidence and pressing on toward Christ
- Philippians 4, rejoicing, prayer, contentment, and generosity

The letter teaches the church how to live under the lordship of Christ in a crooked world, with courage, holiness, and peace. Its call is very practical, rejoice in the Lord, pray instead of anxiously worrying, and learn contentment in Christ who strengthens His people (Philippians 4:4-7; Philippians 4:11-13).

In what ways was Moses like Jesus?

Moses was like Jesus in that both were chosen deliverers, mediators between God and His people, and faithful servants in God’s house. The New Testament explicitly presents Moses as a type pointing forward to Christ, while also showing that Jesus is greater than Moses, the Son over God’s house, not merely a servant in it, Hebrews 3:1-6.

A few key ways they are alike:

- Both were preserved in infancy from a ruler’s death decree, Exodus 1:22-2:10; Matthew 2:13-18.
- Both came to deliver God’s people from bondage, Moses from Egypt, Jesus from sin and death, Exodus 3:7-10; Matthew 1:21.
- Both were mediators of a covenant between God and His people, Exodus 24:3-8; Luke 22:20.
- Both led God’s people through a “waters” moment, Moses through the sea and Jesus through baptism at the start of His public ministry, Exodus 14:21-31; Matthew 3:13-17.
- Both fed God’s people in the wilderness, Moses with manna by God’s provision and Jesus with bread miraculously multiplied, Exodus 16:4-35; Matthew 14:13-21.
- Both taught God’s word and revealed God’s will to the people, Deuteronomy 18:15-19; John 12:49-50.
- Both were rejected by many of their own people, Exodus 2:13-14; John 1:11.
- Both were associated with a mountain where God’s truth was revealed, Exodus 19:3-6; Matthew 5:1-2.

But the greatest point is this, Moses was a servant and a prophet, while Jesus is the eternal Son, the final and perfect Mediator, and the greater Prophet promised by God, Hebrews 3:5-6; Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22-23. Moses could lead Israel out of slavery, but only Christ can save sinners fully and forever through His cross and resurrection, Romans 5:8-10; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

What is Socinianism?

Socinianism is a heretical system that denies the Trinity, the deity of Christ, and the substitutionary atonement, teaching instead that Jesus was a mere man and that salvation is not by Christ bearing our sins. That stands against Scripture, which teaches one God in three persons, the full deity of Christ, and that Jesus died for our sins and rose again, as in John 1:1-14; Colossians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

Historically, Socinianism arose in the 16th century through Fausto and Laelio Sozzini, and it shaped later Unitarian thought. Biblically, it cannot be reconciled with passages like Matthew 28:19, John 20:28, and 2 Corinthians 5:21.

Can an unmarried man be a deacon or elder?

Yes, an unmarried man can be a deacon or elder, because Scripture requires that he be qualified in character, not that he must be married, though if he is married he must be a faithful husband and household leader, as seen in 1 Timothy 3:2, 1 Timothy 3:4-5, 1 Timothy 3:12, and Titus 1:6.

For elders, the Bible says he must be “the husband of one wife,” which means a man who is above reproach in his marital faithfulness if he is married, not that marriage is required for the office. The same is true for deacons in 1 Timothy 3:12, and the emphasis is on proven maturity, self-control, and integrity.

A single man may serve faithfully if he meets the biblical qualifications, but the church should carefully examine whether he has demonstrated the household wisdom, sobriety, and spiritual maturity the office requires. Is it better, spiritually, to be poor than to be rich?

Not in itself. Scripture warns that poverty can tempt a person to steal or despair, and wealth can tempt a person to pride and self-reliance, so the spiritual issue is not money itself but the heart’s response to God, “for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” and some “have wandered away from the faith” because of it, while the poor are also called to trust the Lord, not merely their lack of possessions (1 Timothy 6:9-10; Proverbs 30:8-9).

Jesus blesses “the poor in spirit,” meaning those who know their need before God, and He also warns that “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 5:3; Matthew 6:21). So a poor person is not automatically closer to God, and a rich person is not automatically farther away, but both must repent, believe the Gospel, and learn contentment in Christ, who “though He was rich, yet for your sakes became poor” for our salvation (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Will the sun really be turned to darkness and the moon to blood (Joel 2:31)?

Yes, Joel 2:31 speaks of real cosmic signs, and the New Testament treats that prophecy as ultimately pointing to the day of the Lord and the return of Christ, when God will judge the world and set all things right. Peter quotes Joel in Acts 2:20, and Jesus also speaks of sun-darkening and heavenly shaking in connection with His coming and final judgment, which shows this is not mere poetry detached from history, but prophetic language about a real future intervention of God.

At the same time, prophetic books often use vivid, apocalyptic imagery to describe God’s judgment in ways that are both literal and symbolic in force, so faithful Christians have sometimes differed on the exact timing and sequence. But the main truth is clear: God will not ignore sin forever, and history is moving toward His appointed day, when Christ will return bodily, judge with justice, and make all things new, Matthew 24:29-31; Revelation 6:12-17.

If this raises fear, let it also point you to mercy: the same Lord who will judge is the One who died for sinners and rose again. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and life.
How can I overcome spiritual apathy?

Spiritual apathy is often a sign that your heart has grown dull to the glory of Christ, but it is not beyond the Lord’s restoring grace. God calls the lukewarm to repent and return to Him, because He is patient, faithful, and ready to renew a weary soul, and Scripture says, “Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you” (James 4:8; Revelation 3:15-20).

Begin with honest repentance, not self-reliance. Ask God to expose what is numbing you, then bring yourself back under the means of grace, regular hearing of the Word, prayer, fellowship, and the Lord’s Supper in a faithful church (Romans 10:17; Acts 2:42; Hebrews 10:24-25). Often apathy grows when we stop beholding Christ clearly, so meditate on His cross and resurrection, where love and holiness meet, and remember that He died and rose for sinners who were cold and distracted, not just for those who felt spiritually strong (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8).

A good next step is to set one small, concrete daily practice for two weeks, for example, read one Gospel passage, write one sentence about what it shows you about Jesus, and pray honestly before God about your coldness. Also, tell a mature believer or one of your church elders, because light often returns through confession, prayer, and encouragement from the body of Christ (James 5:16).

If your apathy is tied to guilt, despair, or hidden sin, do not stay distant from Christ. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose to forgive and restore you. What has been most draining your heart lately, busyness, sin, disappointment, or something else?

I’m so sorry you’re carrying this pain. Healing after an abortion can feel complicated, with grief, guilt, fear, anger, and even numbness all tangled together, but there is real hope in Christ.

If this abortion was a sin in your conscience, do not hide from God, bring it into the light, confess it honestly, and trust that Christ’s blood is sufficient to forgive and cleanse.

What does God mean when He says, “Seek me and live” (Amos 5:4)?

In Amos 5:4, God is calling His covenant people to turn from empty religion and return to Him in repentance, because only He gives life, not the idols or injustices they were chasing. In context, “seek me and live” means to seek the Lord Himself, His presence, His ways, and His mercy, not merely outward worship, because true life is found in covenant fellowship with the living God.

Amos is speaking to a people who had religious activity but rebellious hearts. God had already said, “Seek the LORD and live” (Amos 5:6), and later, “Seek good and not evil” (Amos 5:14). So seeking God includes turning from sin, loving justice, and clinging to Him in humble faith. This is not salvation by performance, but a call to repent and return to the God who alone can forgive and restore.

For Christians, this points forward to the full Gospel: we are sinners who need God’s mercy, and that mercy comes through Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again bodily (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The call is still the same in substance, seek the Lord by turning from sin and trusting in Christ alone for forgiveness and life.

If aborted babies go to heaven, why is abortion wrong?

Abortion is wrong because it is the intentional taking of innocent human life, and Scripture treats the unborn as known by God, made in His image, and not morally disposable, even if we trust God to show mercy to children who die before birth. Psalm 139:13-16; Exodus 20:13; Genesis 1:27.

The hope that God receives unborn children does not make the act of killing them good any more than God’s mercy toward other victims of evil makes murder acceptable. The moral issue is the act itself, and God’s clear command is, “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), while He also says He formed us in the womb and numbered our days (Psalm 139:13-16).

Christians may differ on how to explain the salvation of those who die in infancy, but the Bible is clear that we must not do evil so that good may come, and we are to protect the weak and helpless. Romans 3:8; Proverbs 24:11-12.

Should communion be open or closed?

Communion is a non-essential where faithful Christians disagree, but I would recommend a close communion practice, meaning it is open to all baptized believers in good standing with a gospel-preaching church. Many Christians argue for open communion because the Lord’s Table is a means of grace for believers, while others argue for closed communion because of the church’s responsibility to guard the Table and examine participation carefully, as in 1 Corinthians 11:27-29.

My position is close communion, because the New Testament links the Supper with the church’s discernment, covenant membership, and pastoral oversight, not merely private sincerity, and the table should not be treated casually. At the same time, the emphasis must be on self-examination, faith in Christ, and repentance, not on creating unnecessary barriers for true believers.

Who wrote the book of 2 John? Who was the author of 2 John?

The book of 2 John was written by the apostle John, the same John who also wrote 1 John, 3 John, and the Gospel of John.

He identifies himself simply as “the elder” in the letter, which fits the apostle John in his later years, writing to a church or a Christian woman and her children, likely from a pastoral and authoritative position. The letter’s strong emphasis on truth, love, and obedience is very much in line with John’s other writings, such as 1 John 1:1-4 and John 13:34-35.

What is false guilt, and how can I avoid it?

False guilt is the heavy feeling of being condemned for something God has not condemned, or for sins that Christ has already forgiven in repentance and faith. Scripture says that in Christ, “there is now no condemnation” for those who are in Him, and that God “is greater than our hearts” when our conscience accuses us unfairly (Romans 8:1; 1 John 3:20).

To avoid false guilt, first ask whether you are actually guilty before God, or merely feeling shame, fear, or pressure. Compare the situation with Scripture, confess any real sin plainly, and then rest in Christ’s finished work, because “if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9), and “by one offering He has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14).

A helpful practice is to name the accusation, search the Bible for what God says, and then replace the lie with truth. If the guilt comes from your past, remind yourself that Jesus truly bore sin on the cross and rose again, so the believer is not under condemnation but under grace through faith alone in Christ alone (1 Peter 2:24; Romans 5:1).

Are baptism and communion means of grace?

Yes, baptism and communion are means of grace in the sense that God uses them as ordained channels to strengthen faith and bless His people, though Christians differ on the exact way that grace is given. Scripture shows baptism as connected with union with Christ and cleansing, and the Lord’s Supper as a covenant meal that proclaims Christ’s death and nourishes believers in faith, for example Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3-4; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26.

A strong historic Christian view is that these ordinances are not empty symbols, but neither do they work automatically apart from faith. Another major historic view, especially in sacramental traditions, says they are true means by which God conveys grace more directly, and they appeal to passages like John 6:53-56 and 1 Peter 3:21.

My own view is that they are means of grace because Christ appointed them for the good of His church, but their benefit is received by faith, not by mere outward participation. So the practical call is to come to baptism and the Table with repentance, faith, and reverence, asking God to use them to deepen your communion with Christ and His people.
What is the spirit of the law?

The “spirit of the law” is the law’s true intent and heart, the righteous purpose God meant it to serve, not merely the external wording. Jesus exposed this when He showed that God’s commandments reach to the inside, like anger beneath murder and lust beneath adultery, not just outward compliance, in Matthew 5:21-28.

In Scripture, the law’s spirit is summed up in love for God and love for neighbor, because “love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10; Matthew 22:37-40). That means God is not satisfied with bare rule-keeping, but desires a heart transformed by grace, obedience from the inside out.

So the spirit of the law is the moral meaning and holy aim of God’s commands, fulfilled perfectly in Christ and then worked into His people by the Holy Spirit. Practically, that means asking not only, “Did I avoid the act?” but also, “Does my heart, motive, and speech reflect God’s holiness and love?”
Should pastors be paid a salary?

Yes, pastors may and often should be paid, because Scripture teaches that those who labor in preaching and teaching are worthy of material support, even while they must not serve for greedy gain. Paul says, “The elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching,” and “the worker is worthy of his wages” (1 Timothy 5:17-18), and he also says, “the Lord has commanded that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).

At the same time, a salary must never turn ministry into a business or make a pastor “greedy for gain” (1 Peter 5:2; Titus 1:7). The best biblical pattern is faithful support, transparent stewardship, and a pastor who serves willingly, not for money, but out of love for Christ and His flock.

What does it mean that man shall not live by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3)?

Deuteronomy 8:3 means that God’s people must not think physical food is their deepest need, because human life depends above all on God’s word, God’s provision, and God’s faithful care. In context, Moses is reminding Israel that the wilderness was meant to teach them humility and dependence, “that you might know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3).

The point is not that bread is unimportant, but that bread is not enough. God can sustain, direct, and give life by His spoken word, and He was training Israel to trust Him rather than their own resources. Jesus later quoted this verse when He was tempted in the wilderness, showing that true life is found in obedient dependence on the Father, not merely in satisfying bodily hunger (Matthew 4:4).

For us, this means we should receive daily bread with gratitude, but seek God Himself even more. A helpful next step is to read Deuteronomy 8:1-5 and ask God to expose where you are trusting material things more than His word.
What does the Bible say about parenting?

The Bible teaches that parenting is a God-given calling to bring children up in the “discipline and instruction of the Lord” with love, steadiness, and example, not harshness or neglect. Fathers are especially warned not to provoke their children to anger, but to nurture them in a way that reflects God’s own fatherly care, as seen in Ephesians 6:4 and Colossians 3:21.

At the heart of biblical parenting is discipleship: parents are to teach God’s words diligently, speak of them in daily life, and model obedience in the home, as in Deuteronomy 6:6-7 and Proverbs 22:6. The goal is not merely well-behaved children, but hearts formed toward the Lord, which includes loving correction, patience, and prayerful dependence on God’s grace.

A few key biblical emphases stand out:
- Children are a heritage and gift from the Lord, not a burden, as Psalm 127:3-5 says.
- Parents should train and discipline with wisdom, not anger, as Proverbs 13:24 and Proverbs 29:15 teach.
- Discipline is meant for loving formation, like the Lord’s own discipline of His people, not abuse or humiliation, as Hebrews 12:5-11 shows.
- Parents are called to model sincerity, faith, and repentance before their children, because example teaches as much as words do.

Who was Jeremiah in the Bible?

Jeremiah was a prophet of God in the Old Testament, called to speak God’s word to Judah during the years leading up to Jerusalem’s destruction and exile, around the late seventh and early sixth centuries BC. He is often called the “weeping prophet” because he faithfully warned of judgment, grieved over sin, and also proclaimed hope for restoration.

God called Jeremiah from before his birth, saying, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” and appointing him as a prophet to the nations, and Jeremiah 1:4-10 shows both his calling and his weakness before God’s strengthening grace. He preached repentance, announced the coming Babylonian judgment, and urged the people to trust the Lord rather than false security.

Jeremiah is also important because he foretold the New Covenant, where God would write His law on His people’s hearts and forgive their sins, a promise fulfilled in Christ, who secures that covenant by His blood, as seen in Jeremiah 31:31-34; Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6-13.

Why did Jesus allow the demons to enter the herd of pigs?

Jesus allowed it to show His authority over demons, to reveal the terrible destructive nature of evil, and to make the man’s deliverance unmistakable to everyone there, not just private and invisible. In the account, the demons beg Jesus for permission, which shows they are not equal rivals but subject to His command, and the pigs’ destruction becomes a living picture of what evil does when it is left unchecked (Mark 5:12-13; Luke 8:32-33).

It also exposed the value Jesus places on a single human soul. The herd was large, but the delivered man mattered more, and the people’s reaction shows that some will fear the loss of possessions more than they welcome the mercy of Christ (Mark 5:15-17). In context, the event is a sign of Christ’s lordship over the spiritual realm, and it points to His power to save completely, which fits the broader biblical truth that He came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8).

What are the Analects of Confucius?

The Analects of Confucius is a collection of sayings and short dialogues attributed to Confucius and compiled by his followers after his death. It is one of the foundational texts of Confucian thought, focusing on ethics, proper conduct, family duty, social harmony, and good government.

In plain terms, it teaches how a person should live with virtue, self-discipline, respect, and reverence for tradition. Its influence has been immense in Chinese and East Asian history, especially on education, politics, and moral philosophy.

From a Christian perspective, it is a significant historical and philosophical work, but it is not Scripture and does not reveal the gospel of Jesus Christ. The Bible alone is God’s inspired Word, and it teaches that true righteousness comes through faith in Christ, not through moral self-cultivation alone, because all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again for sinners, not by works (Romans 3:23-24; Ephesians 2:8-9; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Can faith change God's plan?

Faith does not change God’s eternal plan, but God truly uses faith and prayer as ordained means by which He brings about His purposes. Scripture shows both that God’s counsel stands forever and that He responds to His people’s praying and believing in real, meaningful ways, without ever being surprised or overruled by them (Isaiah 46:9-10; James 5:16; Matthew 21:22).

So the biblical picture is not that faith forces God’s hand, but that faith submits to God’s will and receives what He has already wisely purposed to give in Christ. In other words, God is sovereign, and prayer is not pointless, it is one of His appointed instruments.

A good next step is to read James 4:13-17 and 1 John 5:14-15, then pray honestly that God would align your desires with His will.
What is Pneumatology?

Pneumatology is the study of the Holy Spirit, His person, His work, and His relationship to the Father and the Son. In Scripture, the Spirit is not an impersonal force, but God Himself, fully divine and active in creation, revelation, regeneration, sanctification, and empowering the church, as seen in John 14:16-17; Acts 1:8; Romans 8:9-16.

This matters because true Christian life depends on the Holy Spirit applying the work of Christ to us. The Spirit convicts of sin, gives new birth, seals believers, and grows them in holiness, which is why theology about the Spirit is never merely academic, but deeply pastoral and practical.
What does the Bible say about children's church?

The Bible does not command or forbid a separate “children’s church” program, so this is a matter of wisdom and church practice, not a core doctrine. What Scripture clearly does teach is that children should be taught God’s Word faithfully, and that the church should gather as God’s people for worship and instruction, with children included under the care of their families and the congregation, as seen in Deuteronomy 6:6-7, Ephesians 6:4, and Colossians 3:16.

A strong biblical case can be made for children being present with the whole church when possible, because God’s people gathered together to hear His Word read and explained, and the whole assembly, including children, was addressed in covenant settings such as Joshua 8:35 and Nehemiah 8:2-3. At the same time, the Bible also highlights parents as the primary disciplers of their children, especially fathers in the home, which means any children’s ministry should support, not replace, parental responsibility, Ephesians 6:4.

My view is that children’s church is a permissible helpful structure if it serves the church’s teaching ministry and does not detach children from the gathered body or weaken parental discipleship. The best test is whether it helps children hear Scripture clearly, learn to worship reverently, and belong visibly to the life of the church.

If your church uses children’s church, a good next step is to ask, does it strengthen family discipleship and the child’s eventual participation in corporate worship, or does it unintentionally train them that the church is for adults only?
Why is the humanity of Jesus important?

Jesus’ true humanity is essential because only a real man could obey in our place, suffer and die for us, and be the mediator between God and sinners, while still being without sin. The Bible says, “Since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity” so that through death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death, the devil, and “He had to be made like His brothers in every way” to become a merciful and faithful High Priest, able to help those who are tempted (Hebrews 2:14-18).

This matters for the gospel: the eternal Son did not merely appear human, He took on a true human nature, a real body, mind, emotions, and will, without sin. That means His obedience counts for us, His cross is a real substitutionary atonement, and His resurrection is the resurrection of our representative head, not of a phantom. “There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

It is also a comfort for believers, because Jesus understands human weakness without sharing our sin. “We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). So when you struggle, you are not coming to a distant Savior, but to One who truly knows human life from the inside.

What is the new birth?

The new birth is God’s work of giving a sinner new spiritual life, also called being “born again,” so that the person turns from sin and trusts in Christ. Jesus said, “Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3), and “the Spirit gives birth to spirit” (John 3:6).

It is not a self-improvement project or merely religious excitement, but a supernatural regeneration by the Holy Spirit. God removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh, so that a person now loves God, hates sin, and begins to walk in new obedience (Ezekiel 36:26-27; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

This new birth is necessary because we are all sinners and cannot save ourselves. Christ died for sins and rose bodily from the dead, and all who repent and believe in Him receive forgiveness and new life (John 1:12-13; 1 Peter 1:3). If you are asking because you want to know God, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.
What does the Bible say about education?

The Bible treats education as a good and weighty stewardship: God calls His people to seek wisdom, teach diligently, and train the next generation in truth, but it always places learning under the fear of the Lord, not above it. Proverbs 1:7 says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge,” and Deuteronomy 6:6-7 commands parents to teach God’s words diligently to their children.

Scripture values learning, but it warns that knowledge without godliness can become prideful and empty. Daniel and his friends were trained in the literature and language of Babylon, yet they remained faithful to the Lord, showing that education can be used for service when submitted to God (Daniel 1:17; Daniel 1:20). Jesus Himself grew “in wisdom and stature” (Luke 2:52), which shows that growth in understanding is part of normal human life.

The Bible also makes parents responsible for training children in the Lord. Ephesians 6:4 says to bring children up “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord,” and 2 Timothy 3:14-15 praises Timothy for knowing the sacred writings from childhood. That means the chief goal of education is not merely career success, but wisdom, character, and faithfulness before God.

A Christian view of education therefore includes both academic skill and spiritual formation. Whether in a school, home, or apprenticeship, the question is not only, “What can this person know?” but also, “Will this help them love God and serve others?” Colossians 3:23 says, “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men.”

What is the Edenic covenant?

The Edenic covenant is the covenant God made with Adam in the garden of Eden, where Adam was appointed as humanity’s head under God’s rule, given dominion, and commanded not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, with life promised in obedience and death threatened in disobedience, though the word “covenant” is not used explicitly there (Genesis 1:26-28; Genesis 2:16-17).

Many Christians see this as the foundation for the covenant of works, because Adam stood as a representative man, and his fall brought sin and death to the human race, which helps us see our need for Christ, the last Adam, who obeyed where Adam failed (Romans 5:12-19; 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49).

In practical terms, Genesis teaches that God’s commands are good, human beings are accountable to Him, and true hope for fallen people is not self-repair but redemption through Jesus Christ.
What is Wahhabism? What is Wahhabi Islam?

Wahhabism is a reform movement within Sunni Islam that began in 18th-century Arabia, associated with Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. Wahhabi Islam usually refers to that same movement’s theology and practice, especially its strict emphasis on monotheism and opposition to practices it sees as idolatrous, such as saint veneration and some forms of devotional customs.

Historically, it joined with the Saudi dynasty and became influential in what is now Saudi Arabia. It is a branch of Sunni Islam, not a separate religion.

From a Christian perspective, it matters to distinguish respect for Muslims as people from agreement with Islamic claims. Christians would say that true worship belongs to the triune God, and salvation is found not in religious zeal but in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again, the only mediator between God and man (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). What sort of interfaith ministries are appropriate?

Interfaith ministry can be appropriate in limited forms when it means cooperating for the common good, showing neighbor-love, and speaking with humility and clarity, but it is not appropriate to blur the unique lordship of Jesus Christ or treat all religions as equally saving. Scripture calls us to do good to all people and live peaceably where possible, while still confessing that salvation is found in Christ alone, not in shared spirituality or moral effort, “There is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12; John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5).

A faithful Christian can join humanitarian cooperation, disaster relief, civic peacemaking, and respectful dialogue that seeks understanding, provided the partnership does not require affirming false worship, denying the Gospel, or participating in prayer or worship that confuses Christ’s exclusive claims. The line is crossed when ministry becomes religious syncretism, because true witness must keep both love and truth together, “whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

What is presuppositional apologetics?

Presuppositional apologetics is a way of defending the Christian faith that begins with the truth that God’s revelation in Scripture is the foundation for all reasoning, morality, and knowledge, rather than trying to prove Christianity by standing on supposedly neutral ground. It argues that the Christian worldview is the necessary basis for logic, morals, meaning, and human dignity, because “the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7), and in Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

A simple way to say it is this: presuppositional apologetics asks, “What worldview makes sense of everything else?” It often compares Christianity with unbelieving worldviews and shows that without the Triune God, people cannot ultimately justify truth, reason, or moral obligation. That fits with the biblical teaching that unbelief suppresses the truth, even though God has made Himself known clearly in creation and conscience (Romans 1:18-20).

The main strength of this approach is that it takes God’s authority seriously and refuses to place human autonomy above divine revelation. The caution is that it must be used with humility, patience, and clarity, not as a weapon for winning arguments, because we are called to give a reason for our hope “with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15).

What does the Bible say about chanting? Should a Christian chant?

The Bible does not forbid chanting, and it does show God’s people using repeated, rhythmic, sung speech in worship, especially in the Psalms and in heaven’s worship, but it also warns against empty repetition done as vain ritual. Matthew 6:7; Psalm 136:1-3; Revelation 4:8.

So a Christian may chant if it is used reverently to help sing, pray, or recite Scripture with understanding and faith, but not as a magical formula or mindless repetition. The key issue is the heart, truth, and edification, not the mere form. Colossians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 14:15.

A helpful test is this: does the chant exalt Christ, build up the church, and keep the mind engaged, or does it drift into empty, mechanical performance? If it helps you worship “with the spirit and with the mind,” it can be fitting; if it becomes superstition or distraction, it should be avoided. 1 Corinthians 14:15.

Who is Jesus — Day 4 — Jesus the Prophet

Jesus is the promised Prophet like Moses, the final and fullest revelation of God, who speaks God’s words with divine authority and calls people to hear and obey Him. Deuteronomy 18:15-19 points forward to this promised Prophet, and the New Testament shows that Jesus fulfills it, especially in Acts 3:22-23 and Hebrews 1:1-2.

Jesus is greater than the Old Testament prophets because He does not merely deliver a message from God, He is the Son who reveals the Father perfectly, “The One who has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). That means His teaching is not optional advice, but God’s own truth with authority over our lives.

This matters because if Jesus is the Prophet of God, then we must listen to Him, trust Him, and repent when His words expose our sin. The Gospel He proclaims is that sinners can be forgiven through His death and raised to new life through His resurrection.

What is biblical homemaking?

Biblical homemaking is the God-honoring work of managing a household in a way that reflects Christ, serving your family with wisdom, order, hospitality, and faithful care. Scripture pictures this as a noble calling, especially in Titus 2:3-5, Proverbs 31:10-31, and 1 Timothy 5:14.

At its heart, homemaking is not “just chores.” It is stewardship. A home is a place where faith is taught, children are nurtured, meals are prepared, needs are anticipated, guests are welcomed, and daily life is ordered for the good of others. Titus 2:4-5 links this to loving one’s husband and children, self-control, purity, kindness, and working at home, so that God’s Word is not reviled.

Biblical homemaking is not limited to women folding laundry or cooking, though those may be part of it. It is the broader work of cultivating a home that serves the Lord, supports a marriage, trains children, practices hospitality, and keeps priorities rightly ordered before God. Proverbs 31 shows a woman whose diligence, wisdom, and strength bless her household and honor the Lord.

A helpful way to think about it is this: biblical homemaking is domestic discipleship. The home becomes a small sphere of faithful stewardship where ordinary tasks are done unto the Lord, with love and purpose, not mere maintenance.

A practical next step is to ask, “How can my home better serve worship, peace, hospitality, and discipleship?” Then choose one concrete habit, such as daily Scripture at the table, regular tidying, or intentional welcoming of others.

How should Christians view statues of Jesus?

Christians should view statues of Jesus with caution, because the second commandment forbids making images for worship, and God has not given us an image of Christ to venerate, even though Jesus truly became man. The issue is not art itself, but the temptation to turn a created likeness into a focus of devotion or to misrepresent the glory of the incarnate Son, who is revealed to us in Scripture, not by man-made likenesses (Exodus 20:4-5; John 1:18; Colossians 1:15).

Faithful Christians have disagreed on religious imagery in general, and some distinguish between art as decoration and images used in worship, while others avoid statues of Christ altogether out of reverence and concern for idolatry. My view is that statues of Jesus are at best unnecessary and at worst spiritually dangerous, because they can invite people to imagine Christ according to human preference rather than according to the Word of God.

A good practical step is to ask whether a statue helps you obey the Lord and treasure Christ more, or whether it subtly competes with reverent worship of Him in spirit and truth. If you want, I can also explain how different Christian traditions understand the second commandment and images.
I am in the process of getting a divorce. Can I start dating, or do I have to wait until the divorce is final?

If your spouse is still living and your divorce is not yet final, starting to date would be unwise and would likely cross into sexual and covenantal unfaithfulness, because marriage before God remains binding until it is truly ended, and Jesus treats divorce and remarriage seriously, especially where adultery is involved, in Matthew 5:32 and Matthew 19:9.

The Bible’s plain concern is not merely paperwork, but covenant faithfulness before God, so while civil proceedings may be in motion, you should not move as though you are free to pursue another relationship. What is the importance of the empty tomb?

The empty tomb matters because it is God’s public declaration that Jesus truly rose bodily from the dead, and that His sacrifice was accepted, sin was defeated, and death was conquered. If Christ was still in the grave, our faith would be empty, but because He rose, we have living hope. “He is not here; He has risen, just as He said” (Matthew 28:6); “He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25); “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17).

The empty tomb confirms the gospel, vindicates Jesus as the Son of God, and guarantees the believer’s future resurrection. It is not merely a symbol, it is the bodily resurrection of Christ in history. The right response is to repent and trust in the risen Christ for forgiveness and new life.

What is traducianism?

Traducianism is the view that the human soul is propagated from the souls of the parents along with the body, so each child receives a whole human nature from its parents rather than having the soul newly created by God at conception.

Christians who hold this view usually appeal to passages that emphasize Adam as the head of the human race, such as Genesis 5:3, and the fact that sin and death spread to all people through Adam, Romans 5:12-19. A strong argument for traducianism is that it helps explain the deep unity of body and soul in human generation, though many orthodox Christians have held **creationism** instead, the view that God immediately creates each soul while still preserving the child’s full humanity.

My view is that creationism is the more careful option, because Scripture clearly teaches God as the giver of life and the maker of each person, while traducianism goes beyond what the Bible states plainly. Either way, orthodox Christianity affirms that every human being is fully responsible before God and is born into Adam’s fallen race, needing the new birth in Christ, John 3:3; Romans 5:12-19.

How should a Christian view the intellect?

A Christian should view the intellect as a gift from God, meant to be used in submission to Him, not as a rival to faith. Scripture calls us to love God with all our mind, and also warns that mere human wisdom cannot replace the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of knowledge and wisdom, Proverbs 1:7; Matthew 22:37.

The Bible does not pit truth against faith. Rather, it shows that the renewed mind is part of sanctification, and that believers are to be transformed by the renewing of their minds, Romans 12:2. At the same time, intellect is limited by sin, so we must not trust our own understanding above God’s Word, Proverbs 3:5-6.

So a Christian should cultivate learning, careful thinking, and wisdom, while humbly submitting every thought to Christ, 2 Corinthians 10:5. Practically, that means reading Scripture carefully, thinking truthfully, asking wise questions, and refusing pride. Use your mind in worship, not self-exaltation.

What does the Bible say about being zealous / having zeal?

The Bible treats zeal as a strong, earnest passion that can be either good or dangerous, depending on what it is for and whether it is governed by truth and love. Holy zeal is commendable when it is for God’s honor, the gospel, and obedience to His word, but zeal without knowledge can become destructive, self-righteous, or misdirected, as seen in Romans 10:2 and Proverbs 19:2.

Scripture shows both sides clearly. God Himself is “zealous” for His people and His glory, and Christ’s zeal for God’s house fulfills Psalm 69:9 in John 2:17. Believers are called to be “zealous for good works” and to be “zealous and repent” in Revelation 3:19; Titus 2:14. At the same time, Paul warns that his fellow Jews had “zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” in Romans 10:2, and zeal can even be directed toward false religion, as with Saul before his conversion in Philippians 3:6.

So biblically, zeal is not the problem, misdirected zeal is. The right kind of zeal is a Spirit-shaped fervor joined to truth, humility, and love, producing obedience, holiness, and faithful witness. What is the grace of God?

The grace of God is His undeserved favor toward sinners, shown most clearly in Jesus Christ. Scripture says, “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men” and “By grace you are saved through faith” (Titus 2:11; Ephesians 2:8).

In the Bible, grace is not God ignoring sin, but God giving what we do not deserve, mercy, forgiveness, new life, and righteousness through Christ. That is why grace is tied to the cross and resurrection, where Jesus bore our sins and rose again for our justification, so sinners can be reconciled to God (Romans 3:24-26; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Is it wrong for a Christian husband and wife to attend separate churches?

It is not automatically sin for a Christian husband and wife to attend separate churches, but it is usually unwise if there is no serious reason, because marriage is meant to be a united partnership in worship and discipleship, and believers are called to “not neglect meeting together” and to pursue unity in Christ (Hebrews 10:24-25; Ephesians 4:3).

A faithful argument for attending separate churches is that there may be legitimate practical reasons, such as geography, work schedules, doctrinal conviction about a particular church, or a season of pastoral transition. The strongest argument for attending the same church is that shared worship, shared teaching, shared membership, and shared shepherding help a marriage move in the same spiritual direction.

My view is that, whenever possible, a husband and wife should attend the same local church, because the local church is where they are ordinarily fed by the Word, known by shepherds, and built up together as one flesh under Christ (Ephesians 5:31-32; Colossians 3:16). If separation is happening, it should be treated as a temporary exception, not a normal goal, and both spouses should pray for unity and seek wise counsel from mature elders.

What is the Druze religion?

The Druze are a religious community that originated in the 11th century in the Levant, especially in what is now Lebanon, Syria, and Israel. Their religion is a distinct, closed faith with roots in Ismaili Shi’a Islam, but it developed into a separate system with its own beliefs and practices.

Historically, Druze belief includes strong emphasis on the oneness of God, reincarnation, secrecy of doctrine, and the authority of their own religious texts and leaders. They do not generally accept converts in or out, and many of their teachings are reserved for initiated members.

From a Christian standpoint, the Druze religion is not Christianity, and it does not confess the biblical gospel of Jesus Christ, His atoning death, and His bodily resurrection for sinners. Christians should speak of Druze people with respect and kindness, while remembering that salvation is found only in Christ, who said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6, BSB).

What is an invocation prayer?

What is the spiritual gift of prophecy?

The spiritual gift of prophecy is the Spirit-given ability to speak a message from God for the edification, exhortation, and encouragement of His people, always under the authority of Scripture and never equal to it, because God’s written Word is the final rule for faith and practice, 1 Corinthians 14:3; 2 Timothy 3:16-17.

In the New Testament, prophecy is tied to speaking what God reveals for the good of the church, but it must be tested, because false claims can be made, 1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21. The main historic Christian question is whether this gift continued beyond the apostles or ceased with the completion of the apostolic foundation, Ephesians 2:20.

I would say the safest biblical position is that prophecy was a real revelatory gift in the apostolic era, serving the church’s foundation, and today any word claiming divine authority must be judged strictly by Scripture, not treated as new revelation. What does the Bible say about purification?

The Bible teaches that purification is God’s work of making the unclean clean, both ceremonially in the Old Testament and spiritually through Christ in the New Testament. Ultimately, true purification from sin comes only through the blood of Jesus and the washing of regeneration by the Holy Spirit, not by outward rituals alone, as seen in Hebrews 9:13-14; Titus 3:5; 1 John 1:7.

In the Old Covenant, purification rites reminded Israel that God is holy and that sin defiles, so people needed cleansing to approach Him, as in Leviticus 11:44-45 and Numbers 19:11-13. These ceremonies pointed forward to the greater cleansing Christ would accomplish, because animal sacrifices could not truly take away sin, only foreshadow the perfect sacrifice of the Lamb of God, Jesus Christ.

In the New Covenant, purification is centered on Christ’s atoning death and resurrection. The Bible says Jesus “purified for Himself a people for His own possession” in Titus 2:14, and that His blood “purifies us from all sin” in 1 John 1:7. This is the heart of justification and sanctification, God declaring sinners righteous in Christ and then continually cleansing and transforming them by His Spirit.

Practically, this means we do not cleanse ourselves by willpower or religious performance. We come to God in repentance and faith, confessing sin, trusting Christ, and walking in the light. Does the Bible say that an increase in technology is a sign of the end times?

No, the Bible does not teach that increasing technology itself is a specific sign of the end times. Scripture does speak of signs like deception, wars, lawlessness, persecution, and the preaching of the gospel to all nations, but it does not name technological progress as a marker of Christ’s return, for example Matthew 24:4-14; 2 Timothy 3:1-5.

Some Christians connect modern technology to end-times themes because it can amplify global communication, surveillance, or commerce, and those ideas may help illuminate passages like Revelation 13, but that is an inference, not an explicit biblical sign. My view is that we should be careful not to treat any invention, whether printing presses, radio, internet, or AI, as proof that the end is immediately here, because Jesus tells us to stay watchful and faithful rather than speculative, Matthew 24:36; Matthew 24:42.

What does the Bible say about caring for our old parents?

The Bible teaches that caring for our aging parents is a clear duty of honor, love, and practical provision, not a burdensome extra. “Honor your father and mother” still stands in the New Testament, and Paul says that if someone does not care for his own household, “he has denied the faith” (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:2-3; 1 Timothy 5:8).

Scripture gives both the command and the example: Jesus rebuked people who used religious excuses to avoid supporting their parents, saying they were nullifying God’s word by their traditions (Mark 7:9-13). And when Jesus was dying, He made sure His mother was cared for, entrusting her to John, which shows tender responsibility even in suffering (John 19:26-27).

This does not always mean every child must personally provide every form of care, but it does mean we should not neglect, abandon, or resent our parents. In practice, that may include financial help, time, visits, meals, transportation, medical coordination, and speaking with patience and respect. If your parents are difficult, honor does not disappear, but it may require wisdom, boundaries, and help from your church.

Does salvation affect more than just the afterlife?

Yes, salvation affects this life too, not only the afterlife. In Christ, you are forgiven, reconciled to God, given new life, and brought into a present relationship with Him through the Holy Spirit, so salvation changes your identity, desires, hope, and daily walk now, not just your eternal destiny. See 2 Corinthians 5:17, Romans 5:1, and John 10:10.

The Bible presents salvation as both a future hope and a present reality, justification by faith now, sanctification through the Spirit now, and eventual glorification later. That means Christians are being transformed in their habits, repentance, love, endurance, and peace even before they enter glory.

What is the difference between Judaism and Islam?

Judaism and Islam are both strict monotheistic religions, but they differ at the most important point: Judaism centers on the covenant God made with Israel through Moses and the prophets, while Islam centers on submission to Allah through Muhammad as the final prophet. Christians also differ from both, because the Bible teaches that Jesus Christ is the promised Messiah, truly God and truly man, whose death and resurrection bring salvation, John 1:1-14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4.

A few key differences are clear:

- **Scripture and authority:** Judaism receives the Hebrew Scriptures and, in many forms, the later rabbinic tradition; Islam receives the Quran and the Hadith. Christians hold the Bible as God’s inspired Word, 2 Timothy 3:16-17.
- **Jesus:** Judaism does not accept Jesus as the Messiah or Son of God. Islam honors Jesus as a prophet, but denies His deity, crucifixion as the saving atonement, and resurrection in the Christian sense. The Bible teaches Jesus is Lord and Savior, John 20:28; Romans 10:9.
- **Salvation:** Judaism commonly emphasizes covenant faithfulness, repentance, and obedience to God’s law. Islam emphasizes submission to Allah and judgment according to deeds. The Bible teaches justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works, Ephesians 2:8-9.
- **God’s nature:** Judaism and Islam both affirm one God, but Christianity teaches the Trinity, one God eternally existing in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Matthew 28:19.

What does it mean to trust in the person and work of Jesus Christ?

John 1:1, 14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9.

Who was Plato? How did Platonism / Platonic thought influence society in Bible times?

Plato was a Greek philosopher who lived in the fourth century BC, best known as the student of Socrates and the teacher of Aristotle. His ideas shaped what is often called Platonism, a worldview that emphasized eternal, immaterial realities more than the changing physical world.

In Bible times, Platonic thought influenced society by helping form the intellectual atmosphere of the Greek-speaking world, especially through ideas like the immortality of the soul, the superiority of the unseen realm, and a sharp distinction between body and spirit. By the time of the New Testament, many Jews and Gentiles had been influenced by this broader Greek philosophical climate, even if they were not strict Platonists.

That matters because the Bible does not treat the material world as evil, but as God’s good creation, and it promises not escape from creation but resurrection and renewal, with a bodily resurrection in Christ, not mere release of the soul. Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead, and that future hope is central to Christian faith, not Plato’s idea of the soul escaping the body (1 Corinthians 15:20-23; Philippians 3:20-21).

A careful Christian takeaway is this: Platonism helped shape the culture around Israel and the early church, but Scripture judges all philosophy, and where Plato’s thought clashes with the Bible, the Bible stands above it (Colossians 2:8). Is a virtual/online communion service biblical?

Communion is biblical when it is the gathered church, physically assembled as one body to remember Christ’s death and proclaim it together, so a fully virtual Lord’s Supper is not the pattern we see in Scripture. The New Testament shows believers coming together “as a church” to partake, and the meal is described as a shared participation in one bread and one body, with clear church oversight, discernment, and self-examination, not a detached individual act (1 Corinthians 10:16-17; 1 Corinthians 11:17-34).

A charitable case for online communion says that extraordinary circumstances, like persecution or severe illness, may require creative pastoral care, and that the heart of the ordinance is Christ, not the building. But I would still say the ordinary, biblical practice is embodied, local-church communion under the care of elders, because the signs given by Christ are not merely private reminders, they are corporate means of grace tied to the gathered body.

So my view is that virtual communion should not be treated as the normal or ideal Christian practice. If your church is considering it because of a crisis, the wiser path is to ask your elders to weigh whether it is a temporary concession or whether another pastoral arrangement would better honor the Lord’s Supper as Scripture presents it.

Why do some churches thrive while others die?

Some churches thrive because they remain faithful to Christ, His Word, prayer, repentance, love, and the ordinary means of grace, while churches often decline when they drift from the gospel, neglect holiness, and lose their first love (Revelation 2:4-5; Acts 2:42). Growth in a church is never merely about strategy, but about the Lord blessing humble dependence and biblical faithfulness.

A thriving church is usually marked by clear preaching of Scripture, prayer, Christ-centered worship, loving discipline, and real discipleship. A dying church often keeps the name of life but has little spiritual power because it has substituted comfort, tradition, personality, or programs for obedience to Christ.

That said, outward success is not the final measure, because God may preserve a small faithful flock, and He may allow a visible congregation to wither for His wise purposes. The question is not only, “Is it growing?” but, “Is it faithful to the Lord Jesus?” Jesus told Sardis, “You have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead” (Revelation 3:1), and He called them to wake up, repent, and strengthen what remained.

How much authority should a pastor have over a church?

A pastor should have real spiritual authority, but it is delegated authority under Christ and exercised according to Scripture, not as a personal rule over the flock. The New Testament calls elders to shepherd willingly and by example, not to domineer, and the congregation still has a real role in receiving teaching and exercising discernment, as seen in 1 Peter 5:2-3; Hebrews 13:17; Acts 17:11.

One faithful Christian view is elder-led congregationalism, where pastors lead, teach, and guard doctrine, while the local church retains final responsibility in matters like recognizing leaders and major church decisions. Another historic view is stronger elder oversight, but even there the pastors are still servants of Christ, not lords over believers.

My view is that a pastor should have enough authority to teach sound doctrine, correct error, lead shepherding, and guide the church decisively in ordinary ministry, but not enough to bypass Scripture, silence the congregation’s rightful discernment, or treat the church as his own possession. That fits the pattern of Acts 20:28, where the overseers are to shepherd the church of God, and 1 Peter 5:2-3, where they must not “lord it over those entrusted to you.”

Practically, a healthy church keeps authority clear by having qualified elders, accountable membership, transparent discipline, and decisions made under the Word. If a pastor cannot be corrected by Scripture and the church’s recognized leadership, that is a danger sign, not biblical headship.

What is the satisfaction or commercial theory of the atonement?

The satisfaction theory of the atonement says that sin dishonors God and creates a real debt of justice that humans cannot pay, so Christ, by His obedient life and sacrificial death, satisfies God’s justice on behalf of His people. In historic Christian theology, this is often connected with **penal substitution**, especially in texts like Isaiah 53:5-6, Romans 3:24-26, and 2 Corinthians 5:21.

A related view sometimes called the **commercial theory** is usually associated with Anselm’s idea that human sin robbed God of the honor due to Him, and Christ’s death restores that dishonored order. The key point in both is that the cross is not mere example or moral influence, but a real, objective work that deals with sin before a holy God.

The Bible’s plain teaching is that Christ offered Himself once for all to bear sin, satisfy divine justice, and reconcile us to God, “For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (1 Peter 3:18; see also Romans 5:8-9).

Who are the Shakers?

The Shakers were a Christian sect that began in 18th-century England and later grew in the United States, known for communal living, celibacy, simplicity, and highly energetic worship. Their official name was the United Society of Believers in Christ’s Second Appearing.

Historically, they broke from orthodox Christianity by treating new revelations, especially through their leader Ann Lee, as authoritative in a way that went beyond Scripture. That is a serious issue, because the Bible is God’s inspired and sufficient Word, and believers are to test all claims by Scripture, not by later revelations, “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

A few key marks of the Shakers were:
- celibacy, which meant they did not marry or have children
- communal ownership of property
- plain dress and simple living
- worship that included rhythmic movement, trembling, and singing, which is where the nickname “Shakers” came from

From a Christian perspective, the main concern is that they denied normal marriage and family life as part of their spirituality, even though marriage is a good gift from God, and they elevated extra-biblical authority above Scripture. The Bible honors marriage and family, while also commending singleness as a gift for some, not as a universal command (Genesis 2:18, 24; 1 Corinthians 7:7-9).

What is baby dedication? Is child / baby dedication biblical?

Baby dedication is a church practice where parents publicly commit to raise their child in the fear of the Lord, and the congregation often promises support and prayer. It is not the same as baptism, because baptism in the New Testament is connected with personal repentance and faith in Christ, as seen in Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38; Acts 8:36-38.

Is it biblical? But baby dedication is not commanded as an ordinance of the church, so it should not be treated as a saving rite or a replacement for believer’s baptism.
